docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Welcome to the SoulEngine documentation site! If you have any questions about SoulEngine, the documentation is a good place to start.

This documentation moves at a fast pace and packs in a lot of substance. If something doesn't click on the first read, take a closer look or ask.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
At the very top of the docs is the navigation bar. On the left is the hamburger menu (which appears automatically if the window is too narrow), the title, and the corresponding SoulEngine version number.

On the right there is a moon/sun icon — click it to switch between day and night mode — along with a language button and a search button.

docs.title: Icon Meanings
docs.text:
Some pages are marked with special icons before their title, which mean the following:

  • 🔧 means this content requires additional software to use, such as Tiled.
  • ❕️ means this content has been updated since the previous version.
  • 🚧 means this topic is still under construction and content is yet to be added.

docs.title: Version Number Meaning
docs.text:
The SoulEngine version number follows the general form: a.b.c-d

  • a is the major version. Currently 3. When this increments, it means the engine has received a non-backward-compatible major update, usually accompanied by abrupt code-style changes and project structure adjustments. Migrating old projects is not recommended.
  • b is the minor version. When this increments, it means the engine has received a significant update, but usually with backward-compatible changes, so old projects can be ported.
  • c is the patch version. When this increments, it usually represents a fix or a small update.
  • d is the release channel. It can be stable, alpha, or beta. For stable development, pick a version tagged with stable whenever possible.

docs.title: About Migration
docs.text:
Migration Notes

SoulEngine's migration approach is special — it's more like "applying a patch". It does not migrate old project data into the new version, but rather migrates the new version's other contents into your old project.

If you have questions, please refer to the relevant section.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: Before using SoulEngine, figure out what you actually need — I'm not going to ask you grand questions like "why make a game", but rather practical needs:

docs.title: Which One Are You
docs.text:
Guide for Different Roles

If you are a translator, after finishing Environment Setup (the game needs to run on SoulEngine), you can jump straight to the Localization topic to start translating.

If you are a user learning game development, please follow the recommended path below, or browse as needed.

If you are a member working on the Overworld, after installation jump to the Overworld Main World System topic for the relevant docs.

If you are just curious, wanting to borrow ideas or simply browse the docs, feel free to look around.

docs.title: What's in This Documentation
docs.text:
Listed by topic, with a one-line description of each, so you can jump as needed.

Topic Content Before You Start (this topic) Environment setup, pre-development prep, Lua crash course Quick Start A step-by-step guide from "just downloaded" to "made your first battle / first map" Basic Development Config, scenes, sprites, typewriter, layers, audio, global variables, screen, masks, borders, Tween, the Game area, game logic Battle System Battle init, battle box, player and souls, attacks, enemy turns, bullet patterns, battle scenes Overworld Main World System Maps, STI and tilesets, characters, interaction and dialogue, menus, encounters, shops Intermediate Development JSON library, ShaderToy, shaders, collision library, math tutorial Working with LÖVE Using the native LÖVE API directly 🚧 Developer Tools Tool scenes and dev assistance 🚧 Localization Where language files go, looking up and replacing text Networking GameJolt, Discord Rich Presence, sock multiplayer Export & Release Packaging into exe / APK / web, plus a pre-release checklist

Icon Meanings

The 🔧 / ❕️ / 🚧 before a page title mean "requires extra software", "updated since last version", and "topic under construction", respectively. Full explanation is on the Home page.

docs.title: Recommended Path
docs.text:
Don't start by flipping open the Basic Development manual pages — those are for reference. Reading them cover-to-cover from the start is inefficient.

If you're unsure where to begin, follow this order:

  1. Environment Setup — install LÖVE and the engine so you can open the project in an editor.
  2. Before Development — check the hardware, system, and math prerequisites so you know what to expect.
  3. Lua Tutorial — must-read if you've never written Lua; the pitfalls won't stick until you hit them once.
  4. Quick Start — start actually building here; it tells you what to do at each step.

After that, browse as needed: for battles go to Battle System, for maps and NPCs go to Overworld, and for complex math or shaders go to Intermediate Development.

When your game is done and you want to ship it, see Export & Release.

If you're ready to install, head to the next page.

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text: These four words may sound intimidating, but the setup is actually fairly simple— You don't need to touch the environment at all; you're just installing a few archives.

docs.title: Installing the Engine and SoulEngine
docs.text:
As of now, regardless of whether love 12+ has been delayed or officially released, please download the 12+ version. Click here to download

After that, download SoulEngine

Make sure you have installed at least version 3.0.0 or higher. The most obvious way to verify is to open conf.lua and check the second line—if it contains 3.0.0-stable or a newer version string, then the version is correct.

-- Soul Engine Configuration File
_VER = "3.0.0-stable"      -- ← this is the line

Where is _VER

It is written on line 2 of conf.lua (line 1 is a comment). Note that there is no _VERSION in conf.lua—that is a built-in Lua global and has nothing to do with the engine version. See the configuration file for details.

LOVE 12.0 is still in development

The t.version in conf.lua is set to 12.0. If you only find the 11.x stable version on the official site, you need to download 12.x from the nightly / test build section, otherwise the APIs the engine uses will be missing.

The 3.0.0 APIs are essentially all stable now, so they won't change in future updates.

Next we will branch by operating system, so please follow only the section that applies to you.

docs.title: Windows Development
docs.text:
For Windows, there are many optional programming tools—you can even run the game by writing your own command line.

But if you have to pick the most convenient one, I currently recommend: Visual Studio Code. It is the blue ribbon—don't download the purple one.

docs.title: Linux Development
docs.text:
VSCode is also recommended, but Linux's command line is the main highlight.

After installing LOVE2D, the love command will be automatically registered in the environment.

So for Linux users, you can run the following command in the terminal to launch the game: 

love .

docs.title: macOS Development
docs.text:
You can download from the link above (or the App Store, etc.).

VSCode is still recommended.

docs.title: Android Development
docs.text:
Domestic users can choose MT Manager. Although some of its features are paid, none of them are needed at all throughout SoulEngine development.

Download link: https://mt2.cn.

About MT

This app is harmless; any detection as malicious is a false positive.

Provided you downloaded it from the official site mentioned in the link above.

Foreign users can choose Squircle CE (I honestly don't believe any foreigner would specifically read the Chinese page).

Setting aside the tool choice, you first need to download LOVE for Android.

Two icons will appear on your desktop: one is the main program that launches a specific folder path by default, and the other lets you choose the path yourself, but usually you need to package it as a .love file first and then launch it with the Loader.

So during development, the software should ideally be able to open and modify .love files directly.

docs.title: iOS Development
docs.text:
LOVE2D is paid on the iOS operating system, although SoulEngine will never be paid.

Warning

Decide for yourself whether to purchase it, but I generally do not recommend doing so.

After completing all the setup methods above for the different operating systems, you can continue to the next subsection.

docs.title: Opening the Project with VSCode
docs.text:
First, enter the SoulEngine project root directory, right-click in an empty area, and a menu will pop up—find Open with Code.

Or if you don't see the Open with Code option after opening the menu, you can skip the right-click graphical method. We also have a command-line version:

Open cmd or Powershell in the project directory and run: 

code .

After opening, if a security prompt appears, approve it unconditionally.

Why approve unconditionally?

You are the author—why not approve it unconditionally? Don't you trust the game you're going to make?

After that, you'll see many files in the sidebar—these are all the project's contents.

docs.title: Extension Selection
docs.text:
Why download an extension

The way LOVE2D launches a game is not by opening the program and selecting a folder, but by manually dragging the folder onto love.exe to open it.

Having to repeat this operation every time you debug causes unnecessary trouble. For this reason, we choose an extension in VSCode that can auto-launch the game.

For the extension, I most recommend LOVE Launcher - SK83RJOSH.

The reasons I recommend it:

  1. Use the ALT + L keybind to launch the game directly.
  2. It does not over-interfere with the workspace, has no code completion support, and only offers lightweight quick-launch capability.
  3. It is a lightweight extension that can be directly searched for and downloaded within VSCode.

docs.title: Configuring the Extension
docs.text:
After installation, we need to tell the extension: where is the love.exe I need?

Click the small gear in the bottom-left corner of VSCode, find the Settings option, then follow the settings shown in the image below:

  1. Search for love—this helps us quickly locate the extension.
  2. Change the second option to your love.exe path. (The path is not censored, but don't rigidly copy the settings—the path in the image generally won't work)

docs.title: Launch Verification
docs.text:
After completing this step, press the Alt + L key combination and check whether the game opens normally.

If, after launching, you see the situation shown in the image below, the launch was successful:

docs.title: Wrapping Up
docs.text: At this point, the installation and configuration for all operating systems except Android and iOS are resolved.

docs.title: Developing with MT Manager
docs.text:
MT Manager is relatively simpler, because there is only one choice.

After downloading, you may get a .love file, which is directly usable.

If you downloaded a .zip file, you can also use it directly.

How to open: single-click the LOVE Loader program and select the corresponding archive to launch.

docs.title: Before Development
docs.text:
We highly recommend people with some Lua foundation come to learn.

But we do not reject newcomers either.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
Through continuous testing, we found that even a low-spec machine with an i3 can run Soul Engine without any problem, so you don't need to worry about the engine blowing up your computer.

A minimum of 4G of RAM is sufficient.

docs.title: Operating System Support
docs.text: Apart from the hardware requirements mentioned above, some operations in Soul Engine cannot function properly on systems other than Windows. This will be highlighted with warning boxes in later documentation.

docs.title: Tech Stack Overview
docs.text:
• Lua will be the primary development language.
  • GLSL will be used later when writing Shaders. Don't learn it for now; if interested, you can check the Shader Development topic. But if you're a complete beginner—don't look.

If you want to get a quick feel for how Lua is written and avoid pitfalls later, we recommend the tutorial in the docs.

docs.title: Math Requirements
docs.text:
These contents are not strictly mandatory—I'm not saying you don't need to learn them; on the contrary, being able to apply them proficiently is the ultimate goal.

In the early stages of development, we won't use much math knowledge.

  • Arithmetic—addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division; these are the most commonly used.
  • Trigonometry—the module that requires the most mathematical foundation.
  • Basic middle-school math—sounds fancy, but it's really just things like absolute value.

The above are the most basic mathematical frameworks used in game development.

If you want more advanced or challenging math knowledge, please go to the Math topic for more content.

docs.title: Patience Requirements
docs.text: No matter how fast you learn, you can't master everything in a single day, so calm down and follow the documentation step by step.

docs.title: Lua Crash Course
docs.text: This page is not really suited for beginners—it's more like a reference manual to consult as development progresses. Several other pages will later hyperlink back to this one.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
This is the thing you'll interact with most during development. Simply put, the vast majority of files with the .lua extension contain variables internally.

Variable Examples

a = 10          -- single letter
abb = ""        -- multiple letters
_count = 0      -- starts with underscore
playerHP = 20   -- camelCase

All of the above are variables.

docs.title: Naming Conventions (must follow)
docs.text:
1. Variables may not be named with keywords (such as if, end, etc.)
  2. Variables may not be named starting with a number (such as 1var, etc.)
  3. The engine uniformly uses ASCII (English letters, numbers, underscores) for naming.

docs.title: Can Chinese actually be used as variable names?
docs.text:
Yes, but strongly not recommended.

SoulEngine runs on LuaJIT (bundled with LÖVE 12), and LuaJIT's lexer treats bytes above 0x80 as valid identifier characters, so the following actually runs in the game:

​你好​ = ""
​你好​ = "hello"
print(​你好​)          -- hello

function ​打招呼​() return "hi" end
print(​打招呼​())      -- hi

local t = {​名字​ = "Chara"}
print(t.​名字​)        -- Chara

Switch Lua interpreters and it explodes

Standard Lua 5.1 (PUC) will outright reject the above syntax:

lua.exe: t.lua:1: unexpected symbol near 'ä'

Yet the verify_*.lua validation scripts in the engine repo, and parts of the build/export process, use standard Lua. One source, two runners—the half with Chinese identifiers will suddenly throw a syntax error on the other path, and the error location points to bytes rather than the characters you wrote.

So just write ASCII uniformly

Chinese isn't unusable—it's just that you should only put it in strings (as well as in places like Tiled layer names and comments that are "for humans and other tools to read"):

local greeting = "​你好​"      -- ✅ write freely inside strings
local name = "Chara"          -- ✅ variable names use ASCII

All variables, functions, and table fields inside the engine are ASCII—following along will cause no problems.

docs.title: Common Types
docs.text:
1. Numbers: 1, 2, 3
  2. Strings (also called text): "hello", "I am a complete sentence.", "rolling log"
  3. Tables, the most powerful variable (can be treated as both an array or a dictionary at the same time): {1, 2, 3, 4}
  4. Booleans (imagine a switch): true, false
  5. Functions (not mathematical! Used by adding parentheses at the end): cool()

docs.title: Keywords
docs.text:
Variables also have their hierarchy. Although not strictly defined, if you type a special word, that word may get a highlighting effect, indicating it is a keyword.

Let's look at some simple examples and comparisons:

Keywords and non-keywords

if then while for do end elseif else in

IF aaa time var1 incredible

Note: I didn't force the color change—it's caused by keyword highlighting being recognized. Here is a mixed version:

Keyword Highlighting

if time == a then
end

Summary: avoid these keywords when naming.

docs.title: Common Combinations
docs.text:
Here, we won't cover overly complex code blocks—only the most commonly used ones:

  1. Conditional: if a value meets a condition, perform an operation.

if statement

if time == 60 then
    a = a + 1
end

The above executes: when time equals 60, it runs the content wrapped by if - end. (Here, for example, a increases by 1.)

  1. if-chain: continuously matches each condition to determine the final matching branch:

if chain

if     time == 60 then
                         branch one
elseif time == 90 then
                         branch two
elseif time == 95 then
                         branch three
else
                         final branch
end

The above executes: when time equals 60, 90, 95, it enters branches one, two, three respectively. If none match, it enters the final branch managed by else.

  1. Loop: use an abstract number to repeatedly perform an operation:

normal for loop

for i = 1, 10, 1
do
    a = a + 1
end

The above executes: create a new i variable, starting from 1 and increasing by 1 each time until 10. During this period, each time it adds 1, it runs the content wrapped by for - end once.

Simply put, it runs ten times.

An even more powerful loop:

while loop

while i < 10
do
    i = i + 1
end

The above executes: detects that i is less than 10, and continuously runs the i = i + 1 operation, until i no longer meets the condition.

docs.title: Basic Semantics of or
docs.text:
If a exists or is true, then choose a; otherwise choose b. Through this method, we can create a default-value substitution effect.

The format is as follows: 

var = a or b

Example

If test is not given an argument, it will default to the content after or, which in this example is default output.. 

local function test(b)
    print(b or "default output.")
end
test()

docs.title: and or Conditional
docs.text:
If condition a is true, use b; otherwise use c. Through this method, we can complete binary or multi-way selection in a single line.

The format is as follows: 

var = a and b or c

This operation relies heavily on logic and parenthesis handling.

Commonly seen when setting the battle box's minimum size to 16:

Example

If width is greater than 16, use width; otherwise use 16.

local _width = (width > 16) and width or 16

Nested Operation

Each layer is a checkpoint—among the three variables cfg, cfg.db, and cfg.db.host, if any one does not meet the standard, it will force the output localhost.

local config = {
    db = { host = "127.0.0.1" }
}

local function getHost(cfg)
    return (cfg and cfg.db and cfg.db.host) or "localhost"
end

print(getHost(config))                        -- 127.0.0.1
print(getHost({ db = {} }))                   -- localhost
print(getHost(nil))                           -- localhost

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
This page is meant to give complete beginners a reference point, covering everything from just starting out to beginning to make battles / Overworld maps. Read the pages under this topic as needed.

It also includes a FAQ section and more.

In this topic, given everyone's differing skill levels, the pace won't be too fast — so don't worry.

If you've already downloaded SoulEngine and LOVE2D, you might be at a loss next:

Question

What do I do next? What can I actually do?

If you really have this question, then next — after careful thought and gathering many viewpoints — we've put together a learning sequence to make sure you can grow step by step from knowing nothing to a SoulEngine master.

docs.title: Modifying Game Information
docs.text: At the very beginning, we won't learn how to add new elements to the game; we'll prioritize learning how to make the game your own.

docs.title: Modifying the Configuration File (conf.lua)
docs.text:
You only need to look at the content before the love.conf(t) line:

-- Soul Engine Configuration File
_VER = "3.0.0-stable"

-- Set to true when building the game for release
_RELEASED = false

-- The game's information
_INFO = {
    TITLE = "Soul Engine - v3.0.0",
    VERSION = "0.0.0", -- THIS IS YOUR GAME'S VERSION, the "_VER" upon means the engine's version.
    AUTHOR = "end",
    CONTACT = "NaN",
    WEBSITE = "NaN",
}

-- This is your window size. Change these values to set your desired resolution.
LOGICAL_WIDTH, LOGICAL_HEIGHT = 640, 480
CANVAS_WIDTH, CANVAS_HEIGHT = 640, 480

-- How much the GAME SCREEN is scaled. It is ALWAYS kept dead-centre.
--     "integer" → whole-number scaling (pixel-perfect; the default)
--     "auto"    → fill as much of the window / screen as possible
--     false/nil → 1:1, no scaling
SCREEN_SCALE = "integer"

-- Legacy switch, only used when SCREEN_SCALE is nil: true = "auto" while
-- fullscreen and 1:1 otherwise. Prefer SCREEN_SCALE.
FILL_SCREEN = true

-- Enable error handler to show custom error screen
-- If you don't know which error crashed the game. Then you need to set it to false.
USE_ERRHANDLER = true

Modifiable Variables

  • _RELEASED whether the game is a released version; this usually disables all debug features, awaiting export and release.
  • All content of _INFO can be modified:
    • TITLE Does not take effect on Android. This is the game window title.
    • VERSION the game version, modify as needed.
    • AUTHOR who the game author is—change to your own name.
    • CONTACT the author/team's contact information.
    • WEBSITE leave blank or fill in the game's release page.
  • LOGICAL_WIDTH the window's width.
  • LOGICAL_HEIGHT the window's height.
  • CANVAS_WIDTH the in-game screen's width.
  • CANVAS_HEIGHT the in-game screen's height.
  • SCREEN_SCALE how large the in-game screen is drawn; the canvas is always centered: "integer" scales only by whole-number multiples (pixel-perfect, default), "auto" fills as much of the window as possible (allows fractional multiples), a number fixes the multiplier, false keeps 1:1 with no scaling. At runtime you can also switch with the global function SetScreenScale(mode) and read the current multiplier with GetScreenScale().
  • FILL_SCREEN whether to fill the entire screen. Now just a legacy switch—it only takes effect when SCREEN_SCALE is unset (nil); for new projects just change SCREEN_SCALE.
  • USE_ERRHANDLER whether to enable the custom error screen, default true. But this feature is not very stable; issues during drawing may cause a crash. If you want to see all errors, temporarily disable it.

Other Variables

These variables can also be modified, but it's best not to.

  • _VER the engine version identifier; you can modify it without leaving any problem—it just records which engine version it is.

_VERSION is a Lua built-in global used to return the current Lua version number. It is not in conf.lua, so don't go looking for it.

docs.title: Modifying Initialization Configuration (conf_pure.lua)
docs.text:
After modifying the conf.lua file, you also need to initialize settings such as—but not limited to—initial room, main color, and language used.

The initialization configuration is split into two files, and they are layered, not an either/or choice:

File Purpose Root conf_pure.lua Engine default values; lays out all the variables used Game/conf_pure.lua Your game's overrides; executed later, same-named variables overwrite the engine's copy

So the correct approach is: write only the few lines you want to change into Game/conf_pure.lua and leave the engine's copy alone. Variables you don't write automatically inherit the engine defaults; if the Game copy has an error, the engine rolls back entirely to the defaults and prints a [Conf] WARNING, without freezing the game.

Below is the engine's default initialization content (that is, the root conf_pure.lua, excerpted):

-- Initialize
Global.SetVariable("FirstRoom", "Battle.scene_battle_init")   -- same-named variable written several times; the last one wins
Global.SetVariable("MainColor", {1, 1, 1})
Global.SetVariable("Language", "zh_CN")
Global.SetVariable("UseRealTime(dt)", false)
Global.SetVariable("ScreenShaders", {})
Global.SetVariable("FPS", 60)
Global.SetVariable("F2Room", "scene_logo")
Global.SetVariable("Volume", {
    Master = 1,
    Music  = 1,
    Sounds = 1
})

Global.SetVariable("ControllerSimulation", {
    virtualKeyboard = false,
    joystick        = false,
})
Global.SetVariable("ControllerDeadzone", 0.15)

-- Network things
Global.SetVariable("GamejoltID", nil)
Global.SetVariable("GamejoltPK", nil)
Global.SetVariable("DiscordAppID", "1342517648348680202")

Global.SetVariable("SE_MEMORY_SAFETY", true)
Global.SetVariable("OPT_COUNT_SPRITES", 2000)
Global.SetVariable("OPT_COUNT_TYPERS", 300)
Global.SetVariable("OPT_MEMORY_MAXSIZE", 0.8)
Global.SetVariable("OPT_LRU_SPRITES", {false, 180})
Guard = ImportFile("Engine.MemorySafety")

Below is an explanation of all global variables.

docs.title: Normal Initialization
docs.text:
• FirstRoom the initial room; upon entering the engine you'll go directly into this room's path. The engine default is Battle.scene_battle_init; to switch to your own scene, write it again in Game/conf_pure.lua. Scenes live in Scripts/Scenes/; to override an engine-built-in scene, put a same-named file in Game/Scenes/, where the Game area takes priority.
  • MainColor the game's main color tone; most of the engine's attacks and text, etc. will follow the color defined by this variable. If you want to make an Underfell fan game, you can try pink.
  • Language the language the game uses. The engine first checks Game/Localization/, then falls back to Localization/ for missing keys; if there's no specific language, write it yourself.
  • UseRealTime(dt) usually false (off); if enabled, all movement operations will use real time.
  • ScreenShaders no need to worry about it for now.
  • FPS defaults to 60, can be modified.
  • F2Room the scene returned to after pressing the F2 key, defaults to scene_logo.
  • Volume the default volume; if you want to set the global volume later, modify this variable.
  • ControllerSimulation can simulate touchscreen control mode.
  • ControllerDeadzone the gamepad stick deadzone (0 ~ 1); larger means less drift but lower precision. Default 0.15; sensitive can use 0.10, lenient can use 0.20.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
• GamejoltID the game page ID on gamejolt, usually 6 to 7 digits. See Networking → GameJolt for details.
  • GamejoltPK is short for private_key, also viewable on the game release page.
  • DiscordAppID can connect Discord RPC to display game progress and more in your personal activity on Discord. See Networking → Discord RPC for details.

docs.title: Memory Protection
docs.text:
• SE_MEMORY_SAFETY defaults to true (on); enables memory protection to prevent memory leaks.
  • OPT_COUNT_SPRITES the maximum number of sprites that can be created; a warning appears at 2000, and creation is blocked at double that number.
  • OPT_COUNT_TYPERS allows a maximum of 300 typewriters present at once.
  • OPT_MEMORY_MAXSIZE warns when memory usage reaches 80% of total memory.
  • OPT_LRU_SPRITES sprite cache recycling, defaults to {false, 180} i.e. off: the second item 180 is the judgment duration in seconds, but when the first item is false it won't trigger recycling—sprites that enter the cache stay forever. To turn it on, change to {true, 180}; sprites unused for more than 180 seconds will be recycled and re-loaded from disk next time they're needed.

On whether to monitor memory

SE_MEMORY_SAFETY is the master switch. If your game truly needs such a large number of images and typewriters, you can turn this variable off.

But if memory leaks become severe enough to crash the machine, you bear the consequences yourself.

docs.title: Creating and Switching Scenes
docs.text: A scene can be imagined as you creating a new world. All operations within this world are defined by you.

docs.title: Creating a Scene
docs.text:
In SoulEngine, there are two base scene templates: scene_template.lua and scene_template_full.lua.

When first starting out, we just copy the lightweight scene_template.lua.

Place it in the path Scripts/Scenes/, i.e. in the same directory as scene_template.lua. To override an engine-built-in scene, put a same-named file into Game/Scenes/, where the Game area takes priority and the engine directory is the fallback.

Adjust the initialization config

After that, don't forget to change FirstRoom in Game/conf_pure.lua to the name of the scene you just created.

docs.title: Scene Content
docs.text:
local scene = {}

function scene.update(dt)
end

function scene.draw()
end

function scene.clear()
    Layers.clear()
end

return scene

The lightweight scene contains only this code internally. You may notice that this code divides the entire scene into several different parts. Their functions are as follows:

Same-level code

Here, we grade by number of wrapping levels. In short, the region inside a function - end wrapper counts as one level.

If there is a new wrapper block, it adds another level.

  1. The first-level region, outside all function - end regions and before return, executes exactly once the moment you enter the scene.
  2. The second-level region, inside a function, executes under specific circumstances.

In more detail:

  • The region inside scene.update executes every moment (frame), about 60 times per second (default).
  • The region inside scene.draw executes every moment (frame), about 60 times per second (default).

docs.title: Creating the First Feedback
docs.text:
Let's assume you successfully copied and pasted a new scene. Please type the following code in the first-level region range: 

print("This is my new scene")

After that, when you enter the scene, the console will show the text inside print, which means you succeeded.

docs.title: Android Test Feedback
docs.text:
On Android, if there's no console to look at and you don't know whether you've successfully switched to the scene you just wrote, you can copy the following code into the scene's first-level region: 

Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png")

The code above creates a Poseur image at the center of the screen.

docs.title: Creating Sprites
docs.text: All visible parts of a game are "rendered" with color. And the rendered color, in a 2D game like the current one, is carried by sprites.

docs.title: Creating an Image
docs.text:
Just like at the end of the previous page, use Sprites.CreateSprite(path, layer) to create a sprite.

  • path the image path: first look in Game/Resources/Sprites/, then fall back to Resources/Sprites/ (Game area takes priority).
  • layer the layer; can be a number or text. If you enter text and the layer doesn't exist, it defaults to returning 0, and the terminal will show a hint.

Terminal hint

[WARNING] Layers.add: Layer "xxx" not found, defaulting to 0

Case

Below we'll create a poseur image on layer 0. 

Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png", 0)

docs.title: Editing an Image
docs.text:
First you need to master an operation that will also be very common later: assignment. Sounds fancy, but it's actually just making something equal the result of a function call.

You may have thought about creating an image in one go with a long string of parameters, like:

Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png", 0, 320, 240, 0, 1, 0, 0, nil, {1, 1, 1}, 1, 2, 2)

The good news is the engine does not design it this way: Sprites.CreateSprite(path, layer) only takes two parameters. Position, color, scale, etc. are all assigned one by one after you get the sprite.

If it really took a long string of parameters

Suppose the creation function really required you to fill in all properties at once; then to just change xscale you'd have to do this:

Sprites.CreateSprite("a.png", 0, nil, nil, nil, nil, nil, nil, nil, nil, nil, 2, 2)

Tell me within three seconds, which one is the third-to-last nil? Obviously, you can't answer within three seconds, so the engine chose to split it up. That simple.

CreateSprite returns an object, which you can think of as representing this image, so we can write it like this:

Catching the image

image = Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png", 0)

Modifying the image's properties separately after creation:

Changing x/yscale

image.xscale = 2
image.yscale = 2

Below are all the modifiable properties and the concepts they represent. For a more complete explanation, open Basic Development:

Modifiable properties

  • x the horizontal position.
  • y the vertical position.
  • rotation (degrees) the image's angle; increases clockwise as the angle grows.
  • xscale the horizontal scale; default 1, enlarges the image by a multiplier.
  • yscale the vertical scale; default 1, enlarges the image by a multiplier.
  • color the image's color, assigned using a table.
  • alpha the image's transparency (0 ~ 1); the larger the number, the more clearly visible.
  • pixel_snap whether this image does pixel snapping (defaults to following the global sprites.pixel_snap, i.e. on). Set to false to exempt just this image—commonly used for parts in an assembly that shouldn't be individually rounded.
  • velocity the image's velocity

docs.title: Basic Development
docs.text:
Setting aside the headache-inducing advanced features, in this topic we only learn the basics, with the goal of getting the game to run properly.

You can also treat this as a reference page, since it will cover every library's functionality and what it can achieve, from start to finish.

docs.title: Initialization Configuration
docs.text: Here you can set author info, the game icon, the initial Scene, and similar options.

docs.title: Version & Info
docs.text:
Open conf.lua in the directory; this is the file used to fill in information. In most cases, you only need to look at the content before the love.conf(t) function.

_VER = "3.0.0-stable"
_RELEASED = false
_INFO = {
    TITLE = "Soul Engine - v3.0.0",
    VERSION = "0.0.0", -- THIS IS YOUR GAME'S VERSION, the "_VER" upon means the engine's version.
    AUTHOR = "end",
    CONTACT = "NaN",
    WEBSITE = "NaN",
}

LOGICAL_WIDTH, LOGICAL_HEIGHT = 640, 480
CANVAS_WIDTH, CANVAS_HEIGHT = 640, 480
SCREEN_SCALE = "integer"        -- how the game canvas is scaled
FILL_SCREEN = true              -- legacy switch, only takes effect when SCREEN_SCALE is nil
USE_ERRHANDLER = true

Below is an introduction to the main variables:

  • _VER Engine version number. You may change this to your own game version number; this is not required, since it does not matter whether the engine version is displayed. A real game version follows below.
  • _RELEASED Whether this is a released version. Set to true before packaging and exporting. (Though I think most people will forget.)
  • _INFO Info table; this info is shown in the error screen and the window title.
    • TITLE Window title. Not viewable on Android.
    • VERSION Game version. This is the current version of your game; for example, once released, you can give it a label like 1.0.0.
    • AUTHOR Game author. (Will be shown on the error screen)
    • CONTACT Contact info. (Will be shown on the error screen)
    • WEBSITE Game website, which can be a release page or an address for feedback. (Will be shown on the error screen)
  • LOGICAL_WIDTH / HEIGHT Size of the game window, default (640, 480). A second recommended size is (960, 540); this size is for the case with a border.
  • CANVAS_WIDTH / HEIGHT Size of the game canvas, default (640, 480). Modifying the size is not recommended; just keep the default.
  • FILL_SCREEN Whether to let the game scale itself proportionally as the window is enlarged to fullscreen. Now only a legacy switch: it only takes effect when SCREEN_SCALE is not written (nil); for new projects, change the following one directly.
  • SCREEN_SCALE How the game canvas is scaled, default "integer". The canvas is always centered; the border scales together with the canvas, so the window frame and the game image will not be misaligned.
    • "integer" Only scales by integer multiples, pixel-perfect. When the window is 1.5× larger than the canvas, use 1×; when more than 4× larger, use 4×.
    • "auto" Tries to fill the window, allowing fractional multiples.
    • A number means a fixed multiple; false keeps 1:1 with no scaling.
    • During runtime you can switch with SetScreenScale(mode) and read the current multiple with GetScreenScale().
  • USE_ERRHANDLER Whether to enable the custom error screen, default true. If an error occurs it enters the "Doge" (annoying dog) screen. If disabled, the default error style is kept.

Custom error screen:

docs.title: Game Initialization
docs.text:
In the same directory as conf.lua there is another config file: conf_pure.lua. This file is responsible for the various initialization contents of the game.

There are actually two copies of the initialization config, and they are stacked:

File Purpose Root conf_pure.lua Engine defaults; lays out all variables Game/conf_pure.lua Your game's overrides; executed later, same-named variables override the engine copy

So if you only want to change a few lines, just write those lines into Game/conf_pure.lua; anything not written automatically inherits the engine defaults. Even if you break the engine copy it won't freeze — when the Game-region copy errors out, the engine rolls back entirely to the defaults and prints a [Conf] WARNING. Press F2 to re-run both config files.

By function, we divide the content of this file into four sections: initialization, Controller, Network, and memory management.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
Global.SetVariable("FirstRoom", "Battle.scene_battle_init")
Global.SetVariable("MainColor", {1, 1, 1})
Global.SetVariable("EnableFriskDance", false)
Global.SetVariable("Language", "zh_CN")
Global.SetVariable("UseRealTime(dt)", false)
Global.SetVariable("ScreenShaders", {})
Global.SetVariable("FPS", 60)
Global.SetVariable("F2Room", "scene_logo")
Global.SetVariable("Volume", {
    Master = 1,
    Music  = 1,
    Sounds = 1
})
  • FirstRoom Initial Scene. The first Scene after launching the game is this one. The engine default is Battle.scene_battle_init; note that the same variable is written several times in the file, the last one wins — when changing it to your own Scene, remember to write it at the very bottom.
  • MainColor Main color. If you want to make an AU like Underfell, you can set this value to pink; the vast majority of elements will follow this color.
  • EnableFriskDance Enables the "genocide dance" feature in the Overworld; the engine disables it by default (false).
  • Language Language file, currently using zh_CN (Simplified Chinese).
  • UseRealTime(dt) Use real-world time. Including Player movement, nothing is affected by lag.
  • ScreenShaders Screen effects.
  • FPS Frame rate.
  • F2Room The Scene you go to after pressing F2 (see Developer Tools → Engine Hotkeys for what each hotkey does).
  • Volume Volume level.

Battle Scene with the Underfell main color set:

docs.title: Input Control
docs.text:
Global.SetVariable("ControllerSimulation", {
    virtualKeyboard = false,
    joystick        = false,
})
Global.SetVariable("ControllerDeadzone", 0.15)
  • ControllerSimulation Simulates input during the unreleased phase; can simulate a joystick and virtual touchscreen.
  • ControllerDeadzone How large the gamepad deadzone is; if this value is too small the Player may start responding as soon as the stick is barely touched.

For the complete input interface (logical key table, Controller.GetState, etc.) see Input & Controller.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Global.SetVariable("GamejoltID", nil)
Global.SetVariable("GamejoltPK", nil)
Global.SetVariable("DiscordAppID", "1342517648348680202")
  • GamejoltID / PK The game's ID and private key; see Network Development → GameJolt for details.
  • DiscordAppID The app used to display Discord Rich Presence; you can create a new one; see Network Development → Discord RPC for details.

docs.title: Memory Safety
docs.text:
Risk

Disabling this part may cause the game to run out of memory. Please think twice before disabling it.

Global.SetVariable("SE_MEMORY_SAFETY", true)    -- DANGEROUS
Global.SetVariable("OPT_COUNT_SPRITES", 2000)
Global.SetVariable("OPT_COUNT_TYPERS", 300)
Global.SetVariable("OPT_MEMORY_MAXSIZE", 0.8)
Global.SetVariable("OPT_LRU_SPRITES", {false, 180})
Guard = ImportFile("Engine.MemorySafety")
  • SE_MEMORY_SAFETY This protects against the game running out of memory. Without protection, the computer's RAM may be filled up and crash. It can be disabled, but the consequences are yours to bear.
  • OPT_COUNT_SPRITES Maximum number of images allowed at the same time, default 2000; warnings start at 2000, and creation is rejected at 4000.
  • OPT_COUNT_TYPERS Maximum of 300 Typers allowed on screen at the same time.
  • OPT_LRU_SPRITES Sprite cache recycling, default {false, 180}, meaning off: the second item's 180 seconds is the judgment duration, but when the first item is false the recycling is not triggered — once a sprite enters the cache it stays there. To turn it on, change to {true, 180} — any image unused for more than 180 seconds gets recycled, and re-read from disk next time it is used.

Guard is the execution library; after fetching the settings above, it will interfere with operations in the sprite library / typer library.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text:
In Soul Engine, every room can be called a room, or a Scene. By default, every Scene is a pure black area with no additional content shown.

Scene Manager path: Scripts/Libraries/SceneManager.lua

docs.title: How a Scene Runs
docs.text:
Scenes are placed in Scripts/Scenes/ by default. There is also a Game-region copy: Game/Scenes/, where same-named files take priority over the engine directory and fall back only when not found. So if you want to replace an engine-built-in Scene, you don't need to modify the engine — just put a same-named file into Game/Scenes/.

There must be one Scene running at all times; simply put: from the moment you enter the game until you quit, every frame you are inside some Scene, and there is no "void period".

docs.title: Creating a Scene
docs.text:
Open the Scene path and you will see many default Scenes, but in practice you only need to focus on two files to create a new Scene: scene_template.lua and scene_template_full.lua.

One is the lightweight version (use this file for daily development), and one is the full version (use this file when making certain page tools).

If you cannot find them, they may have been accidentally deleted; below are the two versions of the Scene code, which you can copy directly:

template 
local scene = {}

function scene.update(dt)
end

function scene.draw()
end

function scene.clear()
    Layers.clear()
end

return scene
full 
local scene = {}

-- ============================================
-- 1. CORE LIFECYCLE CALLBACKS
-- ============================================

--- Called once when the scene is first loaded.
function scene.load()
end

--- Called every frame to update the scene state.
--- @param dt number|nil Delta time since last update.
function scene.update(dt)
end

--- Called every frame to draw the scene.
function scene.draw()
end

--- Called when leaving the scene.
function scene.clear()
end

--- Called when the game is about to quit.
function scene.quit()
    print("SE.quit: Game is quitting... Goodbye!")
end


-- ============================================
-- 2. KEYBOARD CALLBACKS
-- ============================================

--- Called when a key is pressed.
--- @param key string The key name (e.g., "escape", "a").
--- @param scancode string The scancode of the key.
--- @param isrepeat boolean True if this is a repeated key event.
function scene.keypressed(key, scancode, isrepeat)
    if key == "escape" then
        SE.event.quit() -- Press ESC to quit the game
    end
    print("SE.keypressed: Key '" .. key .. "' pressed")
end

--- Called when a key is released.
--- @param key string The key name.
--- @param scancode string The scancode of the key.
function scene.keyreleased(key, scancode)
    print("SE.keyreleased: Key '" .. key .. "' released")
end

--- Called when text input is received (e.g., from IME or character input).
--- @param text string The input text.
function scene.textinput(text)
    -- Example: append input text to a string
    print("SE.textinput: Text input received: " .. text)
end


-- ============================================
-- 3. MOUSE CALLBACKS
-- ============================================

--- Called when a mouse button is pressed.
--- @param x number X coordinate of the mouse.
--- @param y number Y coordinate of the mouse.
--- @param button number The button number (1 = left, 2 = right, etc.).
--- @param istouch boolean True if the event came from a touchscreen.
--- @param presses number Number of presses in a row (for double-click detection).
function scene.mousepressed(x, y, button, istouch, presses)
    print(string.format("SE.mousepressed: Button %d pressed at (%d, %d)", button, x, y))
end

--- Called when a mouse button is released.
--- @param x number X coordinate of the mouse.
--- @param y number Y coordinate of the mouse.
--- @param button number The button number.
--- @param istouch boolean True if the event came from a touchscreen.
--- @param presses number Number of presses in a row.
function scene.mousereleased(x, y, button, istouch, presses)
    print(string.format("SE.mousereleased: Button %d released at (%d, %d)", button, x, y))
end

--- Called when the mouse is moved.
--- @param x number Current X coordinate.
--- @param y number Current Y coordinate.
--- @param dx number Change in X since last frame.
--- @param dy number Change in Y since last frame.
--- @param istouch boolean True if the event came from a touchscreen.
function scene.mousemoved(x, y, dx, dy, istouch)
    -- Mouse move events are frequent; avoid printing debug info here.
    -- Use this to update mouse-related logic (e.g., hover states).
end

--- Called when the mouse wheel is scrolled.
--- @param x number Horizontal scroll amount.
--- @param y number Vertical scroll amount.
function scene.wheelmoved(x, y)
    print(string.format("SE.wheelmoved: Scrolled dx=%.1f, dy=%.1f", x, y))
end


-- ============================================
-- 4. WINDOW & SYSTEM CALLBACKS
-- ============================================

--- Called when the window gains or loses focus.
--- @param f boolean True if the window gained focus, false if it lost focus.
function scene.focus(f)
    if f then
        print("SE.focus: Window gained focus")
    else
        print("SE.focus: Window lost focus")
    end
end

--- Called when the window is resized.
--- @param w number New window width.
--- @param h number New window height.
function scene.resize(w, h)
    print(string.format("SE.resize: Window resized to %dx%d", w, h))
    -- Use this to recalculate UI layout or camera viewport
end

--- Called when the window visibility changes (minimized/restored).
--- @param v boolean True if the window is visible.
function scene.visible(v)
    if v then
        print("SE.visible: Window is now visible")
    else
        print("SE.visible: Window is now hidden")
    end
end


-- ============================================
-- 5. DRAG & DROP CALLBACKS
-- ============================================

--- Called when one or more files are dragged and dropped onto the window.
--- @param file SE.File The dropped file object.
function scene.filedropped(file)
end

--- Called when a directory is dragged and dropped onto the window.
--- @param dir SE.File The dropped directory object (also a SE.File).
function scene.directorydropped(dir)
end

return scene

After copying, paste it in the same directory and rename it (into Scripts/Scenes/; to override an engine-built-in Scene put it in Game/Scenes/, same name takes priority).

docs.title: Switching Scenes
docs.text:
Use the Scenes.switchTo(scene, ...) function to switch to another Scene.

  • scene The Scene to go to, with the path counted from Scripts/Scenes/.
  • ... Variable parameters; you can put some values in here to pass to the target Scene. Normally you can use global variables instead, but this is more convenient.

The example below shows switching Scenes with parameters; you will most likely see the input 320, 240 printed to the terminal:

Switching Scenes with parameters

Scenes.switchTo("scene_gameover", 320, 240)

scene_gameover: 

function scene.load(...)
    print(...)
end

docs.title: Clearing a Scene
docs.text:
When leaving a Scene, you need to clear all the images / audio / typer assets you created in the Scene, to prevent them from carrying into the next Scene.

The scene.clear() function is responsible for this. Normally, we write the Layers.Clear() function inside it, which thoroughly clears all visible content in the Scene.

For audio, we use the Audio.Clear() function to clear it.

Clearing audio and images

function scene.clear()
    Layers.Clear()
    Audio.Clear()
end

docs.title: Clearing the Cache
docs.text:
Aside from the above, the most important and also the easiest-to-forget part to clean up is the cache.

When entering a Scene, each Scene produces a cache due to the require operation, and that cache cannot be fully cleared simply by clearing Layers and Audio.

Symptom: the second time you enter a Scene, some variables remain in the state they were when you last left.

Cache residue

Back in Soul Engine v1.1.0 it was the cache that did us in, so I pay special attention to this.

1.Use package.loaded to unload the cache:

package.loaded

package.loaded["Scripts.Libraries.Beat"] = nil

Note: the key name here uses a dot (.), not a slash (/). The keys in package.loaded are the module names used in require, e.g. require("Scripts.Libraries.Beat") produces the key Scripts.Libraries.Beat. Writing "Scripts/Libraries/Beat" will not error, but it also clears nothing — it is one of the easiest pitfalls.

If you get stuck on a beat in some Scene, and then re-enter the Scene and find the starting beat is several hundred, now at the very beginning it will be reset to zero properly.

2.Use ClearModuleTree(path) to clear the cache of all contents in a folder.

CMT function

ClearModuleTree("Scripts.Libraries.Attacks")
ClearModuleTree("Scripts.Libraries.Battle")

After use, all libraries in these two folders will have their cache cleared; you no longer need to write out each file path one by one.

3.Use ClearGameTree(sub_root) to clear the cache of the Game/ tree.

CGT function

ClearGameTree("Souls")       -- clears Game.Souls.*
ClearGameTree("Animations")  -- clears Game.Animations.*
ClearGameTree()              -- no parameter = clears the entire Game region

Game/ is a second tree independent of Scripts.Libraries. Things like Game/Souls/, Game/Animations/, Game/Encounter/, Game/Attacks/, Game/Waves/ cannot be cleared using only ClearModuleTree("Scripts...") — they must be cleared separately with this. (Both trees are provided by Scripts/Libraries/Engine/PathDefiner.lua, and neither touches Game/Hacks/ or Game/Logics/.)

Note: a Scene does not need to unload itself additionally; SceneManager will actively clear the Scene itself, but the main thing is to write the unloading process for other libraries well inside the Scene's clear function.

docs.title: Some Examples
docs.text:
logo walkthrough

Path: Scripts/Scenes/scene_logo.lua

local scene = {}
Audio.Clear()
Camera:reset()

local logo = Sprites.CreateSprite("Logo.png")
local time = 0
local alpha = 0

Audio.PlaySound("snd_intro.ogg")
local font = Fonts.New("determination_mono.ttf", 13, "mono")
font:setFilter("nearest", "nearest")

local tip = Fonts.New("Mars Needs Cunnilingus.ttf", 13, "mono")
tip:setFilter("nearest", "nearest")

function scene.update(dt)
    time = time + 1
    if (time >= 180 and time % 60 == 0) then
        alpha = 1 - alpha
    end

    if (Controller.GetState("confirm") == 1) then
        Scenes.switchTo("Battle.scene_battle_init")
    end
end

function scene.draw()
    SE.graphics.setFont(font)
    SE.graphics.setColor(0.4, 0.4, 0.4, alpha)
    SE.graphics.printf("[PRESS Z OR ENTER]", 0, 320, 640, "center")

    SE.graphics.setFont(font)
    SE.graphics.setColor(1, 0, 0, 1)
    SE.graphics.printf("Undertale By Toby Fox © 2015", 0, 445, 640, "left")

    SE.graphics.setColor(0.4, 0, 1, 1)
    SE.graphics.printf("SoulEngine By Anskiyy © 2024", 0, 460, 640, "left")

    SE.graphics.setColor(1, 1, 1, 1)
    SE.graphics.printf(_VER, 0, 460, 640, "right")
end

function scene.clear()
    Audio.Clear()
    Layers.clear()
end

return scene

At the start it resets the audio and Camera, and creates the logo. It also plays the audio snd_intro.ogg (similar to a "thud" opening).

draw renders the small corner text and the prompt.

When update's time keeps increasing to 180, the prompt PRESS Z OR ENTER starts to light up and blink (done by controlling the alpha alpha).

When the Player presses Z or ENTER, it switches to the scene_battle_init Scene in the Battle folder, executing the content in scene.clear() to clear the scene and leave.

clearing the cache

Path: Scripts/Libraries/Battle/init.lua

function battle.Clear()
    -- Clear the game module tree so it re-queries Localize on next load
    if battle.gameName then
        ClearModuleTree(battle.gameName)
    end

    -- Clear all loaded attack pattern modules. attack_paths holds resolved
    -- module names, so both roots (Game.Attacks.* and
    -- Scripts.Libraries.Battle.PlayerAttacks.*) are covered.
    for i = #battle.attack_paths, 1, -1
    do
        ClearModuleTree(battle.attack_paths[i])
    end
    ClearGameTree("Attacks")

    -- Game region has its own tree: only clearing Scripts.Libraries.Battle
    -- leaves these behind, and next time you enter battle you'd get the last
    -- encounter / monster animation / soul module, bringing state along.
    ClearGameTree("Encounter")
    ClearGameTree("Animations")
    ClearGameTree("Waves")
    ClearGameTree("Souls")

    if (Battle._wave) then
        Battle._wave._end = false
        Battle._wave.objects = {}
        Battle._wave._paths = {}
    end
    Battle._wave = {}
    -- public wrapper; internally clears both Game.Waves. and Scripts.Waves. prefixes
    Battle.ClearWaveModule(Battle.wave)
    battle.restoring_arena = false

    -- Clear the entire Battle library tree (UI, buttons, Player, Arenas,
    -- game_apis, Waves, PlayerAttacks, Souls, etc.) in a single pass.
    ClearModuleTree("Scripts.Libraries.Attacks")
    ClearModuleTree("Scripts.Libraries.Battle")
end
When called: clears the game files, attack files, the Game region's attacks / encounters / monster animations / waves / souls, and the entire battle library tree's cache.

Ensures everything is normal next time you enter.

Note: Battle.ClearWaveModule(Battle.wave) is a dedicated method provided by the Battle library; it clears the same-named cache under both the Game.Waves. and Scripts.Waves. prefixes at once, which is more reliable than writing ClearModuleTree by hand — even if the round script was moved between the two locations, no old version remains.

docs.title: Sprites
docs.text:
All art assets are handled through the Sprite library.

Some people may be used to calling a Sprite a "sprite sheet"; in fact they mean the same thing.

Path of all sprites: Resources/Sprites/ Sprite library path: Scripts/Libraries/Sprites.lua

If you want to override an engine-built-in sprite (e.g. replace the default px.png), just put your own same-named image into Game/Resources/Sprites/; the Game region takes priority, with the main directory as fallback.

docs.title: Creating a Sprite
docs.text:
Use Sprites.CreateSprite(path, layer) to create a sprite:

  • path The sprite's path; lookup starts from Resources/Sprites/ as the root directory, and you need to add the .png extension when creating.
  • layer The sprite's Layer, which can be a number or a string. If the corresponding Layer is not found via the string, it will not error; instead it automatically sets the layer to 0.

Creating an image

Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png", 0)

By default, this image is generated at the exact center of the screen, i.e. position (320, 240).

docs.title: Sprite Properties
docs.text:
Properties are set in two types: direct properties and method calls.

In direct properties, we use a dot (.) to set properties; In method calls, we use syntactic sugar, using a colon (:) to set properties.

Direct properties

  • x Horizontal coordinate of the image; larger means further right.
  • y Vertical coordinate of the image; larger means further down.
  • rotation Rotation angle of the image, in degrees; the image rotates clockwise as the angle increases.
  • xscale Horizontal scaling factor of the image, default 1, meaning original size.
  • yscale Vertical scaling factor of the image, default 1, meaning original size.
  • layer The image's Layer; a larger number means a higher Layer.
  • velocity The image's velocity; setting it once lets the image keep moving at that speed:
    • x Horizontal speed.
    • y Vertical speed.
    • r Rotation speed.
  • xpivot Horizontal pivot point of the image, default 0.5, representing the horizontal center.
  • ypivot Vertical pivot point of the image, default 0.5, representing the vertical center.
  • xpivot_px Horizontal pivot point of the image, set by pixels.
  • ypivot_px Vertical pivot point of the image, set by pixels.
  • xanchor Adjusts the horizontal offset relative to the parent object, when it has a parent.
  • yanchor Adjusts the vertical offset relative to the parent object, when it has a parent.
  • color The image's color, made of a table of three numbers 0 ~ 1. For example {1, 0, 0}, representing red, green, blue respectively.
  • alpha The image's transparency, made of a number 0 ~ 1; the smaller the number, the more transparent the image.
  • visible Whether the image is visible, default true.
  • pixel_snap Whether this image does pixel snapping. Defaults to following the global switch sprites.pixel_snap (default true); writing true / false directly overrides only this one. See "Pixel Snapping" below.
  • outline The image's outline color and thickness, made of five parameters {r, g, b, a, thickness}, representing {red, green, blue, alpha, thickness} respectively.
  • follow_mode Settings for following the parent object, supporting two: position: follow position only, parent rotation does not interfere; the second is full: follow both the parent's position and rotation.
  • isBullet Whether it is a damageable type (bullet type); a sprite becomes a bullet through this variable, default false.
  • HurtMode What type of damage the bullet deals, e.g.: orange, blue, red, green...

Method calls

  • GetPivotOffset() Gets the current anchor's pixel offset.
  • GetFilter() Gets the rendering method currently used by the image.
  • Dust(sound, remove, time) Turns an image into dust.
    • sound Whether to play a sound effect.
    • remove Whether to remove the image after the dust animation finishes.
    • time How many seconds the dust animation plays.
  • Outline(r, g, b, a, t) Sets the sprite's border.
    • r, g, b, a Color and alpha, all values 0 ~ 1.
    • t Border thickness; normally you can use 2, thickening as needed.
  • SetFourPointMode(enabled) Whether to enable four-corner vertex mode, i.e. the common leg stretch deformation.
  • SetFourPoint(p1x, p1y, p2x, p2y, p3x, p3y, p4x, p4y) The coordinates of the four points in four-corner vertex mode; just fill them in order.
  • SetFourPointP(index, x, y) Sets the coordinate of the index-th point among the four to (x, y).
  • Move(x, y) Moves the sprite at speed (x, y).
  • MoveTo(x, y) Moves the sprite to position (x, y).
  • Set(p) Sets the sprite's image to the image at path p. (Include the .png extension)
  • SetAnimation(frames, interval, mode) Sets the image's animation; animations are all composed of individual images.
    • frames The image sequence used by the animation.
    • interval How many seconds between each switch.
    • mode What mode the animation plays in, supporting loop loop, oneshot play once, empty play once and clear.
  • Scale(x, y) Sets the sprite's scaling size in horizontal and vertical directions to (x, y).
  • Pivot(x, y) Sets the sprite's anchor offset in horizontal and vertical directions to (x, y).
  • PivotPixel(x, y) Sets the sprite's anchor pixel offset in horizontal and vertical directions to (x, y).
  • Anchor(x, y) With a parent object, sets the sprite's anchor offset in horizontal and vertical directions to (x, y).
  • AnchorPixel(x, y) With a parent object, sets the sprite's anchor pixel offset in horizontal and vertical directions to (x, y).
  • SetParent(spr) Sets a certain sprite as the current sprite's parent object; spr is a created sprite object.
  • SetChildren(children) Sets multiple sprite objects as the current sprite's child objects.
  • AddChild(child) Adds an additional child object child to the child group.
  • RemoveChild(child) Removes child sprite object from the child group.
  • GetPosition() Gets the image's coordinates, returns x, y, normally can be caught with two variables.
  • GetPositionParent() Gets the parent object's coordinates, returns x, y, normally can be caught with two variables.
  • SetStencils(stencils) Sets the sprite's Mask, multiple masks can be used.
  • SetShaders(shaders) Sets the sprite's Shader to shaders, multiple shaders can be used.
  • GetShaders() Gets the shaders in use.
  • ClearShaders() Clears all shaders of the sprite.
  • AddShader(shader) Adds an additional shader at the end.
  • InsertShader(index, shader) Inserts a shader at position index.
  • RemoveShader(shader) Removes the shader shader from the shader list.
  • Solid(axis, box) Adds a collision body to the sprite.
    • axis Can be x direction, y direction, or xy direction, representing having a collision volume only in this direction.
    • box Can fill width and height parameters, e.g.: {width = 1, height = 1}, this is a 1*1 collision box.
  • UnSolid() Removes the collision body from the sprite.
  • IsSolid() Returns whether the sprite currently has a collision body.
  • GetImagePath() Returns the image path currently used by this sprite (the resolved real path).
  • GetAnimationPath() Returns the current animation's frame sequence path, returns nil when there is no animation.
  • SetPPCollision(enabled) Toggles this image's perfect pixel collision, returns (success, rectangle count). See "Perfect Pixel Collision" below.
  • IsPPCollision() Returns whether this image has perfect pixel collision on.
  • Destroy() / Remove() Deletes the sprite.

Setting color and position

local a = Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png", 0)
a.color = {1, 0, 0}
a:MoveTo(320, 0)

You will most likely see a red poseur with only its legs left at the top of the screen.

docs.title: Library-level Methods
docs.text:
All the above are methods of "a certain sprite"; the following are attached to the Sprites library itself:

Library-level methods

  • Sprites.CreateSpriteQuad(path, quad, layer) Creates a sprite taking only the block specified by quad from the image; quad is filled as {x = , y = , width = , height = }. Useful for tileset cropping.
  • Sprites.MultiDust(sprs, sound, remove, time) Turns a whole group of sprites into dust together, diffusing across the bounding box, more natural than calling Dust one by one.
  • Sprites.ShakeSprite(sprite, magnitude, duration, speed) Shakes the sprite for a period of time. magnitude can be a number or {x = , y = }.
  • Sprites.ShadowSprite(sprite, target_scale, duration, speed) Generates a shadow that follows the sprite and scales up while fading out; returns that shadow sprite object.
  • Sprites.GetCacheInfo() Returns (cache count, detail list), useful to see who is currently in the image cache.
  • Sprites.CleanupCache() Manually runs an LRU cleanup (under the normal flow the engine runs it automatically per OPT_LRU_SPRITES).

docs.title: Pixel Snapping
docs.text:
Pixel art most fears "half-pixel jitter": the sprite coordinate carries a decimal, and the sampled edges flicker bright and dark. The engine does this for you by default.

The global switch is sprites.pixel_snap (default true), and can also be changed with Sprites.SetPixelSnap(enabled); a single image can override it itself:

sprites.pixel_snap = false      -- turn off globally
Sprites.SetPixelSnap(true)      -- turn on globally
spr.pixel_snap = false          -- let only this one through

The snapping rule is snap the edges, not the center: what actually gets rounded to an integer is the coordinate of the four edges of the quad, not the image's center point. These two only coincide exactly when the image size is even, so odd-sized sprites would be off by half a pixel if you just rounded the center.

For composite bodies (like bones made of head / body / tail pieced together) you must round the shared anchor only once: set each part to pixel_snap = false, then use Sprites.SnapEdge(centre, offset) to snap the anchor, then place the parts according to the anchor. If you let each part round on its own, the seams will misalign.

  • Sprites.SnapCoord(v) Rounds a single number, equivalent to math.floor(v + 0.5).
  • Sprites.SnapEdge(centre, offset) Snaps the "edge" to an integer: centre is the center coordinate, offset is this edge's offset relative to the center (e.g. half-width), returns the snapped center coordinate.

Rotated sprites don't recognize 'edges'

Once a sprite is rotated, the quad is no longer parallel to the axes, so that SnapEdge stuff becomes meaningless. The correct approach for rotated parts is "don't snap", as long as you ensure its geometry is exactly the same as when snapping is off.

docs.title: Perfect Pixel Collision
docs.text:
The default collision judgment uses a bounding box: a 32×32 heart-shaped image is judged as a 32×32 square. To make the judgment follow the sprite's real pixel shape, turn this on for that image:

spr:SetPPCollision(true)    -- returns ok, rectangle count
spr:SetPPCollision(false)   -- back to normal bounding box
spr:IsPPCollision()         -- query current state

The judgment itself uses Sprites.PPCollide(a, b):

local ok = Sprites.PPCollide(bullet, Player.sprite)
-- true  = really collided
-- false = did not collide
-- nil   = neither side has perfect pixel on; use the bounding box conclusion

That is, it only gives an answer when at least one side is on; when it returns nil, do not treat it as "did not collide".

Judgment gets bigger once turned on

Perfect pixel judges using the sprite's opaque pixels. A 16×16 heart-shaped image with perfect pixel on will have a judgment range much larger than the default centered {4, 4} small box. If you want to "graze" use _hitbox; only turn this on when you want "shape-following" — pick one of the two.

Related helpers:

  • Sprites.GetPPRects(sprite) Gets all rectangles of this image in local coordinates.
  • Sprites.GetPPShapes(sprite) Gets the shapes after converting to world coordinates.
  • Sprites.GetHitbox(sprite) Gets "bounding box + _hitbox override" in one step; the battle uses this for the Soul judgment.
  • Sprites.ClearPPCache() Clears the rectangle cache. Call once after hot-reloading the library or sprite.

The underlying rectification algorithm is in Scripts/Libraries/PerfectPixel/, with two versions: a C backend (cpp.dll) and a pure Lua version (pure.lua); the former is about 10× faster and auto-enables when available. To turn on the F7 collision-box overlay to see the judgment shapes, see Battle System → Battle Scene.

docs.title: About Color
docs.text:
Here, color is divided into three basic colors red, green, blue, and all subsequent colors are mixed from these three.

Some commonly used colors are introduced below:

  • {1, 0, 1} KR's big pink, mixed from red and blue in equal proportions.
  • {0.4, 0, 1} Purple, but slightly deep blue.
  • {0, 1, 1} Cyan bone color of blue attacks.
  • {1, 0.5, 0} Orange attack.
  • {1, 1, 0} Yellow confirm.

docs.title: Light and Dark Colors
docs.text:
When it comes to light and dark, we generally mix by adding white or black into a color, so we can do this:

Red is {1, 0, 0}, if you want a dark color, what should you do? The answer is to add black to this color, and black is {0, 0, 0}.

We start adding and taking the average:

  • (1 + 0) / 2 = 0.5 The first color becomes 0.5.
  • (0 + 0) / 2 = 0 The second color becomes 0.
  • (0 + 0) / 2 = 0 The third color becomes 0.

Finally the dark red is: {0.5, 0, 0}.

We do the same for light colors:

  • (1 + 1) / 2 = 1 The first color becomes 1.
  • (0 + 1) / 2 = 0.5 The second color becomes 0.5.
  • (0 + 1) / 2 = 0.5 The third color becomes 0.5.

Finally the light red is: {1, 0.5, 0.5}.

But normally, this mixing method may go too far, so you can change the added 1 to 0.5 etc.

docs.title: Rainbow Color
docs.text:
Applying a periodic trigonometric transformation to {r, g, b}, and adjusting the phase, you can make a rainbow color effect.

r = math.sin(time / 8 + 0)
g = math.sin(time / 8 + 8)
b = math.sin(time / 8 + 16)

If you apply rgb to the color of an image, that image will start a rainbow color transformation.

docs.title: ❕️ Typers
docs.text:
Typer location: the Scripts/Libraries/Typers/ folder.

There are four kinds of Typers: InstText is only responsible for drawing the whole text directly, and the other three EText / NText / SText can all type out character by character normally.

All text on screen can be drawn through Typers, but we also have an additional way, which will be covered on the next page.

docs.title: Creating a Typer
docs.text:
The three character-by-character Typers are divided by "how tags are handled", namely EText, NText and SText.

The fourth, InstText, has no typing animation, and its usage differs a lot from them, so it is placed separately at the end of this section.

docs.title: EText Typer
docs.text:
EText stands for Easy Text; its feature is that the style is written inside the text, similar to bbcode.

Use Typers.EText.New(text, position, layer, size, mode) to create an etext mode typer.

  • text The text to type; can be a string or a table; if a table is used, the text is split into a pageable type.
  • position The position of the first character of the typer.
  • layer The typer's Layer.
  • size The size of the dialog box shown by the typer.
  • mode The typer's mode: manual switch to the next sentence manually, none cannot be manually intervened, only switch to the next sentence through code. If no parameter is given at creation, the default is manual mode.

Creation example

local t = Typers.EText.New({"This is the first sentence", "This is the second sentence"}, {320, 240}, 0)

Modifying style:

Set the style by adding tags with square brackets [] in the sentence.

Usage case

local t = Typers.EText.New({"[colorHEX:ff0000]This is a red sentence."}, {320, 240}, 0)
All tags
  • [wait:x] Makes the typer wait x seconds; only a direct number is allowed, no expressions like 1 / 2.
    • The wait uses its own timer, so even if a [speed:] appears later, it cannot swallow this pause.
    • When the Player presses cancel to fast-forward, or this sentence carries [skip], the wait is skipped directly and the remaining characters are typed out immediately.
  • [speed:x] Sets the typer's typing interval to x seconds; only a direct number is allowed, no expressions. Default value is 1/15=0.0667 seconds.
  • [size:x] Changes the font size of the following text to x; only a direct number is allowed. Characters already typed keep the size at creation, so text on screen will not "rewind" to shrink or grow. bondfont is not turned off by this; each character's scaling and spacing still apply.
  • [colorRGB:r, g, b] Sets character color in RGB format (0 ~ 255).
  • [colorHEX:rrggbb] Sets character color in hexadecimal (00 ~ ff).
  • [font:x] Sets the font to x. The path starts from Resources/Fonts/, but Game/Resources/Fonts/ is checked first; same-named files in the Game region take priority. Setting the font conveniently turns off bondfont; to restore it you must turn it on again yourself.
  • [effect:name, int] Sets the character's effect.
    • name The effect name: shake vibrates in place, rotate does a slight rotation, other names mean no effect.
    • int Effect intensity, default 1; larger number means stronger.
  • [outline:r, g, b, a, t] Sets the text's outer border.
    • r, g, b, a Border color and alpha.
    • t Border thickness.
  • [voice:name] Sets the typing sound effect; files are in Resources/Sounds/Voices/, just write the file name.
  • [portrait:frames|interval|mode] Sets the animation played simultaneously while typing, generally a character playing a speaking animation while talking.
    • frames Frame images, separated by English commas, e.g. a.png, b.png.
    • interval Seconds per frame, default 1/30.
    • mode Playback mode, default looponce (return to the first frame after one round).
    • The three segments are separated by |; only frames is required: [portrait:a.png, b.png|0.05|looponce].
  • [portrait:remove] Removes the speaking animation (writing hide / clear / none has the same effect).
  • [skip] Fast-forwards this sentence; takes no value. Fast-forward skips all [wait:] waits.
  • [noskip] Forbids this sentence from being fast-forwarded by the cancel key, the opposite of [skip].
  • [next] After this sentence finishes typing, immediately turn to the next sentence, without waiting for the Player to press confirm; also takes effect in manual mode.
    • A bubble belongs to "the sentence that displays it", so [next] clears the bubble together with the text; if you want to keep using the bubble in the next sentence you must re-[showbubble:].
  • [showbubble:dir, pos] Shows the bubble dialog box. dir is the tail direction, can be left / right / up / down (default left); pos is the tail's position along the border 0 ~ 1, default 0.5.
  • [hidebubble] Hides the bubble dialog box.
  • [func:name] Calls a function named name. Lookup order: first check this typer's funcs registry (registered with typer:SetFunc), if not found fall back to the _G[name] global. So local / closure / upvalue functions, as long as registered first with :SetFunc, can also be called from text, without polluting the namespace by attaching to global.
  • [func:name|a, b, c] Calls a function named name, and can pass parameters, separated by English commas. Lookup order is the same as above.
    • Numeric strings are auto tonumber'd into numbers; other parameters are passed as strings as-is.
    • Function execution errors are wrapped in pcall, only printing [EText] func callback error: ... without interrupting typing.
    • When not found, prints [EText] function not found in typer.funcs or _G: <name> and skips.
  • ^ This symbol can be used to directly reset all styles to default.

Instance methods

  • typer:SetFunc(name, fn) Registers function fn into this typer's funcs table, so [func:name] can call local / closure / upvalue.
    • name String name (corresponds to [func:name] in text); empty string or non-string returns directly.
    • fn When it is a function, registers it; when nil is passed, clears that name's entry.
    • Returns the typer itself, supporting chaining: t:SetFunc("shake", shake):SetFunc("heal", heal).
    • Registration timing: must be completed before the text scans the [func:] tag — usually just register immediately after creating the typer.
    • The old global function style is still compatible (_G[name] fallback), existing text need not change.

Tags can be written consecutively

[font:x][colorHEX:ffff00][effect:shake, 2] written consecutively like this is fine; effects stack in order.

docs.title: NText Typer
docs.text:
NText stands for Neutral Text; its feature is that the style is written in a style table, separated from the text, which makes it more convenient to modify the text.

Use Typers.NText.New(text, position, layer, size, opts, mode) to create an ntext mode typer.

  • text The text to type; can be a string or a table; if a table is used, the text is split into a pageable type.
  • position The position of the first character of the typer.
  • layer The typer's Layer.
  • size The size of the dialog box shown by the typer.
  • opts Style table, with independent style settings inside.
  • mode The typer's mode: manual switch to the next sentence manually, none cannot be manually intervened, only switch to the next sentence through code. If no parameter is given at creation, the default is manual mode.

Usage case

local text = Typers.NText("&* ​这​&​是​一句​话​^...", {320, 240}, 0, {0, 0}, {
    {
        color = {1, 0, 0},
        outline = {0, 1, 1, 1, 2},
    },
    {
        color = {0, 1, 0}
    }
}, "manual")

Modifying style:

Modify the style by adding & and ^ symbols in the sentence.

All styles
  • font The font used; setting it auto-releases bondfont.
  • size Font size.
  • color The text's color, using {r, g, b}.
  • alpha The text's transparency (0 ~ 1).
  • outline The text's outer border, using the {r, g, b, a, t} format.
  • scale The text's scaling factor, default 1. Wide characters like Chinese are auto-handled by bondfont, drawn at 2×.
  • autowrap Whether to auto-wrap.
  • wait Pause for how many seconds before continuing. Same as [wait:x], uses an independent timer, later styles cannot override it, skipped during fast-forward.
  • effect Character effect, format {name = "shake", intensity = 3}.
  • voice Single typing sound file name, placed under Resources/Sounds/Voices/.
  • voices Typing sound list, randomly picks one per character to play.
  • skip Fast-forward settings table, can fill canskip (whether it can be fast-forwarded by cancel key), skipping (whether currently fast-forwarding), skipcount (how many characters per fast-forward), absolute.
  • portrait Character speaking expression switch, supports three ways of writing:
-- 1. Full form
portrait = {
    files = {"a.png", "b.png"},
    interval = 0.02,        -- seconds per frame, default 1/30
    mode = "looponce"       -- default looponce: return to first frame after one round
}

-- 2. Directly give a list of image paths (interval and mode use defaults)
portrait = {"a.png", "b.png"}

-- 3. Remove the speaking animation
portrait = "remove"         -- writing "hide" / "clear" / "none" has the same effect

docs.title: SText Typer
docs.text:
SText stands for Sequence Text, a sequence typer; its feature is that the text is gradually concatenated during typing, which is very suitable for situations with multiple checking conditions.

Usage case

local hp = 5
local text = Typers.SText.New(function (self)
    self:addText("Hello")
    self:nextSentence()

    if (hp) then
        self:addText("HP is now " .. hp .. ".")
    else
        self:addText("I am blind and cannot see HP.")
    end
end, {80, 60}, 0, {200, 100})

Below are all the functions available during construction:

Construction functions

  • self:addText(text) Adds text to the current sentence.
  • self:addSkipText(text) Adds text that needs to be typed instantly (appears immediately during fast-forward).
  • self:setFont(name) Sets the font. Setting the font conveniently turns off bondfont; to restore it you must turn it on again yourself.
