  • self:setWaitTime(time) Pause for how many seconds before continuing. Uses an independent timer, later setSpeed cannot swallow it, skipped during fast-forward.
  • self:setSpeed(interval) Sets the typing interval (seconds).
  • self:setEffect(name, intensity) Sets the character effect; name is shake or rotate, intensity default 1.
  • self:setColor(r, g, b) Sets color, 0 ~ 1 or 0 ~ 255 is auto-recognized by the engine.
  • self:setColorHEX(hex) Sets color in hexadecimal form, e.g. "ff0000".
  • self:setOutline(r, g, b, a, t) Text border, drawn behind the character with 8-direction offset copies.
  • self:setVoices(voices) Sets the typing sound; can pass a file name, or a list.
  • self:setPortrait(frames, interval, mode) Sets the character speaking animation. frames is the image path string (or just a single file name), interval default 1/30, mode default looponce.
  • self:removePortrait() Removes the speaking animation.
  • self:showBubble(visible, dir, pos) Shows / hides the bubble (visible false means hide).
  • self:nextSentence() Ends the current sentence and waits for Player confirm; after confirm, clears text and starts the next sentence.

docs.title: InstText Typer
docs.text:
InstText stands for Instant Text; its feature is no typing animation: the whole text is already drawn on screen the instant it is created.

It is suitable for text that exists long-term but does not need to appear character by character — battle menu buttons, the money readout in a shop, status bars, etc. Because it pre-renders each character into a sprite and caches across instances, drawing the same text for any length costs no extra performance, cheaper than running printf once per frame.

Use Typers.InstText.New(text, position, layer, size) to create.

  • text The text to display. Passing a table only takes item 1; to wrap lines you must write \n yourself (or turn on auto-wrap).
  • position The position of the text's top-left corner.
  • layer Layer.
  • size {width, 0}, the first item is the auto-wrap box width, default {640, 0}; the second item is currently unused.

Creation example

local label = Typers.InstText.New(
    "* " .. Localize.localizeText("Battle.Spare"),
    {90, 270},
    "UponArena"
)
label:SetAlign("center")
label.fontsize = 24

Instance methods

  • SetText(new_text) Changes the text. Re-pre-renders, does not touch color.
  • SetAlign(mode) Alignment, "left" (default) / "center" / "right". Alignment is computed relative to position by whole-line width.
  • Rebuild() Forces a re-layout once. After manually changing size or auto_wrap you must call it yourself.
  • SetColor(r, g, b) Changes color, 0 ~ 1 or 0 ~ 255 both accepted.
  • UseBondFont(config) Switches to a different Chinese/English font config, same structure as EText's bondfont.
  • Destroy() / Remove() Destroys. Decrements the character's reference in the cache by one, can be called repeatedly.
  • t.font / t.fontsize These two properties are written directly; writing them conveniently re-lays out once, no need to Rebuild() yourself.

Color is baked into the character: change color first, then text

InstText pre-renders each character into a sprite, and does not re-color at draw time. So the order must be SetColor → SetText (or SetColor → Rebuild()). Reversing it — change text first then color — will produce no change on screen.

Auto-wrap

local t = Typers.InstText.New("A very very long text that certainly won't fit...", {320, 60}, 0, {200, 0})
t.auto_wrap = true
t:Rebuild()          -- ← after changing auto_wrap / size you must re-layout yourself
  • Default off. If not turned on it always lays out a single line, so existing calls in the engine will not reflow at all.
  • After turning on, it wraps by size[1], with rules consistent with EText / NText: English wraps by word (the whole word goes to the next line, not split in half), Chinese and other equal-width characters wrap character by character; only when a single word itself is wider than the box will it hard-break.
  • Like EText, it does not recognize square-bracket tags; things like [wait:] will be drawn as text as-is.

It does not need updating every frame

InstText registers itself into the Layer and is drawn directly by Layers, not going through Typers.Update, so you don't need to manage it in love.update — after changing content it redraws itself.

Remember to destroy it yourself

Layers.clear() / Typers.ClearAll() will clear it together, but calling Destroy() yourself is safest. Creating repeatedly without destroying, the character sprites in the cache will only keep growing. Typers.InstText.ClearCache() can clear all character cache at once — but instances currently being drawn are also released together, use with caution.

docs.title: Layers System
docs.text:
Besides sprites and Typers, we can also directly use Layers to create content, managed directly under the Layers.

Management file path: Scripts/Libraries/Layers.lua.

Note: this library was written relatively early, so you will most likely see functions named in snake_case, while other libraries use camelCase naming.

docs.title: Creating a Layer
docs.text:
Use Layers.new_layer(name, layer) to create a Layer.

  • name The Layer's name.
  • layer Roughly which level this Layer is.

Since the created Layer is only for convenient direct use during development, it ultimately has to be categorized into a number, after all only numbers are most convenient for Layer ordering.

Layer creation in the battle system

Layers.new_layer("BOTTOM", -1000)
Layers.new_layer("Background", -10)
Layers.new_layer("UI", 0)
Layers.new_layer("ArenasExtraW", 10)
Layers.new_layer("ArenasExtraB", 10.01)
Layers.new_layer("UponArena", 11)
Layers.new_layer("BelowPlayer", 12)
Layers.new_layer("Player", 13)
Layers.new_layer("BelowBullets", 25)
Layers.new_layer("Bullets", 30)
Layers.new_layer("ArenasCoverW", 50)
Layers.new_layer("ArenasCoverB", 50.01)
Layers.new_layer("TopAll", 60)
Layers.new_layer("TOP", 1000)

If the Layer with the entered name does not exist (most likely not created or mistyped), it is automatically defined as 0.

When mistyped, a warning pops up in the sidebar and does not affect gameplay:

Terminal hint

[WARNING] Layers.add: Layer "xxx" not found, defaulting to 0

docs.title: Editing a Layer
docs.text:
Besides creating, you can also perform operations like removal; the table below gives all methods:

Layer operations
  • get_layer(name) Returns the Layer with this name, returns nil directly if it does not exist.
  • remove_layer(name) Deletes the Layer matching this name.
  • set_layer_active(name, active) Whether to enable the Layer with this name.
  • add(obj) Adds an object to a Layer.
  • remove(obj) Detaches obj from the Layer system — only detaches, does not destroy. To also destroy, use the following line: 
    Layers.get_layer("Bullets"):remove(obj)   -- remove from the specified layer, and call obj:Destroy()
  • add_external(draw_func, layer) Draw function and Layer height.
  • remove_external(t) Since add_external returns a table, put it in this function to delete it.
  • remove_externals(list) Clears all external content written in list.
  • remove_external_by_layer(layer) Clears all external draw content of a certain layer.
  • clear_external() Clears all external draw operations across all Layers.
  • sort() Not commonly used; sorts objects inside a Layer by Layer size.
  • make_dirty() Not commonly used; re-issues the sort signal to make sort run.
  • draw() Located in main.lua; here it draws all sprites and Typers.
  • clear() / Clear() Commonly called when cleaning up and exiting a Scene.
  • count() Returns how many objects are now in the Layer.
  • external_count() Returns how many external draw operations are now in the Layer.
  • find_by_id(id) Finds a Layer, object, or external draw operation via the unique _id property.
  • debug() Prints the Layer's current internal info, including how many objects, how many layers, how many external draw operations, etc.

docs.title: Drawing Directly with Layers
docs.text:
As said at the beginning, this part is actually the focus.

Use Layers.add_external(draw_func, layer) to draw content.

  • draw_func The draw function. For more detail on how to draw and what methods are available, see With LOVE Development → Graphics; only a case is provided here.
  • layer The Layer height it is at.

draw_func case

local font = Fonts.New("determination_mono.ttf", 27, "mono")

Layers.add_external(function ()
    SE.graphics.setFont(font)
    SE.graphics.printf("Name the fallen human", 0, 40, 640, "center")
end, 0)

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
In the engine, audio is divided into two categories:

One is music, mainly characterized by being long (over 20 seconds), .ogg format; The other is sound effects, mainly characterized by being short, mostly .wav format, but also no lack of .ogg format.

The reason for separating them is: these two types have different loading methods.

Audio library location: Scripts/Libraries/Audio.lua

The sound effect main directory is Resources/Sounds/, and the music main directory is Resources/Music/. If you want to override engine-built-in audio, put the same-named file into Game/Resources/Sounds/ or Game/Resources/Music/; the Game region takes priority, with the main directory as fallback. This step is done automatically by Audio.ResolvePath; just write the file name when calling.

Both sound effects and music go through Audio.ResolvePath; the writings below behave identically (Game region always checked first):

Writing Actual lookup order Audio.PlaySound("snd_slam.wav") Game/Resources/Sounds/snd_slam.wav → Resources/Sounds/snd_slam.wav Audio.PlaySound("Blaster/snd_intro.wav") Game/Resources/Sounds/Blaster/snd_intro.wav → same-named file in main directory Audio.PlaySound("/Voices/uifont.wav") Game/Resources/Sounds/Voices/uifont.wav → Resources/Sounds/Voices/uifont.wav

Starting with / means "relative to the audio main directory" (the typer voice uses this writing), so the Game-side override path for voices is Game/Resources/Sounds/Voices/. Paths that already write out Resources/Sounds/ or Game/Resources/Sounds/ are also recognized, without duplicating the prefix.

docs.title: Playing Audio
docs.text:
About loading methods:

Sound effects use the static loading mode; since sound effect files are generally small, loading them all at once saves a lot of overhead. In contrast, music uses the stream loading mode; music files are usually loaded while playing.

docs.title: Playing a Sound Effect
docs.text:
Use Audio.PlaySound(path, volume, loop) to play a sound effect; the path starts from the Resources/Sounds/ folder.

  • path Audio path, needs the extension.
  • volume The volume when playing, automatically multiplied by the engine's set volume; see the Game Initialization section in Initialization Configuration in the same directory for details.
  • loop Whether to loop; normally sound effects are not looped.

Normally, we can also just fill in the first parameter, i.e. what audio to play:

Playing a sound effect

Audio.PlaySound("snd_slam.wav")

docs.title: Playing Music
docs.text:
Use Audio.PlayMusic(path, volume, loop) to play a sound effect; the path starts from the Resources/Music/ folder.

  • path Audio path, needs the extension.
  • volume The volume when playing, automatically multiplied by the engine's set volume; see the Game Initialization section in Initialization Configuration in the same directory for details.
  • loop Whether to loop; normally music is looped.

Playing music

Audio.PlayMusic("mus_gameover.ogg")

docs.title: Querying Music
docs.text:
To know whether a certain piece of music is playing now, use Audio.FindMusic(path):

if (Audio.FindMusic("mus_gameover.ogg")) then
    -- playing
end

Internally it follows the exact same resolution order as Audio.PlayMusic (i.e. the table above), so the Game-region-overridden version is also recognized.

docs.title: Editing Audio
docs.text: When audio is created, it is not just the audio file itself, but also comes with a controller; we can manipulate the audio through the controller, or directly manipulate the audio file.

docs.title: Manipulating Audio
docs.text:
For audio operations, this part belongs to LOVE2D, so only a few of the most-used will be explained; for the rest see With LOVE Development → Audio System.

The object we need to manipulate now is mus, code as follows: 

local mus = Audio.PlayMusic("mus_gameover.ogg")

Methods
  • mus:pause() Pauses the audio.
  • mus:play() Plays the audio; if the audio was paused it actually resumes from where it was paused.
  • mus:resume() Already gone; still recommended to use the play() function.
  • mus:stop() Stops playback and automatically adjusts the position to the beginning.
  • mus:rewind() Resets the playback position to the beginning.
  • mus:setVolume(v) / mus:getVolume() Set / get volume.
  • mus:setPitch(p) / mus:getPitch() Set / get pitch.
  • mus:setLooping(bool) / mus:isLooping() Set / query whether to loop.
  • mus:seek(offset, unit) / mus:tell(unit) Set / get current playback position. (In seconds or samples)
  • mus:isPlaying() Whether the audio is playing.
  • mus:isPaused() Whether the audio is in a paused state.
  • mus:isStopped() Whether the audio is in a stopped state.
  • mus:getDuration() Gets the total audio duration. (Seconds)
  • mus:getType() Returns the audio loading type (static or stream).
  • mus:clone() Clones a copy to use, and the newly cloned audio is in stop state.

docs.title: Manipulating the Controller
docs.text:
The object we need to manipulate now is ins, code as follows: 

local mus, ins = Audio.PlayMusic("mus_gameover.ogg")

ins methods
  • ins:VolumeTransition(startVolume, targetVolume, duration) Automatic audio fade, just execute once.
    • startVolume Starting volume (0 ~ 1).
    • targetVolume Target volume (0 ~ 1).
    • duration Execution duration (seconds).
  • ins:PitchTransition(startPitch, targetPitch, duration) Automatic audio fade, just execute once.
    • startPitch Starting pitch size.
    • targetPitch Target pitch size.
    • duration Execution duration (seconds).
  • ins:FadeIn(duration, targetVolume) Volume fade in.
    • duration Execution duration (seconds).
    • targetVolume Target volume size.
  • ins:FadeOut(duration, targetVolume) Volume fade out.
    • duration Execution duration (seconds).
    • targetVolume Target volume size.
  • ins:Pause() Same as mus:pause().
  • ins:Resume() Similar to mus:play().
  • ins:Stop() Same as mus:stop().
  • ins:SetLoopingPoint(introEndTime, outroStartTime) Sets two loop points; the audio loops between them.
  • ins:FollowLoop() After Intro ends, jumps into the loop section.
  • ins:FollowOutro() After this loop, jumps out of the loop section into Outro.

docs.title: Global Variables
docs.text:
Global variables usually refer to variables that can be obtained or modified anywhere in the game, including stored variables.

Global library path: Scripts/Libraries/Global.lua

docs.title: In-Game Global Variables
docs.text:
These game variables disappear and are cleared after quitting the game; they are usually only used for operations like dividing phases within the game.

Use Global.SetVariable(name, value) to set a global variable named name.

  • name The global variable's name.
  • value The global variable's value. Supports: strings, numbers, booleans, tables, functions... almost all types can be stored, including files opened by io.

Setting a global variable

Sets the name to Chara. 

Global.SetVariable("name", "Chara")

Use Global.GetVariable(name) to get the value of a global variable named name.

Getting a global variable

Can get the Player's global variable. 

Global.GetVariable("player")

Use Global.EnsureVariable(name, value) to get an existing global variable; if no existing one, it creates a global variable with value value.

EnsureVariable returns nil on the 'create' call

This function only returns the value when it already exists; the actual creation call only assigns, without returning a value. So don't write local x = Global.EnsureVariable("x", 1) and then use x — the first call will tell you x is nil.

To get the value, add a GetVariable:

Global.EnsureVariable("config", {master = 1, sfx = 1})
local config = Global.GetVariable("config")

Ensuring a global variable

If config does not exist yet, create a config variable with value {master = 1, sfx = 1}; if it exists, read config directly. 

Global.EnsureVariable("config", {
    master = 1,
    sfx = 1
})

If you don't use the EnsureVariable feature, you can also manually check nil and GetVariable:

Primitive method

If you don't yet understand what or does outside of conditional judgments, see the Short-circuit selection topic. This can catch the value directly because SetVariable returns what was set. 

local config =  Global.GetVariable("config") or
                Global.SetVariable("config", {
                    master = 1,
                    sfx = 1
                })

docs.title: Local Stored Variables
docs.text:
The variables under this section are all stored locally, suitable for game Save / Load operations. Note: this is not the Save / Load attack of PS Flowey; this is a separate battle effect.

Function differences

  • For easy memory, all set, get, ensure operations have a save appended at the end.
  • Only supports storing: strings, numbers, tables.

Below are all the function names directly; the usage is the same as the previous section:

  • Global.SetSaveVariable(name, value)
  • Global.GetSaveVariable(name)
  • Global.EnsureSaveVariable(name, value)
  • Global.DeleteSaveVariable(name)

The extra Delete operation can clear storage, which can also be used in a real reset operation.

The library used for storing tables is dkjson; see Intermediate Development → JSON Library for details

docs.title: Canvas & Screen
docs.text:
The screen's position or size is determined by CANVAS (the canvas) together with the Camera.

Canvas location: main.lua, conf.lua Camera location: Scripts/Libraries/Camera.lua

docs.title: Main Canvas
docs.text:
Note: this content should be used together with With LOVE Development → Graphics.

The canvas size is written in conf.lua, mentioned in Initialization Configuration. The vast majority of elements are drawn through CANVAS, except for Border Border.

Canvas drawing code 
SE.graphics.setCanvas({MAIN_CANVAS, stencil = true})
SE.graphics.clear(0, 0, 0, 1)

Camera:apply()
Layers.draw()
if (scene_.draw) then
    scene_.draw()
end
Camera:unload()

local shaders = Global.GetVariable("ScreenShaders") or {}
local source = MAIN_CANVAS
local target = INTERMEDIATE_CANVAS

if (#shaders > 0) then
    for i, shader in ipairs(shaders) do
        SE.graphics.setCanvas(target)
        SE.graphics.clear(0, 0, 0, 0)
        SE.graphics.setShader(shader)
        SE.graphics.draw(source)
        SE.graphics.setShader()
        source, target = target, source
    end
end

SE.graphics.setCanvas()
SE.graphics.clear(0, 0, 0, 1)
--Border.Draw()      -- commented out by default, see the "Border" section

SE.graphics.push()
SE.graphics.translate(DrawX, DrawY)
SE.graphics.scale(ScreenScale, ScreenScale)

SE.graphics.setColor(1, 1, 1, 1)
SE.graphics.draw(source)
local prevLineStyle = SE.graphics.getLineStyle()
SE.graphics.setLineStyle("rough")
SE.graphics.setLineWidth(1)
SE.graphics.setColor(1, 1, 1)
SE.graphics.rectangle("line", -1, -1, CANVAS_WIDTH + 2, CANVAS_HEIGHT + 2)
SE.graphics.setColor(1, 1, 1, 1)
SE.graphics.setLineStyle(prevLineStyle)
SE.graphics.pop()

Before drawing, mount all content onto the canvas MAIN_CANVAS and enable the stencil feature, then draw the canvas.

Simplified code 
SE.graphics.setCanvas({MAIN_CANVAS, stencil = true})
Layers.draw()
SE.graphics.setCanvas()

SE.graphics.draw(MAIN_CANVAS)

docs.title: Canvas Scaling (SCREEN_SCALE)
docs.text:
The canvas itself is always CANVAS_WIDTH × CANVAS_HEIGHT; what changes is only how big it is drawn into the window. This is determined by SCREEN_SCALE in conf.lua, and the canvas is always centered (the border also scales together with the canvas, so the window frame and game image will not be misaligned).

Value Meaning "integer" Only scales by integer multiples, pixel-perfect. Uses 1× when the window is only 1.5× larger, 4× when over 4× larger; scales down proportionally if the window is smaller than the canvas "auto" Tries to fill the window / screen, allowing fractional multiples A number Fixed to this multiple false / nil Keep 1:1 with no scaling

The default value in conf.lua is "auto".

It can also be changed at runtime, using two global functions provided by main.lua:

SetScreenScale("integer")   -- switch scaling mode
print(GetScreenScale())     -- read current multiple (e.g. 2)

The old FILL_SCREEN is now only a legacy switch: it only takes effect when SCREEN_SCALE is nil (meaning "use auto when fullscreen, otherwise 1:1"). New projects should just use SCREEN_SCALE.

docs.title: Intermediate Canvas
docs.text:
This canvas is not responsible for drawing content on screen directly; it has only one purpose: Shaders.

When you set a shader for the entire screen, the intermediate canvas comes in handy, responsible for the overlay operation of shaders, allowing at least two shaders to be displayed on screen at the same time.

See Intermediate Development → Shaders for the detailed shader topic.

A brief introduction to the drawing flow, which I call the ping-pong method. The process is similar to switching all shaders back and forth between these two canvases, hence the name ping-pong method: 

1. First hit the first shader onto canvas 2.
2. Switch canvas; canvas 2 inputs into canvas 1, plus an extra shader.
3. The two canvases swap; canvas 1 now has two layers of effects stacked, inputs into canvas 2, plus another shader.
4. The two canvases swap again, back to step 2.
5. Repeat these two steps until all shaders are added.

This process takes very little time.

Note: most so-called templates or engines that support multiple shaders at the same time basically also use this method; it's like I'm sharing part of the approach.

docs.title: Camera
docs.text:
The canvas does not move, always standing in place, while the Camera's role is to offset the content inside the canvas.

By default, a Camera has already been created, called Camera; below are its properties and methods:

Camera properties

  • x / y The Camera's horizontal and vertical coordinate position, default at (320, 240), i.e. the center of the screen.
  • w / h The Camera's view size, i.e. how large an area the Camera can see starting from the center, default (640, 480), i.e. the whole screen.
  • xscale / yscale The Camera's scaling in horizontal and vertical directions, default (1, 1), i.e. original size.
  • r The Camera's angle, default 0.
  • shaker A variable used to make the Camera shake.

Below are the commonly used Camera methods; some methods already correctly used and not needing a second call will not appear here:

Common Camera methods

  • Camera:setPosition(x, y) Moves the Camera to (x, y).
  • Camera:setSize(w, h) The Camera's width/height view.
  • Camera:setScale(x, y) The Camera's view stretch multiple.
  • Camera:setBounds(min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y) Sets the Camera's bounds, restricting the Camera within the rectangular bounds formed by the two points (min_x, min_y) and (max_x, max_y).
  • Camera:setBoundsBox(x, y, width, height) Sets the Camera's bounds, restricting it within a rectangle centered at (x, y) of size width × height.
  • Camera:unBounds() Removes all the Camera's bounds.
  • Camera:reset() Restores the Camera entirely to its birth state (position, view, scale, angle, bounds all reset).
  • Camera:setAngle(r) Sets the Camera's angle.
  • Camera:shake(mag, duration, decay) Issues a Camera shake task.
    • mag Maximum amplitude.
    • duration Shake duration.
    • decay Whether the shake weakens over time.

About creating a Camera: A newly created Camera will not be used unless you actually modify main.lua so there is no longer a single Camera main camera determining offset and scale.

docs.title: About Overworld Boundary Framing
docs.text:
In v3.0.0 and later versions, all Overworld maps automatically add the practice of detecting the map boundary to frame the Camera, without needing to manually enter functions like setBounds again.

Specific flow: 

Draw the map → engine counts non-empty tiles → computes the union → insets by half a viewport → sets the bounds

The key code is in the AutoCameraBounds function in Scripts/Libraries/Overworld/init.lua; the code is long so it is collapsed by default:

Auto-set border 
function overworld.AutoCameraBounds()
    local m = overworld.map._map
    if (not m) then return end

    local tw = m.tilewidth
    local th = m.tileheight

    -- Covered pixel rectangle (min/max), built from the non-empty tiles.
    local min_px_x, min_px_y, max_px_x, max_px_y
    local function union(x0, y0, x1, y1)
        if (not min_px_x) then
            min_px_x, min_px_y, max_px_x, max_px_y = x0, y0, x1, y1
        else
            min_px_x = math.min(min_px_x, x0)
            min_px_y = math.min(min_px_y, y0)
            max_px_x = math.max(max_px_x, x1)
            max_px_y = math.max(max_px_y, y1)
        end
    end

    for _, layer in ipairs(m.layers) do
        if (layer.type == "tilelayer" and layer.visible ~= false) then
            if (layer.chunks) then
                -- Infinite map: each chunk sits at an absolute (maybe negative)
                -- tile coordinate; its own data grid is 1..width x 1..height.
                for _, chunk in ipairs(layer.chunks) do
                    if (chunk.data) then
                        for cy = 1, chunk.height do
                            for cx = 1, chunk.width do
                                local tile = chunk.data[cy] and chunk.data[cy][cx]
                                if (tile) then
                                    union(
                                        (chunk.x + cx - 1) * tw,
                                        (chunk.y + cy - 1) * th,
                                        (chunk.x + cx)     * tw,
                                        (chunk.y + cy)     * th
                                    )
                                end
                            end
                        end
                    end
                end
            else
                -- Regular map: tile (x, y) renders at layer.x/y + (x-1)*tile.
                local ox = layer.x or 0
                local oy = layer.y or 0
                for ly = 1, layer.height do
                    for lx = 1, layer.width do
                        local tile = layer.data and layer.data[ly] and layer.data[ly][lx]
                        if (tile) then
                            union(
                                ox + (lx - 1) * tw,
                                oy + (ly - 1) * th,
                                ox + lx * tw,
                                oy + ly * th
                            )
                        end
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end

    if (not min_px_x) then return end

    -- Convert the covered pixel rectangle into overworld units (*2).
    local sx_l = min_px_x * 2
    local sx_r = max_px_x * 2
    local sy_t = min_px_y * 2
    local sy_b = max_px_y * 2

    -- The visible world area equals the internal canvas (1:1 camera zoom).
    local view_w = CANVAS_WIDTH
    local view_h = CANVAS_HEIGHT
    local hw = view_w * 0.5
    local hh = view_h * 0.5

    local min_x, max_x
    if ((sx_r - sx_l) >= view_w) then
        min_x = sx_l + hw
        max_x = sx_r - hw
    else
        min_x = (sx_l + sx_r) * 0.5
        max_x = min_x
    end

    local min_y, max_y
    if ((sy_b - sy_t) >= view_h) then
        min_y = sy_t + hh
        max_y = sy_b - hh
    else
        min_y = (sy_t + sy_b) * 0.5
        max_y = min_y
    end

    Camera:setBounds(min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y)
end

docs.title: Mask
docs.text:
Simply put, a Mask is an object used to focus the Player's attention; for example, when you battle a monster, the bullets are framed within the battle box by a Mask.

Or when making a UI, with multiple options crammed into one window, an elegant method is to use a Mask to frame the range, so all options are only drawn within this range.

Mask library location: Scripts/Libraries/Masks.lua

docs.title: Creating a Mask
docs.text:
On the surface it is creating a Mask, but in fact it only temporarily creates a table, so there is no need to worry about recycling.

Use Masks.New(shape, x, y, w, h, r, value) to create a new Mask.

  • shape Can be rect / rectangle, creating a rectangular Mask; can also be ellipse / circle, creating an elliptical Mask; image / img creates a sprite-shaped Mask (see the "Sprite Mask" section below for details).
  • x / y The Mask's position, usually no need to set extra since there are methods to follow a sprite later.
  • w / h The Mask's width/height, also no need to set extra.
  • r Angle.
  • value This feature can specify rendering onto a specific layer; normally just set to 1.

docs.title: Following an Image
docs.text:
After creating it, there is no need to manually set position and width/height; just use the Follow function to follow a sprite.

Use mask:Follow(spr) to make the Mask follow a spr.

Following the battle box

This practice is common during rounds; you can directly make the Mask follow the black area. 

local mask = Masks.New("rect", 320, 320, 155, 130, 0, 1)

function wave.Update(dt)
    mask:Follow(Arena.black)
end

docs.title: Image Usage
docs.text:
Use sprite:SetStencils({mask}) to set the sprite's Mask; multiple masks can be placed inside, e.g.: sprite:SetStencils({mask1, mask2, mask3}).

Below is a case of a big dog bullet using a Mask:

docs.title: Sprite Mask
docs.text: Although rectangular and elliptical Masks cover most scenes, there are always some shapes that cannot be drawn with one or two love.graphics primitives — such as a heart shape, a star shape, or even a certain monster silhouette. In this case you can use a sprite Mask.

docs.title: Principle
docs.text:
Inside Masks.Draw it calls love.graphics.setStencilState("increment", "always", 1) and disables color writing; at this point all "drawn" primitives add +1 to the stencil buffer. The key point: when love.graphics.draw draws an image, the transparent fragments discarded by the default sprite shader do not participate in the stencil action, so the Mask's shape is exactly equivalent to the pixel region with "non-zero alpha" in the ImageData.

In short: the sprite's alpha determines the Mask's shape; fully opaque means full Mask, fully transparent means no Mask, semi-transparent parts are written proportionally — this is consistent with what the human eye sees.

docs.title: Creation
docs.text:
Just append an image parameter at the end of Masks.New:

local img = love.graphics.newImage("Sprites/shapes/heart.png")
local mask = Masks.New("image", 320, 320, 0, 0, 0, 1, img)
  • image Can pass a love.Image object, or an engine sprite table (the return value of Sprites.GetSprite etc.); the latter auto-takes its .image field.
  • At this point w / h is used to scale the sprite as a whole to the target size (e.g. 64×64); fill 0 to keep the original size. That is, the sprite Mask still supports Follow to follow the sprite's size changes.
  • For finer scaling control, you can directly assign to mask.scaleX / mask.scaleY, which overrides the w / h conversion.
  • mask.ox / mask.oy can customize the drawing origin, defaulting to the image's geometric center, making (x, y) correspond to the sprite center — consistent with the "geometric center at (x, y)" semantics of rectangular/elliptical Masks.

Sprite requirements

  • Must have an alpha channel. PNG is recommended.
  • The alpha threshold is exactly 0 — semi-transparent pixels between 0~255 will be written to the raster per the GPU's blending rules, and will not form a "hard edge".
  • Since the engine uses nearest filtering and disables mipmap for sprites by default, the Mask edges will not have unexpected blur; if you want anti-aliasing, pre-apply suitable alpha correction to the image yourself.

Performance

An image Mask rebuilds the sprite drawing cost every frame; multiple large image Masks may slow down stencil writing. If possible, reuse the same ImageData / love.Image.

docs.title: Usage and Following
docs.text:
The sprite Mask also follows the standard flow of Masks.Draw -> Masks.Use -> draw content -> Masks.Clear, and can also go through sprite:SetStencils({mask}) to hand it to the sprite pipeline.

Cropping bullets with a heart-shaped sprite

local img = love.graphics.newImage("Sprites/shapes/heart.png")
local mask = Masks.New("image", 320, 320, 64, 64, 0, 1, img)

function wave.Update(dt)
    mask:Follow(Arena.black)
end

bone_sprite:SetStencils({ mask })

The sprite Mask can also be mixed with rectangular/elliptical Masks; as long as their value is consistent, Masks.Draw accumulates them one by one into the stencil buffer, and the final crop is the union of the several shapes.

docs.title: Border
docs.text:
Perhaps you have played or seen works like Undertale BNP. Besides a centered game screen, their game also has a ring of outer border.

Border library location: Scripts/Libraries/Utils/Border.lua

docs.title: Registering a Border
docs.text:
The engine registers a border, but only the ruins and default borders are usable. The bad news is, due to offset and scaling issues, the idle border is not recommended. There used to be an alternative — drawing a 1px white line around the canvas — but it is now also turned off together with the border (see below).

Setting that aside, use Border.RegisterImage(name, path) to register a border, similar to a global variable, and it will need to be called by name later.

  • name The border's code name.
  • path The border's path, counted from the Resources/Sprites/Border/ folder.

docs.title: Enabling the Border
docs.text:
The border and that white line are not drawn now

In main.lua's love.draw both places are commented out:

  • Border.Draw() — the border image itself. It was originally drawn at a fixed window size, and the offset and scaling don't match.
  • The 1px white line around the canvas (rectangle("line", -1, -1, CANVAS_WIDTH + 2, CANVAS_HEIGHT + 2)) — the "big white frame" that used to replace the border image.

So the current default screen is clean, with no decoration around it. To restore either one, uncomment the corresponding lines, or call Border.Draw() manually in a Scene. The library itself is perfectly fine: it scales with SCREEN_SCALE and centers with the canvas.

If you want to see the border effect in the fastest time, use the following two functions:

Use Border.SetEnabled(true) to enable the border. Use Border.FadeIn(dur) to set the fade-in duration (seconds).

Other functions

  • SetImage(img) Switches the border to a registered image name.
  • SetAlpha(a) Sets the border's transparency, also an important approach for fade in/out.
  • FadeOut(dur) Spends dur seconds fading out and disappearing.
  • SetOpening(x, y) Manually specifies the top-left pixel coordinate of the "window opening" (i.e. where the game image is) on the border image.
  • GetOpening(imgW, imgH) Returns the offset of the window opening relative to the border image's top-left. When not manually set, it is auto-computed by canvas centering.

docs.title: Other Operations
docs.text: If you want to draw something else in the border area, modify the Border.Draw function, but note you can only use love2d's official drawing methods; see With LOVE Development → Graphics for details.

docs.title: Tween
docs.text:
Use the tween library to enrich various animations.

Tween library path: Scripts/Libraries/Tween.lua

docs.title: Create a Tween Task
docs.text:
Use Tween.CreateTween(variableSetter, easingType, direction, begin, final, duration, delay, destroyAfter) to create a tween task operation.

  • variableSetter callback function that keeps executing during the tween.
  • easingType the type of easing, e.g. Quad, Bounce, etc. Case-insensitive (all lowercase supported).
  • direction the direction: In, Out, or InOut. Case-insensitive.
  • begin the starting value of the tween.
  • final the final value of the tween.
  • duration the duration of the tween task (in frames).
  • delay the delay before the tween task starts (in frames).
  • destroyAfter how many frames after starting the tween task is cleared (in frames). Defaults to duration; it is automatically reclaimed once finished.

Image example

The following example moves poseur from x = 320 to 640 via a 60-frame bounce out tween.

During the movement you will see the terminal constantly printing poseur.x until the animation ends after 60 frames.

local poseur = Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png", 0)
Tween.CreateTween(
    function(value)
        print(value)
        poseur.x = value
    end,
"Bounce", "Out", poseur.x, 600, 60)

Any variable example

Since the first parameter of CreateTween is a callback function, you can assign any variable you want inside it.

In the code below you can see poseur turning red-hot after 60 frames.

local poseur = Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png", 0)
Tween.CreateTween(
    function(value)
        poseur.color = {value, 0, 0}
    end,
"Quad", "Out", 0, 1, 60)

docs.title: Function Easing
docs.text:
Use Tween.CreateCustomTween(name, easingFunc) to define a custom tween.

Example

Tween.CreateCustomTween("smooth", function(t)
    return t * t * (3 - 2 * t)
end)

Tween.CreateTween(function(value)
    print(value)
end, "smooth", "", 0, 100, 60)

docs.title: Bézier Easing
docs.text:
You can either hand-roll a Bézier easing or generate it from a scene.

For scene-based generation, see Developer Tools → Tool Scenes.

Use Tween.CreateBezierEasing(name, points) to create a Bézier curve easing.

points format: 

{
    {x = 0, y = 0},
    {x = ..., y = ...},
    {x = 1, y = 1},
    ......
}

Summary: the start point must be 0 and the end point must be 1.

Example

Tween.CreateBezierEasing("mybezier", {
    {x = 0, y = 0},
    {x = 0.25, y = 0.1},
    {x = 0.25, y = 1},
    {x = 1, y = 1},
})

Tween.CreateTween(function(value)
    print(value)
end, "mybezier", "", 0, 100, 60)

docs.title: Game Area and Asset Override
docs.text:
Game/ is the root directory of content that belongs to each game itself — this is the Game area repeatedly mentioned throughout this documentation. All engine-bundled assets live in their own original directories; your own content goes into the Game area instead.

The only purpose of this separation is: engine updates will not wipe out your game content.

docs.title: Division of Labor Between Two Paths
docs.text:
Engine directory Game area Purpose Default content bundled with the engine Content for your specific game When updating the engine Replaced wholesale Preserved as-is Priority Low (fallback) High (preferred)

Therefore, follow one iron rule while developing: do not modify anything directly under the engine directory.

If you really need to change engine-bundled behavior or assets, the correct approach is to copy it into the Game area and edit that copy. Keep the engine-directory copy untouched, so you can simply overwrite it when upgrading the engine later — your changes will not be lost.

docs.title: General Rule: Game First, Main Directory as Fallback
docs.text:
Except for a few things that only read from the Game area, all other resources follow the same lookup order:

  1. First check whether the Game area has a file with the same name.
  2. If yes → use the Game area copy directly (override takes effect).
  3. If no → fall back to the engine-directory copy.

This order applies to paths, regardless of file type: scenes, sprites, audio, translations, wave scripts, maps, attack patterns, Souls, item tables all go through this logic.

docs.title: What Supports Override
docs.text:
Content Game area path Engine fallback path Scene Game/Scenes/<name>.lua Scripts/Scenes/<name>.lua Sprite Game/Resources/Sprites/ Resources/Sprites/ Sound effect Game/Resources/Sounds/ Resources/Sounds/ Music Game/Resources/Music/ Resources/Music/ Font Game/Resources/Fonts/ Resources/Fonts/ Translation (key overlay) Game/Localization/ Localization/ Wave script Game/Waves/<name>.lua Scripts/Waves/<name>.lua Attack Pattern Game/Attacks/<name>.lua Scripts/Libraries/Battle/PlayerAttacks/<name>.lua Soul Game/Souls/<name>.lua Scripts/Libraries/Battle/Player/Souls/<name>.lua Map Same relative path under Game/ Maps/ Item table Game/Logics/items.lua Scripts/Logics/items.lua

Two easy pitfalls

  • For fonts, just write the filename: Fonts.New("determination_mono.ttf", 27) will first look in Game/Resources/Fonts/. All font loading in the engine goes through this entry, so you don't need to change any call code — drop in a file with the same name and it gets swapped.
  • The engine fallback directory Scripts/Logics/ for the item table does not currently exist (the engine does not ship this file), so in practice the item table now only has Game/Logics/items.lua as its single source. The same-directory Game/Logics/init.lua is even a hard require, with no fallback at all.

docs.title: What Only Reads From the Game Area
docs.text:
The following content has no available same-named engine-side directory. It is game-specific data — just write it directly in the Game area, no need to worry about overrides:

Content Path Encounter Game/Encounter/ Monster animation Game/Animations/ Game logic data Game/Logics/ Hack scripts Game/Hacks/ Whole-module replacement map Game/Overrides.lua Configuration override Game/conf_pure.lua

This is also why these items appear with only a single path in the docs — they are yours by nature, and the engine provides no default version.

Among these, Game/conf_pure.lua is "layered" rather than "fallback", unlike the others: the engine always runs the root conf_pure.lua first to lay down all default values, then runs your copy to override the same-named variables. So you only need to write the few lines you want to change. If your copy errors out halfway through, the engine will roll back entirely to the defaults and print [Conf] WARNING: ... exists but failed to load; using the engine defaults ..., and the game will still start.

What goes in game logic

World rules (level curve, how max level expands, story switches, chest contents) have their own page: Game Logic and World Rules.

Don't confuse Game/Logics with Game/Hacks

Both directories have "logic"-like names, but their responsibilities are completely different: Game/Logics/ holds data (level tables, chest contents), while Game/Hacks/ holds code (rewriting engine behavior). The next section covers the latter.

docs.title: Rewriting Engine Internals With Hacks
docs.text:
All the methods above share one premise: the content itself must be "placeable elsewhere." But some things don't belong to any category — such as the battle UI layout, the battle flow state machine, or the internal behavior of the sprite library. They live in Scripts/Libraries/, and previously the only way to change them was to touch the engine.

The Game area provides two supported entry points:

docs.title: 1. Game/Overrides.lua — declarative whole-module replacement
docs.text:
A map of ["engine module name"] = "Game module name", suitable for "I want to rewrite this whole module":

-- Game/Overrides.lua
return {
    ["Scripts.Libraries.Battle.UI"] = "Game.UI.Battle",
}

docs.title: 2. Game/Hacks/*.lua — imperative patching
docs.text:
Executed once each at startup in filename numeric-prefix order, suitable for "I only want to change one or two functions":

-- Game/Hacks/010_my_battle.lua
return {
    name = "My battle tweak",
    apply = function(Hack)
        Hack.After("Scripts.Libraries.Battle", function(battle)
            -- runs once after the engine finishes loading Battle
        end)
    end
}

Available primitives: Hack.Replace (whole-module replace), Hack.After (post-load callback), Hack.Wrap (wrap a function), Hack.Set, and the more internal Hack.Patch. Full docs and caveats are in Game/Hacks/README.md.

Filename rules

Every .lua in Game/Hacks/ is treated as an entry and executed; only files beginning with an underscore _ are skipped. So if you want to put a whole module in this directory as replacement material, the filename must include an underscore (e.g. _my_ui.lua), otherwise it will be run as an entry and then complain "this file returns neither a function nor a {apply = ...}".

Press F5 after editing

Both entry points first undo and then re-apply on hot reload, so after editing the config pressing F5 takes effect without restarting.

docs.title: What Happens When an Override Breaks
docs.text:
This point is important enough to state on its own: override failures are always reported, never silently.

When the engine looks up a resource it strictly distinguishes "file does not exist" from "file exists but errored on load," yielding three possible outcomes:

Three outcomes

1. Normal override — the Game area has it and it loads fine. No output; the Game area copy is used directly.

2. Override not found, fallback succeeded — the Game area doesn't have it, the engine-directory copy is used:

[Battle] WARNING: 'bones.wave1' not found in Game.Waves. (fell back to Scripts.Waves.bones.wave1).

This is normal — just confirm "I indeed didn't write this override."

3. Override exists but is broken — the Game area has this file, but it errors on load:

[Battle] WARNING: 'Game.Waves.bones.wave1' exists but failed to load; using Scripts.Waves.bones.wave1 instead.
[Battle]   <the actual error message>

Seeing exists but failed to load means your override did not take effect, and the actual error is printed too — just fix it accordingly.

Different subsystems use different warning prefixes; just look for the words exists but failed to load:

Prefix From [Battle] Encounter, wave, attack pattern, Soul [Scenes] Scene [Overworld] Map, item table [Conf] Game/conf_pure.lua [Hack] Game/Hacks/ and Game/Overrides.lua

Why 'not found' and 'broken' must not be conflated

Early versions used the success/failure of pcall(require, ...) to decide whether a module exists. The problem is that pcall returning false has two completely different causes: the file does not exist, and the file exists but its top-level code errored. Treating the latter as "does not exist" causes two bad things at once: the fallback chain is silently truncated (you think the override took effect, but the old version runs), and the real error is swallowed without display. So now it is check whether the file exists first, then decide whether to require it. A few extra lines buy you the guarantee that once something breaks, you will definitely see it.

docs.title: Some Caveats
docs.text:
• Always use forward slashes / for paths, starting from the project root directory.
  • Filenames must match exactly — override is "same-name replacement," not "nearest merge." Once you put px.png in the Game area, the engine-directory px.png is no longer used at all.
  • Map image references are relative paths. The engine's map .lua references tiles via ../images/..., so when overriding a map, the Game area copy must also bring its own corresponding ../images/ directory tree, otherwise tiles will be missing.
  • When an override doesn't take effect, check the terminal first. The third case above will always print a warning — don't guess.

docs.title: Game Logic and World Rules
docs.text:
Game/Logics/ is the part unique to your game: what the world looks like at the start, how levels rise, what the story switches are called, what's inside chests. Changing this does not require touching the engine.

Paths: Game/Logics/init.lua (the world's initial state and rule tables), Game/Logics/items.lua (the item table).

This page covers the "world rules" layer. How each DATA field is used at runtime is documented in Overworld → Initialization and Scene Skeleton; how the item table is used is in the ITEMS section of that same page; the Game area override order is in Game Area and Asset Override.

docs.title: How It Is Loaded
docs.text:
-- Scripts/Libraries/Overworld/init.lua
DATA  = DATA or require("Game.Logics")
FLAG  = DATA.flags
CHEST = DATA.chests

This file has no engine fallback

The engine hard-requires Game.Logics — unlike sprites or waves, which "fall back to Scripts/ if the Game area lacks it." A missing Game/Logics/init.lua means the entire main world cannot start.

This table IS the save

The save page runs Global.SetSaveVariable("Overworld", DATA) — the entire DATA is written to disk. So adding a field in Logics is equivalent to adding a field to the save.

items.lua is the exception — it goes Game-first: Game.Logics.items → Scripts.Logics.items (the engine copy does not exist in the current project, so in practice only the Game area copy exists).

docs.title: File Skeleton
docs.text:
local path = (...):match("(.-)[^%.]+$")
local logic = {}

Global.SetVariable("FUN", math.random(0, 100))   -- ① globals can be set at top level

logic = { ... }            -- ② the world's default state (player, position, inventory…)
logic.flags   = { ... }    -- ③ story switches
logic.chests  = { ... }    -- ④ what's in chests
logic.lv_data = { ... }    -- ⑤ world rules: level curve

-- Global.DeleteSaveVariable("Overworld")          -- ⑥ force a new save during debugging
if (Global.GetSaveVariable("Overworld")) then
    logic = Global.GetSaveVariable("Overworld")    -- ⑦ if a save exists, use that copy
end

return logic
  • ① You can set globals directly at the top level. FUN is the "fun value" from UNDERTALE, re-randomized each time a new save is started.
  • ⑦ If a save exists, it entirely replaces the defaults — so changes to Logics not taking effect is caused by this; see the DATA section in Overworld → Initialization and Scene Skeleton. During debugging, comment out that line, or use ⑥ to delete the save outright.

docs.title: lv_data: The Growth Curve
docs.text:
This is the most typical "world rule" — max level, HP per level, and EXP per level are all in this one table.

Field Meaning lv Level hp Max HP at this level (directly overrides maxhp) at Attack → written into DATA.player.atk df Defense → written into DATA.player.def totalExp Cumulative EXP required to reach this level (not "how much for this level") The engine-bundled 20-level table 
logic.lv_data = {
    { lv = 1,  hp = 20,  at = 10,  df = 10, totalExp = 0      },
    { lv = 2,  hp = 24,  at = 12,  df = 10, totalExp = 10     },
    { lv = 3,  hp = 28,  at = 14,  df = 10, totalExp = 30     },
    { lv = 4,  hp = 32,  at = 16,  df = 10, totalExp = 70     },
    { lv = 5,  hp = 36,  at = 18,  df = 11, totalExp = 120    },
    { lv = 6,  hp = 40,  at = 20,  df = 11, totalExp = 200    },
    { lv = 7,  hp = 44,  at = 22,  df = 11, totalExp = 300    },
    { lv = 8,  hp = 48,  at = 24,  df = 11, totalExp = 500    },
    { lv = 9,  hp = 52,  at = 26,  df = 12, totalExp = 800    },
    { lv = 10, hp = 56,  at = 28,  df = 12, totalExp = 1200   },
    { lv = 11, hp = 60,  at = 30,  df = 12, totalExp = 1700   },
    { lv = 12, hp = 64,  at = 32,  df = 12, totalExp = 2500   },
    { lv = 13, hp = 68,  at = 34,  df = 13, totalExp = 3500   },
    { lv = 14, hp = 72,  at = 36,  df = 13, totalExp = 5000   },
    { lv = 15, hp = 76,  at = 38,  df = 13, totalExp = 7000   },
    { lv = 16, hp = 80,  at = 40,  df = 13, totalExp = 10000  },
    { lv = 17, hp = 84,  at = 42,  df = 14, totalExp = 15000  },
    { lv = 18, hp = 88,  at = 44,  df = 14, totalExp = 25000  },
    { lv = 19, hp = 92,  at = 46,  df = 14, totalExp = 50000  },
    { lv = 20, hp = 99,  at = 48,  df = 14, totalExp = 99999  }
}

docs.title: How Leveling Is Settled
docs.text:
When a battle ends, ReturnData() in Scripts/Scenes/Battle/scene_battle_ow.lua writes the results back into DATA:

DATA.player.exp = DATA.player.exp + (Battle.EXP or 0)
DATA.player.gold = DATA.player.gold + (Battle.GOLD or 0)
DATA.player.hp = math.max(0, math.min(DATA.player.maxhp, Player.hp))

while (DATA.lv_data[DATA.player.lv + 1] and
       DATA.player.exp >= DATA.lv_data[DATA.player.lv + 1].totalExp) do
    local old_max = DATA.player.maxhp
    DATA.player.lv = DATA.player.lv + 1

    local row = DATA.lv_data[DATA.player.lv]
    DATA.player.maxhp = row.hp
    DATA.player.atk = row.at
    DATA.player.def = row.df

    -- UNDERTALE rule: current HP rises by the same amount max HP rose
    DATA.player.hp = math.min(DATA.player.maxhp, DATA.player.hp + (DATA.player.maxhp - old_max))
end

Settlement rule summary

  • A single battle can level up multiple times (it's a while, not an if).
  • maxhp / atk / def are overridden by the table, not accumulated; whatever the table says is what you get.
  • The amount of max HP gained is also added to current HP (leveling heals).
  • weapon / armor / gold / exp are not governed by the level table.

watk / edef are currently display-only

player.watk (weapon attack) and player.edef (armor defense) only appear in the STAT menu display; the engine does not add them to atk / def. To make equipment actually take effect, you must add it yourself at settlement or damage calculation.

docs.title: Want to Expand to LV 30? Just Add Rows
docs.text:
The cap is entirely determined by table length — the loop condition is DATA.lv_data[lv + 1] existing, so:

{ lv = 21, hp = 106, at = 50, df = 15, totalExp = 150000 },
{ lv = 22, hp = 113, at = 52, df = 15, totalExp = 220000 },
-- ... keep going up to 30

After adding them, no engine code needs to change — the menu, level-up settlement, and EXP display will all follow along.

Opening the STAT menu at max level crashes

Overworld.CalcNextEXP() is written like this:

local next_total = DATA.lv_data[DATA.player.lv + 1].totalExp   -- no nil check

At max level lv_data[lv + 1] is nil, and indexing nil directly errors — the symptom is that opening the STAT page after reaching max level crashes. Two fixes: write one extra row in the level table (e.g. if max is 20, write up to 21, keeping totalExp at a large enough value), or add a nil check to CalcNextEXP yourself (return 0 or "--").

Don't write the EXP threshold backwards

totalExp is cumulative EXP, not "how much this level needs." Level 20's 99999 means "a total of 99999 EXP accumulated to reach level 20," not "fight 99999 more."

docs.title: flags: World Switches
docs.text:
logic.flags = {
    test_killed = 0
}

The engine exposes it as the global FLAG, just use it directly:

FLAG["test_killed"] = 1
if (FLAG["test_killed"] == 1) then
    -- story branch
end

Since the entire DATA is saved, flags are naturally story switches that persist in saves, requiring no extra work.

docs.title: chests: What's in Chests
docs.text:
logic.chests = {
    chest = { "Spider" },   -- key name corresponds to the chest id
    chest1 = {}
}

This is also exposed as the global CHEST. On opening a chest, the list is fetched by id; remember to clear it afterward, or it can be opened repeatedly (see Menu · Save · Chest).

docs.title: Two Things to Consider When Adding Fields
docs.text:
Old saves lack new fields

Saves are stored as the entire table. After you add sanity = 100 to player, that field is nil in previously saved games. When reading, either provide a default (DATA.player.sanity or 100), or during development just delete the save and start fresh.

getcell is force-enabled by the engine

player.getcell is written as false in Logics, but Scripts/Libraries/Overworld/stat.lua has DATA.player.getcell = true at the top level which overrides it. As a result the CELL (phone) menu is ON by default, and changing Logics has no effect.

docs.title: Why This Layer Exists Separately
docs.text:
Keeping "world rules" in one file has the benefit of tuning values without touching the engine:

What you want to change Where to change Max level 20 or 30 Add/remove rows in lv_data HP / ATK / DEF per level hp / at / df of lv_data How fast leveling is totalExp of lv_data Name at start / items / spawn point player and room / marker / position Where story branches are recorded flags What chests give chests Which items exist items.lua in the same directory

In other words, worldview-level settings (is this a "world capped at level 20" or "level 30") are fully decided in Game/Logics/, with the engine completely untouched.

docs.title: Beat
docs.text:
Align in-game events to the beat of the music.

Beat library path: Scripts/Libraries/Beat.lua

This is a standalone library you must wire up yourself

main.lua does not automatically load Beat, nor does it call Update for it every frame. To use it, you must first obtain the module yourself, then advance it every frame:

local beats = ImportFile("Beat")   -- equivalent to require("Scripts.Libraries.Beat")

docs.title: Basic Concepts
docs.text:
The music timeline is measured in BPM (beats per minute):

  • beats.beat is an accumulator starting at 0 that keeps growing with Update, representing "which beat we've reached."
  • 1 beat = 60 / BPM seconds. At 120 BPM a beat is 0.5 seconds, at 180 BPM it is 1/3 second.
  • Integer beats are the common "beat 1, beat 2"; fractional beats (e.g. 2.5) mean half a beat.

docs.title: Set Speed SetBPM(bpm)
docs.text: beats.SetBPM(180)   -- falls back to 120 when omitted or nil

docs.title: Advance Each Frame Update(dt)
docs.text:
Must be called once per frame. It is responsible for accumulating beats.beat and checking whether all registered events should trigger. Put it in the scene's scene.update:

function scene.update(dt)
    beats.Update(dt)
end

docs.title: Trigger Callback on Beat CreateEvent(target, call, offset)
docs.text:
Executes call once at beat target, then auto-removes itself (one-shot).

  • target the target beat, supports fractional values.
  • call the callback executed when the beat is hit.
  • offset extra offset in milliseconds, positive means pushed later. When omitted, uses the module-level default beats.offset (default 0).
beats.CreateEvent(4, function()
    print("beat 4")
end)

-- 200 milliseconds after beat 4
beats.CreateEvent(4, function()
    print("beat 4 +200ms")
end, 200)

docs.title: Beat Check OnBeat(target)
docs.text:
The current implementation has a pitfall; do not use it for timing

OnBeat internally uses floating-point exact equality (beats.beat == target), while beats.beat is a frame-by-frame accumulated float, which almost never hits exactly. Testing: running 600 frames each at 60 / 30 / 144 FPS produced 0 hits every time. To "do something at a certain beat," use CreateEvent instead.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
The "execute a batch of events at a certain beat" style of event.lua, once wired up, looks roughly like this:

local beats = ImportFile("Beat")

function scene.load()
    beats.SetBPM(120)

    -- Beat 1: a batch of events fire together
    beats.CreateEvent(1, function()
        EventU1()
        EventU2()
        EventU3()
        EventU5()
    end)

    -- Beats 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4: each fires once
    for b = 2, 4, 0.5 do
        beats.CreateEvent(b, Event2)
    end
end

function scene.update(dt)
    beats.Update(dt)
end

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• One-shot: events registered with CreateEvent are immediately removed from the internal table after firing. To repeat, re-register.
  • State does not auto-reset: beats.beat is an in-module accumulator; when switching songs or restarting a scene you must reset beats.beat to 0 yourself and re-set BPM as needed.
  • offset is converted by BPM: the offset is converted to beats using the current BPM at trigger-check time, so changing BPM midway simultaneously affects the offsets of not-yet-fired events.

docs.title: Timer
docs.text:
Execute some code after a number of frames or seconds.

Timer library path: Scripts/Libraries/Timer.lua

Needs to be wired up manually

Like the Beat library, this repo's main.lua does not load Timer, nor does it call its Update every frame. Before using it, obtain the module yourself and advance it every frame:

local timers = ImportFile("Timer")   -- equivalent to require("Scripts.Libraries.Timer")

docs.title: Two Time Units
docs.text:
Timers come in two families; the only difference is whether they count in frames or in seconds.

Purpose By frames By seconds Execute at intervals runFrame runSecond Execute continuously after delay duringFrame duringSecond

The frame-based versions add +1 to an internal counter each Update, so an interval of 60 means "every 60 frames"; the second-based versions accumulate dt, so 1.5 means "every 1.5 seconds."

docs.title: Execute at Intervals: runFrame / runSecond
docs.text:
timers.runFrame(func, interval, count)
timers.runSecond(func, interval, count)
  • func the callback executed when due.
  • interval the interval. runFrame is in frames (default 60); runSecond is in seconds (default 1.0).
  • count how many times to execute in total (default 1).

Example

-- Triggers once every 30 frames, 4 times total
timers.runFrame(function()
    print("tick")
end, 30, 4)

-- Triggers once every 0.5 seconds, 3 times total
timers.runSecond(function()
    print("half second")
end, 0.5, 3)

docs.title: Execute Continuously After Delay: duringFrame / duringSecond
docs.text:
timers.duringFrame(func, delay, during, afterfunc)
timers.duringSecond(func, delay, during, afterfunc)

Waits delay (frames / seconds) first, then executes func every frame for the next during (frames / seconds), then calls afterfunc once after the whole segment ends (optional).

  • delay the delay, default 0.
  • during the duration, default 1.
  • afterfunc the end callback, may be omitted.

Example

-- Wait 1 second, then run every frame for 2 seconds, then clean up
timers.duringSecond(function()
    -- runs every frame
end, 1, 2, function()
    -- end callback
end)

docs.title: Advance Each Frame Update
docs.text:
function scene.update(dt)
    timers.Update(dt)
end

docs.title: The Returned Timer Object
docs.text:
All four functions above return a timer object that you can control mid-flight:

Timer fields and methods

  • t.time the current accumulation (frames or seconds).
  • t.count how many times it has fired.
  • t.running whether it is running (becomes false when paused).
  • t.active whether it is still alive (when false, it is reclaimed on the next Update).
  • t:pause() / t:unpause() / t:togglePause() pause / resume / toggle.
  • t:isPaused() whether it is paused.
  • t:stop() stop and reclaim immediately.
  • t:restart() reset and restart (both time and count return to the start).
local t = timers.runSecond(function()
    print("loop")
end, 1, 999)

t:pause()     -- don't run yet
t:unpause()   -- resume

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Must Update every frame: without calling it, the timer stays frozen in place forever.
  • The frame-based version follows the frame rate: the "frames" of runFrame are determined by how often Update is called; dropped frames / different machines will change it accordingly. For stable rhythm, use runSecond.
  • Auto-reclaim: runFrame / runSecond end on their own after firing count times; during* ends after the duration segment runs out. After ending, they are removed on the next Update.

docs.title: Input and Controller
docs.text:
The engine unifies keyboard, gamepad, and touchscreen into a single input interface.

Input library path: Scripts/Libraries/Controller/ (contains Keyboard.lua, Joystick.lua, VirtualKeyboard.lua, Controller.lua).

docs.title: Four Modules
docs.text:
Module Hardware wrapped Global name Controller/Keyboard.lua Keyboard + mouse + touch point Keyboard Controller/Joystick.lua Gamepad / joystick Joystick Controller/VirtualKeyboard.lua On-screen virtual buttons / joystick (mobile) VirtualKeyboard Controller/Controller.lua Merges the above three into a unified query Controller

The per-frame update order (written in love.update, order must not be changed): poll the gamepad first, then map the gamepad to the keyboard, then settle the keyboard and virtual keyboard states uniformly.

Joystick.Update()  →  Controller.Update()  →  Keyboard.Update()  →  VirtualKeyboard.Update()

docs.title: State Semantics
docs.text:
All devices' GetState share the same set of return values:

Value Meaning 1 Just pressed this frame 2 Held down -1 Just released this frame 0 Not pressed

So to check "pressed once" use == 1, and to check "is held" use >= 1.

docs.title: Unified Query Controller
docs.text:
Game code should always read input through Controller, not directly from Keyboard — otherwise the gamepad won't be picked up.

Common interfaces

  • Controller.GetState(name) query the state of a logical name (0 / 1 / 2 / -1).
  • Controller.IsDown(name) whether it is held (i.e. GetState(name) >= 1).
  • Controller.GetAxis(name) read the analog value of a gamepad axis (deadzone-applied and re-normalized).
  • Controller.GetVector() returns the (x, y) movement vector, left stick preferred, falling back to the d-pad.
  • Controller.GetDevices() which devices are currently connected (keyboard / gamepad count / virtual keyboard).
  • Controller.GetSource(name) which device provided this input (for debugging).
  • Controller.AllowPlayerInput(bool) toggle all device player input at once.
  • Controller.SetDeadzone(v) set the joystick deadzone.
  • Controller.SetMirrorEnabled(bool) toggle the "gamepad mapped to keyboard" bridge (on by default).

Example

if (Controller.GetState("confirm") == 1) then
    -- confirm was just pressed this frame
end

local x, y = Controller.GetVector()

docs.title: Logical Key Map
docs.text:
Logical names are decoupled from specific hardware: keyboard and gamepad each bind a set, and queries only recognize the logical name.

Logical name Keyboard Gamepad confirm return, z a cancel x, shift b menu c, ctrl start, y, back shift lshift, rshift leftshoulder, rightshoulder ctrl lctrl, rctrl — alt lalt, ralt — up / down / left / right corresponding arrow keys d-pad + left stick arrows up / down / left / right d-pad + left stick letter a ~ z — number 0 ~ 9 —

Custom bindings

To add your own logical name, bind it once for keyboard and once for gamepad:

Keyboard.Bind("dash", "lshift", "rshift")
Joystick.Bind("dash", "leftshoulder", "rightshoulder")

docs.title: Gamepad Axes and Virtual Buttons
docs.text:
Gamepad analog axis names: leftx / lefty / rightx / righty / triggerleft / triggerright.

  • Read an axis: Controller.GetAxis("leftx").
  • Once a stick / trigger crosses the deadzone, a set of virtual button names also emerges (e.g. leftstickleft, triggerright), which can be queried directly like confirm.

The default deadzone is 0.15, adjustable via Controller.SetDeadzone(v) or the ControllerDeadzone config option.

docs.title: Touchscreen and Virtual Keyboard
docs.text:
On mobile, the on-screen virtual buttons open automatically (an 8-direction stick pad at bottom-left + Z / X / C at bottom-right). To test on desktop, use ControllerSimulation from Initialization Configuration:

Global.SetVariable("ControllerSimulation", {
    virtualKeyboard = true,   -- open the virtual keyboard, mouse drag = finger swipe
    joystick        = false,  -- pretend a gamepad is plugged in
})

You can also toggle manually in code: VirtualKeyboard.SetEnabled(true), VirtualKeyboard.SetVisible(false), VirtualKeyboard.SetAlpha(0.4).

docs.title: Related Configuration
docs.text:
• ControllerDeadzone gamepad deadzone size.
  • ControllerSimulation.virtualKeyboard / .joystick desktop input simulation.

See Initialization Configuration → Input Control.

docs.title: ❕️ GUI Library
docs.text:
The engine's built-in UNDERTALE-style graphical interface library, providing components such as windows, text, buttons, sliders, text inputs, and dropdowns, plus an input helper that maps mouse coordinates from window space to canvas space.

Library path: Scripts/Libraries/GUI/ (folder form, init.lua is the entry).

Loading: in main.lua do GUI = ImportFile("GUI"), must be after Typers (Label wraps Typers.InstText). After loading, you can call the global GUI directly from any scene.

Dependencies:

  • Typers — text in Label / Button / Slider / TextInput / Dropdown all goes through Typers.InstText, auto-routing Chinese/English.
  • Layer System — all drawing is registered via Layers.add_external, no sprites created.

docs.title: Coordinates and Layer Conventions
docs.text: Convention Description Coordinate semantics Top-left (x, y) + width/height (w, h); Window:SetCenter switches to center-point semantics (compatible with battle-box semantics). Default layer 1000 (above battle elements); adjustable via :SetLayer, or pass layer at New. Mouse coordinates love's mouse coordinates are in window screen space; GUI is in 640×480 canvas space. The two are converted via GUI.Input.ScreenToCanvas (see below). Pixel snapping internal math.floor(v + 0.5) snapping, consistent with Sprites.snapCoord. Color restore restores white after each draw, so color does not leak to other layers in the same frame (pitfall #7).

docs.title: Font Conventions
docs.text:
Through testing, only the following font sizes render clearly. The GUI library reuses Typers.InstText's bondfont mechanism directly, so the caller does not need to handle fonts:

Language Font Size English Resources/Fonts/determination_mono.ttf 27 or 13 Chinese Resources/Fonts/simsun.ttc only 13; for size 27 use scale=2 to enlarge

Mixed Chinese/English layout is auto-routed by Typers.InstText per character byte (charlen judges 1=English / >1=Chinese); GUI.Label is a thin wrapper over it.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
The caller holds the component reference and calls :Destroy() on each one in scene.clear. Layers.clear() stops external drawing but does not release Label's InstText text-cache reference (InstText uses reference counting), so you must call Destroy explicitly, otherwise it leaks and may trigger "Cannot use object after it has been released".

TextInput.Focus opens system text input (love.keyboard.setTextInput); Blur / Destroy must close it, otherwise it still receives input after leaving the scene.

docs.title: Mouse Input Helper GUI.Input
docs.text:
Key point: love's mouse coordinates are in window screen space, while GUI components are in canvas space — they must be converted to hit-test.

GUI.Input uses the globals DrawX / DrawY / ScreenScale (set by updateScreenScale in main.lua) for conversion, and does button edge detection, so the scene can poll IsPressed / IsReleased / IsDown every frame — semantics match the keyboard's hand-written prev table.

State model:

  • held is real-time — OnPressed / OnReleased change it directly, IsDown reflects the current state.
  • pressed / released / wheel are frozen per frame — async events first go into pending, then at the start of Update() are swapped into state and pending is cleared, so IsPressed / IsReleased are true exactly on the next frame.

Scene wiring (main.lua already forwards all mouse callbacks to the scene, when not pausing):

-- the four love callbacks forwarded to the helper
function scene.mousepressed(x, y, button)  GUI.Input.OnPressed(x, y, button) end
function scene.mousereleased(x, y, button) GUI.Input.OnReleased(x, y, button) end
function scene.mousemoved(x, y)            GUI.Input.OnMoved(x, y) end
function scene.wheelmoved(x, y)            GUI.Input.OnWheel(x, y) end

function scene.update(dt)
    GUI.Input.Update()   -- must be at the very start of scene.update, freezes this frame's state

    local mx, my = GUI.Input.GetCanvasMouse()   -- canvas-space coordinates
    if (GUI.Input.IsPressed(1)) then            -- left button = 1; just pressed this frame
        -- hit-test / trigger component
    end
    local wheel = GUI.Input.GetWheel()          -- +1 up / -1 down / 0
end
GUI.Input interface overview
  • ScreenToCanvas(sx, sy) pure conversion: (sx-DrawX)/ScreenScale, (sy-DrawY)/ScreenScale.
  • GetCanvasMouse() current canvas-space cursor position.
  • IsDown(button) whether held (real-time).
  • IsPressed(button) whether just pressed this frame (edge).
  • IsReleased(button) whether just released this frame (edge).
  • GetWheel() this frame's wheel delta (+1 / -1 / 0).
  • OnPressed(sx, sy, btn) / OnReleased(...) / OnMoved(sx, sy) / OnWheel(x, y) called in the love callbacks.
  • Update() called at the start of scene.update.
  • Reset() called in scene.clear — prevents the mouse from being held when switching scenes, where love may not deliver mousereleased to the new scene, causing IsDown to lock up.

docs.title: Window
docs.text:
Visual window: two stacked rectangles (thick outer border + inner fill), purely visual — no collision, no player constraint. Animation uses the same "rate-limited approach to target" as the battle box (smooth_value).

local win = GUI.Window.New{
    x = 200, y = 100, w = 240, h = 120,
    thickness = 5, layer = 1000,
}
win:ResizeWithSpeed(300, 150, 15, 15)   -- smooth resize (must call win:Update(dt) in scene.update)
win:SetCenter(320, 240)                 -- switch to center-point semantics
win:SetVisible(false)
-- scene.clear: win:Destroy()
Window interface
  • New{x, y, w, h, thickness, outer, inner, layer, visible} outer color defaults to MainColor, inner defaults to black.
  • :MoveTo(x, y, imm) / :SetCenter(cx, cy, imm) move; imm=true syncs immediately without animation.
  • :Resize(w, h, imm) / :ResizeWithSpeed(w, h, sw, sh) resize.
  • :SetThickness(t, imm) border thickness.
  • :SetOuterColor(c) / :SetInnerColor(c) / :SetOuterAlpha(a) / :SetInnerAlpha(a).
  • :SetVisible(v) / :SetLayer(layer).
  • :Update(dt) smooth-animation driver (static menus can skip).
  • :GetCenter() / :ContainsPoint(x, y) center point / hit-test.
  • :Destroy() idempotent.

docs.title: Label
docs.text:
Text label, thin wrapper over Typers.InstText, auto-routing mixed Chinese/English.

local lbl = GUI.Label.New("Hello ​世界​", {320, 200})
lbl:SetAlign("center")
lbl:SetText("new text")
lbl:SetColor(1, 1, 0)     -- yellow
lbl:SetAlpha(0.5)
lbl:SetWrapWidth(200)     -- auto-wrap (pass nil/0 to disable)
-- scene.clear: lbl:Destroy()
Label interface
  • New(text, pos, layer, size) pos={x,y}; size={boxWidth,_} enables auto-wrap.
  • :SetText(t) / :SetAlign(mode) ("left" / "center" / "right") / :SetColor(r,g,b) / :SetAlpha(a).
  • :SetPosition(x, y) / :SetWrapWidth(w) (auto Rebuild after width change) / :Rebuild().
  • :Inst() get the underlying InstText directly (advanced use, use with care).

Changing auto_wrap / size does not auto-reflow

After changing InstText's auto_wrap and size you must call :Rebuild(), otherwise lines won't reflow. Label.SetWrapWidth already calls it internally; if you change inst.auto_wrap directly you must Rebuild manually.

docs.title: Button
docs.text:
Button, UNDERTALE-style selected state. Keyboard-selected = prefix "> " + yellow; mouse-hover = yellow without prefix (the two states are visually distinct); unselected uses 2-space monospace padding to prevent text jitter.

local btn = GUI.Button.New{
    x = 200, y = 150, text = "FIGHT",
    w = 200, h = 30,            -- mouse hit area
    onSelect = function() end,
}
btn:SetSelected(true)          -- keyboard-selected
btn:SetHovered(true)            -- mouse-hover
if (confirm) then btn:Trigger() end
Button interface
  • New{x, y, w, h, text, selected, onSelect, layer, prefix, pad, colorNormal, colorSelected}.
  • :SetSelected(v) / :SetHovered(v) / :SetText(t) / :SetPosition(x, y) / :SetOnSelect(fn).
  • :ContainsPoint(x, y) hit-test.
  • :Trigger() trigger the onSelect callback.
  • Color logic: selected or hovered → colorSelected (yellow), otherwise colorNormal (white).

docs.title: Slider
docs.text:
Horizontal slider: track + knob, two rectangles. Pure component that does not read input; the scene drives it via :Move / :SetValue / :DragTo / :Wheel.

local s = GUI.Slider.New{
    x = 200, y = 300, w = 240,
    min = 0, max = 100, value = 50, step = 1,
    focused = true,             -- knob turns yellow
}
-- keyboard: :Move(1) / :Move(-1)
-- mouse: :DragTo(mx, my) drag / :Wheel(dir) wheel / :ContainsPoint hit-test
local v = s:GetValue()
Slider interface
  • New{x, y, w, min, max, value, step, trackH, knobSize, trackColor, knobColor, focusedColor, focused, showLabel, layer}.
  • :Move(dir) +1 / -1 step; :SetValue(v) / :SetRange(min, max) / :GetValue().
  • :DragTo(cx, cy) canvas-space x → value (call while dragging).
  • :Wheel(dir) wheel (same as :Move).
  • :SetFocused(v) knob highlight.
  • :ContainsPoint(x, y) hit-test (with 4px margin).
  • step grid-snapping prevents float drift from continuous Move.

docs.title: TextInput
docs.text:
Single-line text input box: window-style thin border + text + blinking cursor. Focus opens system text input (love.keyboard.setTextInput) so the OS emits character events; the scene routes textinput / keypressed into it.

local ti = GUI.TextInput.New{
    x = 200, y = 100, w = 240, h = 32,
    placeholder = "Name", maxLen = 16,
    onSubmit = function(self) print(self:GetText()) end,
}
-- scene routing:
--   scene.textinput(t)  -> ti:HandleTextInput(t)
--   scene.keypressed(k) -> ti:HandleKeyPressed(k)
--   scene.update(dt)    -> ti:Update(dt)        -- cursor blink
-- click to focus: if (ti:ContainsPoint(mx,my)) then ti:Focus() else ti:Blur() end
TextInput interface
  • New{x, y, w, h, thickness, placeholder, maxLen, layer, onSubmit}.
  • :Focus() / :Blur() / :SetFocused(v) — toggle system text input + setKeyRepeat (backspace long-press repeat).
  • :HandleTextInput(text) append character (filters newlines, truncates by maxLen).
  • :HandleKeyPressed(key) returns whether consumed: backspace deletes one UTF-8 codepoint, escape blurs, return / kpenter triggers onSubmit; other keys return false (not consumed, keyboard navigation works as usual).
  • :SetText(t) / :GetText() / :ContainsPoint(x, y) / :Update(dt) / :SetPosition(x, y).

maxLen counts characters, not bytes

maxLen counts UTF-8 codepoints, so one CJK character counts as 1. Backspace also deletes one codepoint (not one byte).

docs.title: Dropdown
docs.text:
Dropdown box: a trigger button shows the current selection; clicking expands the option list. w is the menu width, buttonW (optional, defaults to w) is the trigger button width. expand="up"|"down" specifies the expand direction.

local dd = GUI.Dropdown.New{
    x = 200, y = 200, w = 180,
    buttonW = 180,            -- optional, default = w
    buttonH = 24, itemH = 24,
    items = {"Red", "Green", "Blue"},
    selected = 1,
    expand = "down",          -- "up" | "down"
    layer = 1001,
    onSelect = function(self, idx, text) print(idx, text) end,
}
-- scene routing (scene.update, after GUI.Input.Update()):
local mx, my = GUI.Input.GetCanvasMouse()
dd:SetHover(mx, my)
if (GUI.Input.IsPressed(1)) then
    local consumed = dd:HandleClick(mx, my)  -- click trigger button = expand/collapse; click option = select+collapse; click outside = collapse but not consumed
end
Dropdown interface
  • New{x, y, w, buttonW, buttonH, itemH, thickness, gap, expand, items, selected, layer, onSelect}.
  • :SetHover(mx, my) call every frame, updates hover highlight.
  • :HandleClick(mx, my) call on click, returns whether consumed.
  • :SetExpanded(v) / :IsExpanded() / :GetSelected() / :GetSelectedText() / :SetItems(items) / :SetPosition(x, y) / :SetOnSelect(fn) / :ContainsAny(mx, my).
  • Selected item = yellow + prefix "> "; hovered item = yellow without prefix; others = white (consistent with Button).
  • Trigger button border turns yellow on hover / expand; menu border stays white.
  • Menu is left-aligned to the trigger button; option row positions fixed at New, expanding only toggles alpha=0/1.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Same-layer occlusion: background cannot share a layer with text
