Layers within the same layer are ordered by _id (registration order); later registration draws later (visually on top). If a component's background (the black inner layer of drawWindow) and a text Label share a layer, and the background is registered later, the black fill will cover the text.

Fix: inside the component put the background on layer and the text on layer+1 (cursor on layer+2). TextInput and Dropdown both do this.

Closure-referenced local must be declared first

If a component's onSubmit / onSelect callback closure references a local variable (e.g. feedback_timer), and that local is declared after the closure, the closure will write to the global instead of that local (Lua does not hoist locals).

-- wrong: the onSubmit closure writes the global feedback_timer, not the local below
local ti = GUI.TextInput.New{ onSubmit = function() feedback_timer = 120 end }
local feedback_timer = 0

-- right: local declared before the closure
local feedback_timer = 0
local ti = GUI.TextInput.New{ onSubmit = function() feedback_timer = 120 end }

luac -p won't catch this (it's a runtime scope issue, not a syntax error).

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Typers Typewriter — the underlying text of Label / Button etc. (InstText, bondfont, character routing).
  • Layer System — add_external / remove_external / clear.
  • Input and Controller — keyboard / gamepad input; GUI's mouse part uses GUI.Input (see above).

docs.title: Battle System
docs.text:
It wouldn't be an exaggeration to call this SoulEngine's most complex module. Here you'll see...

Battle UI Player PlayerAttacks Game Wave Animation — all these libraries working together.

These modules are not standalone libraries, but rather tightly-coupled responsibility layers within the battle system. They cooperate closely through battle state and turn flow. They're separated only to make each part easier to locate and modify, not so they can run independently.

The Game area concept and resource lookup order that recur throughout this topic are explained in one place: Basic Development → Game Area & Resource Override.

First, the flow: 

Enter battle
  ↓
Game provides encounter data
  ↓
Wave initializes the wave
  ↓
UI enters battle state (stateinner)
  ↓
Player receives input → PlayerAttacks resolves
  ↓
Animation plays visuals
  ↓
Wave advances the turn
  ↓
UI updates state / checks for end
  ↓
(loop back to Player or exit)

docs.title: Game
docs.text:
Responsible for customizing encounter data and enemies.

Encounter path: Game/Encounter/.

Game area path: Game/ (the root directory containing Animations, Encounter, Waves, Souls, etc.).

docs.title: Monster Animation
docs.text:
Responsible for playing enemy animations.

Path: Game/Animations/.

docs.title: UI
docs.text:
Path: Scripts/Libraries/Battle/UI/.

All other visible content on screen is directed through the UI library; the most representative is the stateinner.lua library, which handles everything from entering battle at the start, through various options, enemy turns, and ending the game.

Details beyond stateinner will be covered later in UI.

docs.title: Player
docs.text:
Path: Scripts/Libraries/Battle/Player/.

Player's standalone soul path: Game/Souls/ (Game area, takes priority), Scripts/Libraries/Battle/Player/Souls/ (engine default, fallback).

Player attack path: Game/Attacks/ (Game area, takes priority), Scripts/Libraries/Battle/PlayerAttacks/ (engine default, fallback).

docs.title: Turns
docs.text:
Responsible for enemy turns.

Path: Game/Waves/ (Game area, takes priority), Scripts/Waves/ (engine default, fallback).

Following the engine's convention of "Game first, main directory as fallback": it first looks for a same-named wave in Game/Waves/; if found, it's used directly. Only if not found does it fall back to Scripts/Waves/, and a warning is printed to the console.

Bullet library path: Scripts/Libraries/Attacks/.

docs.title: Battle Scene
docs.text:
The contents of the battle scene changed within the past week: instead of certain scenes having their own layers, they are now placed under init.lua by default.

Below is the code that initializes all layers. This is not mandatory — you may adjust the layers as you see fit:

Layers.new_layer("BOTTOM", -1000)
Layers.new_layer("Background", -10)
Layers.new_layer("UI", 0)
Layers.new_layer("ArenasExtraW", 10)
Layers.new_layer("ArenasExtraB", 10.01)
Layers.new_layer("UponArena", 11)
Layers.new_layer("BelowPlayer", 12)
Layers.new_layer("Player", 13)
Layers.new_layer("BelowBullets", 25)
Layers.new_layer("Bullets", 30)
Layers.new_layer("ArenasCoverW", 50)
Layers.new_layer("ArenasCoverB", 50.01)
Layers.new_layer("TopAll", 60)
Layers.new_layer("TOP", 1000)

docs.title: Encounter File
docs.text:
Note: This file involves a lot of localization. See the Localization topic for details.

Strictly speaking, calling this part an Encounter would be more accurate. The main purpose of this file is to initialize the battle scene first, turning the standardized battle scene into a customized version.

It is responsible for defining: player data (when entering battle), enemy data (count, HP, actions, etc.), the item inventory, and some other miscellaneous things. Below is a standard template; it is collapsed by default because it is very long:

Standard Game Template 
local encounter = {
    narration = Localize.localizeText("Battle.Narration.Default"),
    can_flee = true,
    flee_percent = 0.75,
    enemy_id = 1,
    enemies = {
        {
            id = "Poseur",
            name = Localize.localizeText("Battle.EnemiesName.Poseur"),
            animation = require("Game.Animations.Poseur"),

            maxdamage = 400,
            dmg_float = 2,  -- Some random stuff......I hate them

            show_hpbar = true, -- Sans... stop hiding your hp bar.
            maxhp = 100,
            hp = 100,
            gold = 1,
            exp = 1,

            defensetext = "MISS",
            misstext = "MISS",

            canspare = true,
            killable = true,

            position = {320, 140},
            actions = {
                {id = "Check", name = Localize.localizeText("Battle.Actions.Names.Check")},
                {id = "Pose",  name = Localize.localizeText("Battle.Actions.Names.Pose")},
            }
        },
    },

    state = "DEFENDING",
    wave = "bones.wave1",

    player = {
        name = "end",
        lv = 20,
        maxhp = 99,
        hp = 99
    },

    items = {
        {id = "CHOCOLATE", _color = {0.4, 1, 1}, name = "Chocolate"},
        {id = "END", _color = {0.4, 0, 1}, name = "END", _cantdestroy = true},
    }
}

-- Assign internal _id to each statically-defined enemy
for i = 1, #encounter.enemies
do
    local e = encounter.enemies[i]
    e._id = encounter.enemy_id
    encounter.enemy_id = encounter.enemy_id + 1
end

-- The following methods are now provided by Battle.game_apis via metatable:
--   encounter:AddEnemy(data)  — adds a validated enemy with auto-assigned _id
--   encounter:AddItem(item)    — adds a validated item
--   encounter:ForceAttack(id)   — makes the enemy whose string `id` matches
--                                 enter one attack cycle (Battle.attack.Restart)

return encounter

The game body is defined through an encounter table. Below are the properties and methods that the encounter table provides:

Encounter Table Properties

  • narration The narration text printed in the battle box during the player's turn. Here it uses Localize to fetch the text, but you can write Chinese or English directly — both display fine.
  • can_flee Whether to show the Flee option in the Mercy button. Can be disabled in some boss fights.
  • flee_percent The flee probability. Has no effect if can_flee is off.
  • enemy_id Incremented when a new enemy is added, used to give each enemy a new unique id.
  • state The state when first entering battle. This is explained later; it is recommended to pick ACTIONSELECT (player turn) or DEFENDING (go straight to the enemy turn, i.e. an opening kill).
  • wave The turn script when first entering battle, can be used together with the DEFENDING state. See the Turn Script section below for load order.
  • enemies The enemy table, storing the data for all enemies.
    • id The detection id used internally. Usually English; any string works as long as there is no conflict, since this part is not translated.
    • name This is the name that actually gets displayed and will be localized.
    • animation Which animation this enemy uses.
    • maxdamage The maximum damage that can be dealt to the enemy. If later integrated with Overworld, the max damage can be computed by a formula.
    • dmg_float The dealt damage gets a random + 0 ~ dmg_float added on top of the current damage. Default is 2.
    • show_hpbar Whether to show the HP bar. In the original UNDERTALE there is one monster with a special case: Sans does not show an HP bar even while attacking.
    • maxhp The enemy's maximum HP.
    • hp The enemy's current HP.
    • gold The gold the enemy carries, obtained after killing or sparing it.
    • exp The experience the enemy carries, obtained only after killing it.
    • defensetext The text shown when you hit the enemy but deal no damage.
    • misstext The text shown when you miss the input window and fail to hit the enemy.
    • canspare Whether the enemy can be spared (will automatically turn yellow-named).
    • killable Whether the enemy can be killed. If false, the enemy will not die even when its HP bar is empty — useful for extra execution animations.
    • position Where the enemy stands. This is not the enemy's own animation, but rather the coordinate used for the hit reaction animation, i.e. where the player will slash toward.
    • actions The action table, describing what behaviors can be performed on the enemy.
      • id The action id, also not localized.
      • name The action's name, also what is actually displayed on screen.
  • player Player data.
    • name The player's name.
    • lv The player's level.
    • maxhp The player's maximum HP.
    • hp The player's current HP.
  • items The inventory.
    • id Each item's detection id, not localized.
    • name Each item's actually displayed name.
    • _cantdestroy (optional) If true, the item is not consumed when used.

Besides the properties above, the encounter table also has a batch of methods mounted via a metatable (from Scripts/Libraries/Battle/game_apis.lua), which you can call directly using colon syntax:

Encounter Table Methods

  • AddEnemy(data) Adds an enemy. Auto-fills missing fields and assigns a unique _id, returning the completed enemy table.
    • data The enemy data table, with fields identical to those listed under enemies above.
  • AddItem(item) Adds an item. Auto-validates the item format and returns the completed item table.
    • item The item data table.
      • id The item's detection id, not localized. If missing or invalid, replaced with STONE.
      • name The item's actually displayed name. If missing or invalid, replaced with Stone.
      • _color (optional) The item's color, composed of three numbers 0 ~ 1.
      • _cantdestroy (optional) If true, the item is not consumed when used.
  • InitAnimation(index, pos) Initializes the animation of the index-th enemy and returns the animation instance.
    • index The enemy's ordinal in the enemies table.
    • pos The animation's position.
    • Return value: the enemy's animation instance. All subsequent operations are performed on it (anim.SetFace(3)); repeated calls do not rebuild it — they return the same instance as-is.
  • ForceAttack(id) Makes the specified enemy enter one attack resolution cycle (internally calls Battle.attack.Restart).
    • id The enemy's string id (the same style as enemy_id, not the _id number).
    • Note: it only looks up by id; if not found, it simply prints [Battle - forceAttack] WARNING: No enemy found with id = ... and does nothing; moreover, this warning is printed even on success, so don't be fooled by it — judge by whether the enemy actually moved.

Difference Between Properties and Methods

Properties are data, written statically in the table; methods are operations used to append to or modify the data in the table. The difference is: properties are read with a dot (encounter.wave), while methods are called with a colon (encounter:AddEnemy(...)). A field is a method when it is defined as a function, so the table above looks a lot like the property table but is called differently.

A Warning Is Not an Error

When AddItem and AddEnemy find invalid data, they do not halt the game. Instead they print a warning and replace it with a default value:

[Battle - Items] WARNING: Invalid item id.
[Battle - Enemy] WARNING: Invalid enemy id, using default.

The purpose of this is to guarantee the battle always runs, but the replaced field won't tell you which enemy caused the problem, so when you see a warning, go back and check the encounter file yourself.

docs.title: Turn Script
docs.text:
wave holds the name of a turn script (without the .lua extension), e.g. bones.wave1. This name is handed to Battle.LoadWave to resolve. The search order is:

  1. Game/Waves/<name>.lua — the Game area, priority.
  2. Scripts/Waves/<name>.lua — engine default, fallback.

If neither location is found, or the Game-area copy exists but errors while loading, the engine prints a warning and automatically falls back to the default wave script, ensuring the battle won't freeze over a single wave file.

Terminal Output on Fallback

When not found:

[Battle - Wave] WARNING: wave 'bones.wave1' not found. Searched, in order:
    Game.Waves.bones.wave1  (Game/Waves/bones/wave1.lua)
    Scripts.Waves.bones.wave1  (Scripts/Waves/bones/wave1.lua)
[Battle - Wave] Falling back to the default wave (Scripts.Waves.wave).

When the Game-area copy is broken (Note: it still falls back successfully, but it will definitely tell you the override has a problem — it is not silent):

[Battle] WARNING: 'Game.Waves.bones.wave1' exists but failed to load; using Scripts.Waves.bones.wave1 instead.
[Battle]   <the actual error message>

Therefore, whenever you see exists but failed to load, it means your override did not take effect — go fix that file; don't suspect the engine didn't read it.

Available methods:

Turn Script Methods

  • Battle.LoadWave(wave_name) Loads a turn script and returns the finally selected wave table.
    • wave_name The turn script name. Uses the default wave when left empty or nil.
  • Battle.waveModule The full module name that actually loaded successfully last time, e.g. Game.Waves.bones.wave1. Can be used to confirm whether the override took effect.
  • Battle.ClearWaveModule(wave_name) Clears the turn script's cache.
    • wave_name The turn script name. Uses the current Battle.wave when left empty.

Why Clear Cache in Both Locations

ClearWaveModule clears the same-name cache in both the Game area and the engine directory at once. This way, when a script has been moved between the two locations (from Scripts/Waves/ to Game/Waves/), no leftover old version remains.

docs.title: Enemy Animation
docs.text:
Starting with 3.0.0, animations are bound to the encounter file; any operations done to them during battle are received by dedicated functions.

Animation does not use a metatable: New(pos) returns a plain table that uses _class to point back to the module itself. All functions are declared with a dot, and their first parameter is the instance self. Before New returns, it calls Battle.BindAnimation(self, this module), binding these functions onto the instance itself, so external dispatch is written with a dot and does not pass self:

anim.SetFace(3)        -- instead of cls.SetFace(anim, 3)
anim.Update(dt)
anim.cpos[1] = 100     -- position is just a plain field on the instance, read/write directly

Writing it with a colon (anim:Update(dt)) would pass the instance one extra time and the engine would error on the spot. (Sprites are still engine objects, so keep the colon syntax sprite:Set(...)).

Here is a standard animation template:

Animation Template 
local MyMonster = {}

function MyMonster.New(pos)
    local self = {}

    -- The instance uses `_class` to point back to this module
    self._class = MyMonster

    self.running = true
    self.x = 0
    self.y = 0
    self.elements = {}
    self.hurting = false
    self.hurttime = 0
    self.intensity = 16
    MyMonster.Init(self, pos)

    -- Required: bind this module's functions to the instance, so callers can write `anim.Hurt()`
    Battle.BindAnimation(self, MyMonster)

    return self
end

function MyMonster.Init(self, pos)
    local _pos = (pos or {320, 140})
    local sprite = Sprites.CreateSprite("poseur.png", "UI")
    sprite:MoveTo(_pos[1], _pos[2])

    self.sprite = sprite
    self.cpos = {sprite.x, sprite.y}
end

function MyMonster.Hurt(self)
    self.hurting = true
    self.intensity = 16
end

--- OPTIONAL: called the moment an attack is LAUNCHED at this enemy, before the
--- hit lands. Implement it to react (brace / dodge / telegraph / counter, ...).
--- `data` may contain:
---   data.enemy    → this enemy table
---   data.damage   → planned damage for the hit
---   data.perfect  → true when the timing landed in the perfect zone
---   data.offset   → distance from the perfect zone (0 = perfect)
---   data.position → {x, y} of the enemy on screen
---   data.attack   → the attack pattern instance
function MyMonster.OnAttack(self, data)
end

function MyMonster.Spare(self)
end

function MyMonster.Update(self, dt)
    if (not self.running) then
        return
    end

    -- ====================>
    -- TODO: put your monster's animation code here.
    --
    -- Example: react to engine-provided state
    --   if (self.canspare) then ... end            -- spareable?
    --   if (self.dead) then                        -- HP hit 0 and killable
    --       self.sprite:SetAnimation({"death_0.png", "death_1.png"}, 0.1)
    --   end

    -- Default hurt shake: knock the sprite sideways, decaying toward 0.
    if (self.hurting) then
        local p = self.sprite
        p.x = self.cpos[1] + self.intensity
        if (self.intensity > 0) then
            self.intensity = self.intensity - 1
            self.intensity = -self.intensity
        elseif (self.intensity < 0) then
            self.intensity = -self.intensity
        end
    end
    -- <====================
end

function MyMonster.Destroy(self)
    if (not self.sprite) then
        return
    end

    -- TODO: play a death effect here, e.g. sprite:Dust(true, true)
    self.sprite:Dust(true, true)
    self.sprite = nil

    -- Destroy every extra object registered in `elements`.
    for i = #self.elements, 1, -1
    do
        local e = self.elements[i]
        if (e and e.Destroy) then
            e:Destroy()
        end
    end
    self.elements = {}
end

return MyMonster

Next, all the functions are described. The signatures in parentheses are the internal module signatures — the function bodies rely on these self arguments; when called from outside (the scene, waves, attack patterns), always write anim.Foo(...) without passing self, for example anim.Hurt(), anim.Update(dt), anim.SetFace(3).

Function Methods

  • New(pos) The animation's position, returns an independent plain-table instance.
  • Init(self, pos) Animation initialization, responsible for creating the sprite and variables.
  • Hurt(self) Executed when taking damage (the player's weapon sends a Hurt signal).
  • OnAttack(self, data) Executed when the attack key is pressed during calibration; data stores the calibration result, etc.
  • Spare(self) Executed when spared successfully; can produce effects like the enemy turning black.
  • Destroy(self) Executed once when killed, can be used for effects like turning to dust.
  • Update(self, dt) Executed every frame; the vast majority of animation code is written here.

docs.title: Initializing Animation
docs.text:
The initialization flow is semi-automatic: InitAnimation is a method the engine provides through game_apis, and we only need to call it in the battle scene, once per enemy.

index is which enemy (1-based). If you write too large or a wrong number, it won't error — the terminal just emits a warning.

Terminal Warning

[Game - Animation] WARNING: Enemy #x has no animation.

For pos, since each monster's standing position may differ during battle. When initializing and assigning enemies, you need to use the pos parameter to adjust the position.

Usage Example

local mobs = {"froggit", "whimsum", "migosp"}
local ypos = {
    ["froggit"] = 160
    ["whimsum"] = 80
    ["migosp"]  = 200
}

-- After saving ypos, we can decide what to spawn
for i = 1, 3
do
    -- Randomly pick one of these three monsters
    local name = mobs[math.random(#mobs)]

    Game:AddEnemy(
        {
            id = name,
            name = name,
            animation = require("Game.Animations." .. name),

            maxdamage = 400,
            dmg_float = 2,  -- Some random stuff......I hate them

            show_hpbar = true, -- Sans... stop hiding your hp bar.
            maxhp = 100,
            hp = 100,
            gold = 1,
            exp = 1,

            defensetext = "MISS",
            misstext = "MISS",

            canspare = true,
            killable = true,

            -- Set position
            position = {100 + 150 * (i - 1), ypos[name]},

            actions = {
                {id = "Check", name = Localize.localizeText("Battle.Actions.Names.Check")},
                {id = "Pose",  name = Localize.localizeText("Battle.Actions.Names.Pose")},
            }
        },
    )
end

docs.title: Writing Animation
docs.text:
For the vast majority of fan projects, we can drop the Spare feature, and most of our code will be written in the Update function.

function MyMonster.Update(self, dt)
    if (not self.running) then
        return
    end

    -- ====================>
    -- TODO: put your monster's animation code here.
    --
    -- Example: react to engine-provided state
    --   if (self.canspare) then ... end            -- spareable?
    --   if (self.dead) then                        -- HP hit 0 and killable
    --       self.sprite:SetAnimation({"death_0.png", "death_1.png"}, 0.1)
    --   end

    -- Default hurt shake: knock the sprite sideways, decaying toward 0.
    if (self.hurting) then
        local p = self.sprite
        p.x = self.cpos[1] + self.intensity
        if (self.intensity > 0) then
            self.intensity = self.intensity - 1
            self.intensity = -self.intensity
        elseif (self.intensity < 0) then
            self.intensity = -self.intensity
        end
    end
    -- <====================
end

The comments provide a small example: you can switch animations with canspare, or switch to another set with dead — though those comments won't actually run as-is. Without conditional wrapping, we can write another set of ordinary animation.

If you want a detailed tutorial on how to write good animations, go to Advanced Development → Math Tutorial.

Here is a partial explanation, using Sans as a special example:

Sans Animation 
function Sans.OnAttack(self, data)
    local ty = 220
    Tween.CreateTween(function (v)
        self.cpos[1] = v
    end, "Quad", "Out", 320, ty, 40)
    Tween.CreateTween(function (v)
        self.cpos[1] = v
    end, "Quad", "Out", ty, 320, 35, 80)
end

function Sans.Spare(self)
    -- Spared: sans fades out instead of dying.
    for _, sprite in ipairs(Sans.AllSprites(self)) do
        sprite.alpha = 0.5
    end
end

function Sans.Update(self, dt)
    if (not self.running) then
        return
    end

    if (not self.legs or not self.body or not self.head or not self.cpos) then
        return
    end

    -- A "30 FPS frame tick": every counter ported from the original advances by
    -- this much, so the animation speed is frame-rate independent.
    local step = dt * SOURCE_FPS

    -- ====================>
    -- 1) SWAY / BOUNCE ----------------------------------------------------
    -- bounce 0 = still, 1 = idle 8-shape, 2 = medium bob, 3 = tired bob.
    local xoff, yoff = 0, 0
    local bounce = math.floor(self.bounce or 0)

    if (bounce == 3) then
        -- Large, slow vertical breathing (worn-out sans).
        self.siner = self.siner + step
        yoff = math.sin(self.siner / 18) * 2
    elseif (bounce == 2) then
        -- Medium vertical bob.
        self.siner = self.siner + step
        yoff = math.sin(self.siner / 15) * 4
    elseif (bounce == 1) then
        -- Idle: fast vertical + slow horizontal → a small figure 8.
        self.siner = self.siner + step
        yoff = math.sin(self.siner / 3)
        xoff = math.cos(self.siner / 6)
    else
        -- Still.
        self.siner = 0
    end

    local scale = self.bounce_scale or 1
    xoff = xoff * scale
    yoff = yoff * scale
    self.xoff = xoff
    self.yoff = yoff

    -- 2) HURT SHAKE -------------------------------------------------------
    -- Same decay as the reference: flip the sign every tick while the
    -- magnitude shrinks by one unit per tick (0.5 units per frame at 60 FPS).
    local shake_x = 0
    if (self.hurting) then
        shake_x = self.intensity
        if (self.intensity > 0) then
            self.intensity = -(self.intensity - step)
        else
            self.intensity = -self.intensity
        end

        if (math.abs(self.intensity) <= step) then
            self.intensity = 0
            self.hurting = false
        end
    end

    -- 3) HEAD OFFSETS (attack poses) --------------------------------------
    if (self.head_auto_return) then
        local k = math.min(1, (self.head_return_speed or 6) * dt)
        self.headx = self.headx - self.headx * k
        self.heady = self.heady - self.heady * k
        if (math.abs(self.headx) < 0.05) then self.headx = 0 end
        if (math.abs(self.heady) < 0.05) then self.heady = 0 end
    end

    -- 4) BLUE-EYE AUTO-OFF (only for :FlashBlueEye) -----------------------
    if (self._blueeye_timer) then
        self._blueeye_timer = self._blueeye_timer - dt
        if (self._blueeye_timer <= 0) then
            self._blueeye_timer = nil
            if (self._blueeye_flash) then
                self._blueeye_flash = false
                self.facetype = 0
                self.f_i = 0
            end
        end
    end

    -- 5) TORSO IDLE CYCLE --------------------------------------------------
    -- The original only drew the plain torso while no arm animation was
    -- playing (`movearm == 0`); the same flag pauses this cycle.
    if (math.floor(self.movearm or 0) == 0) then
        self.torso_time = self.torso_time + dt
        if (self.torso_time >= TORSO_INTERVAL) then
            self.torso_time = self.torso_time - TORSO_INTERVAL
            self.torsoframe = (self.torsoframe + 1) % TORSO_FRAMES
            self.body:Set(self.torso_frames[self.torsoframe + 1])
        end
    end

    -- 6) FACE / BLUE EYE / SWEAT ------------------------------------------
    Sans.UpdateFace(self, step)

    -- 7) PLACE EVERY PART --------------------------------------------------
    Sans.ApplyOffsets(self, xoff, yoff, shake_x)

    -- 8) DEATH -------------------------------------------------------------
    -- `self.dead` is set by Battle.Update once HP hit 0 and the enemy is
    -- killable. sans has no death sheet yet, so we just freeze the idle sway
    -- and let Destroy() play the dust effect. Add your own animation here.
    if (self.dead) then
        self.bounce = 0
    end
    -- <====================
end

Since it is too long, we only look at the idle left-right sway animation when bounce = 1:

Idle Animation

self.siner = self.siner + step
yoff = math.sin(self.siner / 3)
xoff = math.cos(self.siner / 6)

It uses trigonometric functions to set up periodic movement; /3 and /6 produce two different speeds, meaning the head and body move along an ∞ trajectory.

docs.title: UI
docs.text: Main body init.lua, state hub stateinner.lua, button system buttons.lua

docs.title: Main Body init
docs.text:
This file is responsible for drawing the contents under the battle box and managing the state hub. In the battle scene, it appears as the global variable UI.

Below are the available methods:

UI Methods

  • UI.SetBarMaxLength(length) Set the maximum length of the HP bar (in pixels).
  • UI.SetHPBarColor(color) Set the color of the HP bar.
  • UI.SetMaxHPBarColor(color) Set the color of the HP bar's background trough (i.e. the full-background bar behind the HP bar).
  • UI.ToggleKR(bool) Whether to enable KR. No animation; write your own if needed.
  • UI.GetKRStarted() Get whether KR has already been enabled.
  • UI.newBounceText(text, pos, color) Used in the attack animation; after the attack animation finishes playing, it generates a damage-number text (or MISS text). See Attack Resolution for details.
    • text The text to print. Cannot be Chinese.
    • pos Where the bounce starts.
    • color The color of the bouncing text. Default red {1, 0, 0}.
  • UI.newMissText(text, pos, color) Generates new static text, commonly seen when the player is at the calibration screen but misses the attack by not pressing the attack key.
    • text The text to print. Cannot be Chinese.
    • pos Where the bounce starts.
    • color The text color. Default white {1, 1, 1}, with a built-in black outline.
  • UI.newMonsterBar(pos, start, target) Generates a tweened monster HP bar on the enemy (used during attack resolution).
    • pos The enemy's position; the bar is drawn at its lower-left.
    • start The starting fill ratio (1 is full).
    • target The target fill ratio, which tweens from start to target over 30 frames.
  • UI.SetTextPosition(x, y) Modify the coordinates of the whole line of text starting with the name.
  • UI.GetTextPosition() Return the coordinates of the whole line of text starting with the name.
  • UI.MoveTextPosition(dx, dy) Move the text at a speed of (dx, dy).
  • UI.SetBarPosition(x, y) Modify the coordinates of the HP bar.
  • UI.GetBarPosition() Return the coordinates of the HP bar.
  • UI.MoveBarPosition(dx, dy) Move the HP bar at a speed of (dx, dy).
  • UI.MovePosition(dx, dy) Execute both the Text and Bar move functions at once.
  • UI.SetHPNameLimit(x) Modify the minimum x-coordinate of the HP label to x. Default is 245.
  • UI.GetLayout() Get the entire layout. If you want to systematically modify the layout, this function is recommended.
  • UI.GetHPBar() Return the HP bar representing the current HP.
  • UI.GetMaxHPBar() Return the HP bar representing the maximum HP.
  • UI.GetKRBar() Return the HP bar representing KR.
  • UI.GetBars() Return the three HP bars above.

The state hub and UI are called within the main body, appearing respectively via these variables:

UI.state & UI.buttons

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text:
Responsible only for the logic of the four buttons: Fight, Act, Item, and Mercy. Below are the button methods; when calling them you need to write UI.buttons.xxx():

Button Methods

  • buttons.GetButtons() Get the four buttons (in order).
  • buttons.ResetButtons() Return all buttons to their idle state.
  • buttons.ResetAllState() Return all buttons to their idle state and place the player at the first button.
  • buttons.RemoveButton(id) Remove the id-th button; this button will give no response.
  • buttons.SetLogic(logic) The button switching logic table; its contents are start, end, operation.
  • buttons.SetSprites(sprs) Set the four buttons' images at once; explained in detail below.
  • buttons.SetAnimations(anims) Set the four buttons' images at once; explained in detail below.

docs.title: Switching Images
docs.text:
This is the original button table, laid out in order by button. The first item in each table is the idle image, and the second is the selected image.

sprites = {
    {
        "UI/Battle Screen/spr_fightbt_0.png",
        "UI/Battle Screen/spr_fightbt_1.png"
    },
    {
        "UI/Battle Screen/spr_actbt_center_0.png",
        "UI/Battle Screen/spr_actbt_center_1.png"
    },
    {
        "UI/Battle Screen/spr_itembt_0.png",
        "UI/Battle Screen/spr_itembt_1.png"
    },
    {
        "UI/Battle Screen/spr_sparebt_0.png",
        "UI/Battle Screen/spr_sparebt_1.png"
    }
}

docs.title: Switching Animation
docs.text:
Unlike images, this time we use multiple groups of data, i.e. adding one more layer on top of the table above:

buttons.animations = (anims or {
    idle = {
        {{
            "poseur.png",
            "bullet.png"
        }, 0.1}
    },
    selecting = {
        {{
            "heart.png",
            "Overworld/spr_exc.png"
        }, 0.1}
    }
})

Since what is actually being called is the sprite's SetAnimation operation, you need to pass two values: one is the image group and one is the interval.

docs.title: State Hub
docs.text:
Preliminary Note

Normally this file does not need to be modified, because the underlying supported logic is stable and unchanging. After understanding the state flow, you may move on to the next page.

docs.title: State Flow
docs.text:
The battle system has the following states to determine which UI phase the player is in:

  • ACTIONSELECT The initial state of the player's turn (selecting buttons left/right).
  • FIGHTMENU The first page of the Fight button.
  • ACTMENU The first page of the Act button.
  • ITEMMENU The first page of the Item button.
  • MERCYMENU The first page of the Mercy button.
  • ATTACKING The second page of the Fight button; after selecting FIGHTMENU, pressing confirm again enters the attack calibration screen.
  • ACTIONMENU The second page of the Act button; after selecting ACTMENU, confirm to choose an action.
  • DEFENDING The enemy's turn.
  • DIALOGUERESULT After selecting an Act or Item, the state enters here to wait for narration text. Note the spelling is DIALOGUE, not DIALOG.
  • TRYINGFLEE Executed the instant Flee is pressed.
  • FLEEING Executed continuously after a successful Flee press, until the battle ends; can also be pulled back to the DEFENDING state by other means.
  • WIN Battle won. Plays victory text, hides the Soul, and after the text finishes, fades out and switches to the result scene.

docs.title: Battle Box
docs.text:
The battle box (Arena) is that white frame the player's Soul gets locked inside. In the engine it is an independent, freely modifiable rectangular/elliptical region — not a sprite. Scaling, rotating, punching holes, and moving are all driven by numbers.

Path: Scripts/Libraries/Battle/Arenas.lua. It appears in the battle scene as the global variable Arenas; the main battle box is fixed on Battle.mainarena.

docs.title: Two Modes
docs.text:
mode determines whether this box is a "place you can stand" or a "place you cannot stand":

Mode Meaning Effect plus Plus zone The player is locked inside; hitting an edge gets pushed back minus Minus zone The player is blocked outside; walking in gets ejected to the nearest valid position

The two can be stacked: a large plus box provides the activity area, then stack a few small minus boxes to punch holes in the middle — producing the original-game kind of battlefield with "pillars inside the box".

The Main Battle Box Is plus by Default

On entering battle, Battle.mainarena is a plus rectangle; during the player's turn its size is 565x130 (the battle box itself), and on entering the enemy's turn it automatically shrinks to 155x130 (the bullet box). These two sizes are switched by Battle itself, so normally you don't need to change them manually.

docs.title: Creating a Box
docs.text:
Arena Methods

  • Arenas.New(mode, shape, x, y, width, height, angle) Create a new battle box, returns the box object.
    • mode "plus" or "minus", default "plus".
    • shape The shape; currently only "rectangle" is recommended; "circle" / "ellipse" work in some collision checks, but will not generate a display sprite.
    • x / y Center coordinates, default 320, 320.
    • width / height Width and height, default 155, 130; values below 16 are forced up to 16.
    • angle Rotation angle (degrees), default 0.
  • Arenas.Clear() Destroys all boxes except the main battle box.
  • Arenas.PlayerOnGround(player) Whether the player's "feet" touched the box edge (judged along the gravity direction; works for all four orientations).
  • Arenas.PlayerOnCeiling(player) Whether the player's "head" touched the box edge.
  • Arenas.insts The current instance list of all boxes.
  • Arenas.stencils The current list of all masks, usable for clipping bullets.

docs.title: Box Properties
docs.text:
The created box object can directly read/write these fields:

Arena Properties

  • mode / shape The mode and shape passed in at creation.
  • x / y / width / height / rotation The current values (smoothly moving toward the target values).
  • target The target value table {x, y, width, height, rotation}; change this to make the box move.
  • speeds The change-speed table {x, y, width, height, rotation}, default 7.5 / 7.5 / 15 / 15 / 15.
  • thickness The white-border thickness, default 5.
  • is_active Whether it participates in collision. When off, the box is still on screen but the player passes right through it.
  • is_containing Whether the player is currently inside this plus box.
  • move_player Whether to carry the player along when the box moves, default true.
  • white / black The two sprites that make up the box (outer white, inner black).
  • mask The box's own mask object (only plus has one).

Change Speed Is Per-Frame, Not Per-Second

The values in speeds are how many pixels to advance per frame; the engine does not multiply by dt during smoothing. That is, the same speeds at 60 FPS and 120 FPS will differ by a factor of two in how fast the box scales. When writing waves, tune by the 60 FPS empirical values, or use ResizeWithTime to control precisely.

docs.title: Changing Shape
docs.text:
All the "change the value" functions write to target; the box smoothly moves there on its own. To apply instantly, find the variant with the imm parameter.

Size and Position

  • Resize(w, h, imm) Change width and height. When imm is true, applies immediately.
  • ResizeWithSpeed(w, h, speedw, speedh) Change width and height and specify the speed.
  • ResizeWithTime(w, h, timew, timeh) Change width and height; the speed is auto-computed from "how many frames to arrive".
  • MoveTo(x, y, imm) Move the center point. When imm is true, applies immediately.
  • RotateTo(rotation) Rotate to the specified angle.
  • ResetSpeed() Restore all speeds to default.

docs.title: Single-Side Stretch
docs.text:
Effects like "the box's top edge pushes out a block" in the original game are done with the four functions below; they automatically correct the center point while stretching, keeping the opposite edge fixed:

Single-Side Methods

  • UpSide(value) Extend the top edge upward by value pixels (negative shrinks).
  • DownSide(value) Extend the bottom edge downward.
  • LeftSide(value) Extend the left edge leftward.
  • RightSide(value) Extend the right edge rightward.
Opening/Closing a Box Top and Bottom 
local Arena = Battle.mainarena

-- When the enemy turn starts: push the box taller by 40 pixels, over about 15 frames
Arena:UpSide(40)
Arena:DownSide(40)

-- After some frames, retract again
Arena:UpSide(-40)
Arena:DownSide(-40)

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Appearance Methods

  • SetThickness(t) Set the white-border thickness.
  • OuterColor(color) Set the outer color, default follows the global variable MainColor.
  • InnerColor(color) Set the inner fill color, default black.

docs.title: Getting Coordinates
docs.text:
When writing bullets you often need "fire from somewhere on the box's top edge"; these two functions save you from hand-computing rotation:

Coordinate Methods

  • GetCenterPos(side) Returns the x, y of the midpoint of an edge. side is "up" / "down" / "left" / "right".
  • GetCornerPos(corner) Returns the x, y of a corner. corner is "ul" / "ur" / "dl" / "dr".

Both functions do rotation compensation — however many degrees the box is rotated, the returned point rotates along with it.

docs.title: Followers
docs.text:
Some things (e.g. decorations hanging on the box edge) need to move with the box; use AddFollower to attach them, and they auto-sync coordinates every frame:

Follower Methods

  • AddFollower(sprite, position) Make a sprite follow the box.
    • sprite The sprite object to follow.
    • position Where to attach; values are the same as the two coordinate functions above ("up", "ul", "left" ...).
  • Destroy() Destroy this box and its two sprites.

docs.title: Mask
docs.text:
If bullets are drawn directly, the parts outside the box also show up. The original game relied on a mask to clip the outside-of-box parts:

local wave = ImportFile("Battle.Waves")
local Arena = Battle.mainarena

-- Create a mask that follows the battle box
local mask = Masks.New("rectangle", 320, 320, 155, 130, 0, 0)

-- Make it follow the box every frame (mask syncs when the box scales/moves)
function wave.Update(dt)
    mask:Follow(Arena.black)
end

-- Apply the mask to bullets
bullet:SetStencils({mask})

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
• The box scaled but the bullets didn't get clipped along — you forgot to call mask:Follow(Arena.black) every frame.
  • The player gets ejected to a weird place — after being pushed out by a minus box, if the landing spot is also invalid, the engine searches outward in rings for the nearest valid point; if none is found it stays put. This happens when you place minus boxes too tightly.
  • The box snaps into place instantly — check whether you mistakenly passed imm = true, or gave speeds too large a value.

docs.title: Player and Soul
docs.text:
This page covers two things: the Player itself (HP, taking damage, KR), and the Soul (which decides how the player moves).

Path: Scripts/Libraries/Battle/Player/. It appears in the battle scene as the global variable Player.

docs.title: Player
docs.text:
Player holds the player's battle data and also owns the Soul's sprite.

Player Properties

  • name The player's name.
  • lv Level.
  • maxhp / hp Maximum HP / current HP.
  • kr The current KR (karma, i.e. the purple damage that keeps draining HP over time) value.
  • canMove Whether the player can control the Soul right now.
  • sprite The Soul's sprite object.
  • action The Soul module itself (see the next section).
  • soul The current Soul's name, e.g. "red", "blue".
  • souls The list of extra Souls created via NewSoul.
  • platforms The one-way platform list (built by Player.BluePlatform). Any Soul can use it — see "One-Way Platforms" at the end of this page.
  • platform_ground Whether the player is currently standing on a one-way platform.
  • hurt_time Remaining time of the invincibility frames after taking damage.

Player Methods

  • Player.SetSoul(id, args, use_sound) Switch Soul.
    • id The Soul's name, or numeric shortcut: 1 = "red", 2 = "orange", 6 = "blue".
    • args Extra parameters passed to the Soul's Init.
    • use_sound When true, plays snd_ding.wav.
  • Player.NewSoul(id, args, use_sound) Create an extra independent Soul (its own sprite, its own state), commonly used for effects like twin Souls.
    • args Also passed to Init.
  • Player.SetHitBox(width, height, soul) Set the Soul's collision box, default {4, 4}.
    • soul When omitted, changes the main Soul; when a Soul table is passed, changes that one.
    • Passing 0 or a negative number is silently changed to 1; to "disable collision" you must skip the collision loop yourself.
  • Player.SetPerfectPixel(enabled) Switch the main Soul and every extra Soul in Player.souls to perfect-pixel collision (judged by the sprite's actual pixels rather than the _hitbox rectangle), returns (available, rectangle count).
    • For a 16×16 heart, enabling it makes the hit area larger than the default 4×4 — a feel tradeoff; choose between this and SetHitBox.
  • Player.Heal(amount, use_sound) Heal; won't exceed maxhp.
  • Player.Hurt(amount, time, use_sound) Deduct HP.
    • amount How much to deduct (a negative value heals).
    • time Invincibility-frame duration, default 60; during this time the Soul flickers and no longer collides.
  • Player.AddKR(kramount) Increase KR. Only takes effect when KR is enabled, and won't directly drop HP below 0.
  • Player.AddParticle() Generate a Soul afterimage at the current position.
  • Player.Update(dt) Called by the engine every frame; normally you don't need to call it manually.

HP Reaching Zero Switches Scene Directly

Inside Player.Update it is hardcoded: when hp + kr <= 0, it immediately Scenes.switchTo("scene_gameover"). To make a "locked-HP, can't-die" story battle, manage hp yourself, or clamp the damage inside the OnHit callback.

docs.title: Soul
docs.text:
A Soul is simply a Lua module that must contain at least one Update(dt).

Soul path: Game/Souls/ (Game area, priority), Scripts/Libraries/Battle/Player/Souls/ (engine default, fallback).

Player.action IS the Soul Module Itself

SetSoul does not copy the Soul module; it directly mounts the module table onto Player.action. This means all self.xxx written inside the Soul stay in the module table. The engine re-executes the file every time it loads a Soul, precisely to avoid the previous battle's state leaking into the next — so do not cache things in the Soul that "should only be initialized once"; write every Update as if it's a fresh game.

docs.title: Soul Template
docs.text:
local action = {
    sprite = nil,
    can_move = true,
    is_moving = false,
    -- use_platforms = true,   -- optional: caught by Player.BluePlatform's one-way platforms
}

-- Default vars.
local speed = 2

-- Called once each time we switch to this Soul: bind sprite, color, reset state.
function action.Init(sprite, can_move, args)
    action.sprite = sprite
    if (can_move ~= nil) then
        action.can_move = (can_move ~= false)
    end
    if (sprite) then
        sprite.color = {1, 0, 0}   -- delete this line if you don't want to color it
    end

    speed = 2                       -- your own counter / switch is also reset here
    return action
end

function action.Update(dt)
    if (not action.sprite) then return end
    -- TODO: your movement logic
end

return action

Soul Available Fields

  • sprite The player sprite handed to the Soul by the engine inside Init.
  • can_move Copied in by the engine from Player.canMove at the moment of switching Souls; when false it should not move. Note it is not written back every frame — changing Player.canMove at runtime is the engine clamping movement inside Player.Update itself; you don't need to sync this field.
  • is_moving Maintained by yourself, used to decide whether to play a movement animation.
  • use_platforms Optional field, omitted by default. Only when written as true will it be caught by Player.BluePlatform's one-way platforms; if not written, it passes straight through. See "One-Way Platforms" at the end of this page.

Initialization Is Written Inside the Soul (the Engine No Longer Does It for You)

SetSoul only does three things: resolve the name, call Init(sprite, can_move, args), and record the name into Player.soul. What color the sprite gets, what the starting speed is, which direction it faces — all decided by the Soul itself inside Init. To change these only edit the Soul file; don't touch the engine. Old Souls without Init still run fine: the engine will stuff sprite / can_move in itself and remind you once in the console.

When writing your own Soul, read input uniformly with Controller.GetState("left") and the like, not Keyboard — only gamepads respond.

docs.title: The Four Built-in Souls
docs.text: These four Souls all color their own sprite inside their Init (red {1, 0, 0}, orange {1, 0.5, 0}, blue {0, 0, 1}, yellow {1, 1, 0}); to change the color, edit the Soul file.

docs.title: Red red
docs.text:
The most ordinary eight-directional free movement. Holding cancel halves the speed (the original's "slow walk").

Player.SetSoul(1)   -- or "red"

docs.title: Orange orange
docs.text:
Also eight-directional movement, but can only move along the eight directions (diagonals are also strictly 45°), and leaves a trail of afterimages behind while moving.

Player.SetSoul(2)   -- or "orange"

docs.title: Blue blue
docs.text:
A Soul with gravity; falls downward and can jump. Among the engine's built-in Souls, only it writes use_platforms = true, so only it can stand on one-way platforms by default — other Souls can too if they add this field.

Player.SetSoul(6)   -- or "blue"

Blue Soul Methods

These methods hang on the Soul module, and Player.action is the Soul module itself, so call them all with a dot, without passing self:

Player.action.SlamAuto(0, 1, 10)

Writing Player.action:SlamAuto(...) would error on the spot.

  • Angle(angle) Only rotates the sprite, does not change the gravity direction.
  • AngleDir(direction, angle) Sets both the gravity direction and the sprite angle.
  • AngleAuto(angle) Sets the sprite angle; the gravity direction is auto-derived from the angle (0 = down, 90 = left, 180 = up, 270 = right).
  • Slam(angle, hp, inv) Slam toward the current gravity direction. On landing, calls Player.Hurt with hp / inv.
  • SlamDir(direction, angle, hp, inv) Specify the gravity direction then slam.
  • SlamAuto(angle, hp, inv) Derive the gravity direction from the angle then slam.
  • GetDirection() Returns the current gravity direction.
  • SetDirection(direction) Only changes the gravity direction, leaves the sprite angle alone.
  • GetSpeed() Returns the current vertical speed (positive = falling).
  • SetSpeed(value) Directly change the vertical speed.
  • SetCanJump(value) Lock / unlock jumping.
  • SetJumping(value) Force enter / exit the "jumping" state.
  • Land() Land: zero the speed and restore jumping ability.
  • Reset() Restore all state to default.
  • Init(sprite, can_move, args) Called by the engine when switching to this Soul: colors blue, rotates sprite back to 0, then Reset().
  • Update(dt) Called by the engine every frame.

The hp / inv of the three Slam functions are for "self-damage from slamming": fill them in if you want a "slamming costs you" mechanic; if not, fill 0 or omit.

docs.title: Yellow yellow
docs.text:
Also eight-directional movement, but pressing confirm fires a heart-shaped bullet. The bullet has a bit of gravity, grows as it flies, and disappears off-screen or when it hits another bullet; to catch your own bullet, just add a HitCall function to the target bullet.

Player.SetSoul("yellow")   -- no numeric shortcut, must write the name
  • Firing cooldown is 5 frames; sound is snd_shoot.wav.
  • Bullet image is Soul Library Sprites/spr_heartbullet_1.png.
  • Holding cancel also halves the movement speed.

The Charge Performance Is Hooked Up, but the Big Bullet Itself Isn't Yet

Holding confirm starts charging (total duration 60 frames), with two staged performances:

  1. At 1/3 charged, four small dots spiral inward from the surroundings onto the Soul;
  2. When fully charged, a semi-transparent, pulsing yellow shadow overlays the Soul (the "charge complete" marker, which follows the Soul every frame).

Any release clears the charge to zero, and the two effect layers fade out on their own — so releasing midway leaves no residue.

But releasing won't actually fire a big bullet: that bullet pattern isn't written yet. So this part is currently just a "visible" performance.

To actively clear the residual charge effects on screen (e.g. on wave switch), call:

Player.action.ClearBigshot()

It only clears the effects, not the charge counter. It's already auto-cleared once in Init when switching Souls.

docs.title: One-Way Platforms
docs.text:
A set of platforms that only catch the player from above: the player can jump up through them from below, and won't get mysteriously sucked up when standing beneath them.

The platform itself is Soul-independent; the Player.BluePlatform function name is a historical leftover (it was originally written only for the blue Soul).

Platform Methods

  • Player.BluePlatform(x, y, width, args) Create a platform, returns the platform object.
    • x / y Center coordinates, default 320, 320.
    • width Width (pixels), default 50.
    • args Optional settings table:
      • mode "none" (static) or "move" (auto-moving), default "none".
      • speed {x = n, y = n}, the per-frame displacement when mode is "move".
      • rotation Platform angle, default 0.
      • color Platform color, default {1, 0.3, 1}.
      • layer The layer it sits on, default "BelowBullets".
      • active Whether it participates in collision, default true.
      • surface_offset Extra offset of the collision surface relative to the top edge, default 0.
      • surface_tolerance Half-thickness of the collision band, default 2.
      • line_color / line_alpha The color and alpha of the top highlight line.
  • Player.ClearPlatforms() Destroy all platforms.

Platform Object Methods

  • MoveTo(x, y) Move the platform (the highlight line auto-follows).
  • SetRotation(angle) Set the angle.
  • SetWidth(w) Set the width.
  • Sync() Manually sync the highlight line; normally not needed.
  • Destroy() / Delete() Destroy this platform.
A Platform That Moves Left and Right 
local p = Player.BluePlatform(320, 350, 60, {
    mode  = "move",
    speed = {x = 2, y = 0},
    color = {1, 1, 0.3}
})

-- You can also push it yourself in the wave's Update
function wave.Update(dt)
    p.image.x = 320 + 40 * math.sin(math.rad(Battle.TIME_F))
end

To Be Caught, the Soul Must Write a use_platforms Line Itself

Platforms are opt-in: only a Soul table that writes use_platforms = true gets caught; without it, it passes straight through.

local action = {
    sprite = nil,
    can_move = true,
    use_platforms = true,   -- <- add this line, and Player.BluePlatform will catch it
}
  • Among the engine's built-in Souls, currently only blue has this field — so the default behavior is the same as before: switch to red/orange/yellow and you fall through the platform.
  • The field only falls back to the old check (Player.soul == "blue") when missing, so your own Game/Souls/blue.lua without the field still walks the platform fine; no need to change it.
  • The collision itself (Player.BluePlatformCollide(sprite, vertical speed)) only looks at the sprite and vertical speed, Soul-independent. Souls created via Player.NewSoul are not auto-collided by the engine; if you want its own Update to stand on a platform, call once yourself:
Player.BluePlatformCollide(soul.sprite, soul.GetSpeed())

docs.title: Damage Collision
docs.text:
Collision is not computed by the Soul itself, but uniformly by Player.Update:

  1. During invincibility frames (hurt_time > 0), skip all collision directly.
  2. Otherwise, iterate over all sprites with isBullet, first use Sprites.GetHitbox to get the Soul's hit box (with _hitbox override), and do a rectangular broad-phase check.
  3. After a broad-phase hit, use Sprites.PPCollide(bullet, Player.sprite) for a fine check:
    • Returns true / false and that is authoritative (meaning either the bullet or the Soul has perfect pixel enabled on either side);
    • Returns nil meaning neither side enabled it, falling back to the rectangular conclusion from step 2.
  4. If the final judgment is a hit, call Battle.OnHit(bullet) — this one you write yourself in the scene, see Battle Scene and Callbacks.

To Judge by Real Pixels, Enable Like This

Player.SetPerfectPixel(true)          -- switch main Soul + all extra Souls at once
bullet:SetPPCollision(true)           -- or just let certain bullets use pixel collision
The per-sprite-level switch is sprite:SetPPCollision(enabled) / sprite:IsPPCollision(); details in Sprites → Perfect Pixel Collision.

Bullet Color

The HurtMode field on the bullet object decides whether it counts as damage; common values:

  • "normal" Take damage on contact.
  • "blue" / "cyan" Take damage only while moving; standing still is safe.
  • "orange" Take damage only while standing still; moving is safe.
  • "safe" Completely harmless.

How you write this field into the scene's OnHit is up to you; the engine only hangs it on the sprite and passes it along.

docs.title: Attack Pattern
docs.text:
After pressing the Fight button, picking an enemy, and pressing confirm, the back-and-forth sliding calibration bar that appears in the middle of the screen is the Attack Pattern (PlayerAttack) at work.

It is responsible for three things: drawing the calibration bar, judging the timing of your press, and settling the damage to the enemy.

Path: Game/Attacks/ (Game area, priority), Scripts/Libraries/Battle/PlayerAttacks/ (engine default, fallback).

docs.title: Switching Attack Patterns
docs.text:
The default is stick (a stick, the most basic weapon from the original game). To switch to another weapon (e.g. the Real Knife, the gloves), write your own attack pattern file and switch:

Switching Methods

  • Battle.SetAttackPattern(name) Load and switch the attack pattern by name.
    • name The attack pattern file's name (without .lua).
  • Battle.attack The currently active attack pattern object.
  • Battle.attack_paths The list of already-loaded attack pattern module names; Battle.Clear() clears the cache according to it.

If the specified name can't be found, the engine prints a warning and automatically falls back to stick, ensuring the battle won't freeze:

[Battle - PlayerAttack] WARNING: attack pattern 'real_knife' not found. Searched, in order:
    Game.Attacks.real_knife  (Game/Attacks/real_knife.lua)
    Scripts.Libraries.Battle.PlayerAttacks.real_knife  (Scripts/Libraries/Battle/PlayerAttacks/real_knife.lua)
[Battle - PlayerAttack] Falling back to the default pattern (stick).

docs.title: What an Attack Pattern Must Provide
docs.text:
An attack pattern file is a Lua table; the engine calls the following functions at fixed moments:

Required Interfaces

  • Restart(enemy) Attack starts; the engine passes in the target enemy. Here you create the calibration bar and all sprites.
  • Update(dt) Called every frame; advances the calibration bar, reads the confirm key, settles damage.
  • Destroy() Cleanup: destroy sprites and set _end to true.

Optional Interfaces

  • SetMaxDamage(dmg) Force this attack's damage to a fixed value (skip the formula), used for "always deal full damage" performances.
  • Hurt() Notify the target enemy's animation "you got hit".
  • Attack(data) Notify the target enemy's animation "the attack just launched" (not yet settled); data carries:
    • data.enemy The target enemy table.
    • data.damage The planned damage for this hit.
    • data.perfect Whether it landed in the perfect zone.
    • data.offset Distance from the perfect zone, 0 = perfect.
    • data.position The enemy's on-screen coordinates {x, y}.
    • data.attack The attack pattern object itself.

Fields the Engine Reads

  • _end Whether the attack is finished. The engine only advances to the next enemy turn once it sees this become true.
  • _missed Whether this swing missed.
  • _attacked Whether the confirm key has already been pressed.

docs.title: How the Built-in stick Computes Damage
docs.text:
stick's judgment logic can be copied directly:

  • The calibration bar slides from one side of the screen to the other at a speed of 6 pixels/frame.
  • The distance offset between the cursor and the target marker decides the damage:
    • offset <= 12 → perfect, damage = maxdamage + random(0, dmg_float).
    • Otherwise → damage = max(maxdamage * 0.2, ceil(0.9 * maxdamage * (280 - offset) / 280)).
  • The cursor rushing out of bounds → judged as MISS, no damage added, and a MISS text pops at the enemy position.

When cutting in line with SetMaxDamage(dmg), the formula above is skipped entirely and your given value is used directly; internally it uses a _max flag, which auto-resets after each settlement, so the next swing is unaffected.

Timeline (counted by frames):

Frame What happens Press confirm Stop the cursor, play the slash sound effect and blade flash, call Attack(data) Frame 70 Settle damage: HP bar animation, Hurt(), pop damage number, actually deduct HP Frame 130 Destroy()

The MISS branch is much faster: pop MISS text on frame 1, and it ends on frame 30.

Where the Two Numbers in the Damage Formula Come From

maxdamage and dmg_float are both written in the encounter file, as properties of each enemy itself; see Battle Initialization → Encounter File. The attack pattern only reads them, it doesn't define them.

docs.title: Writing Your Own Attack Pattern
docs.text:
The easiest approach: copy Scripts/Libraries/Battle/PlayerAttacks/stick.lua into Game/Attacks/, rename it, then modify.

Here is a minimal skeleton:

local atk = {_end = false}
local enemy = nil
local attacked = false

function atk.Restart(_enemy)
    atk._end = false
    enemy = _enemy
    attacked = false

    -- Create the calibration bar sprite here
end

function atk.Destroy()
    -- Destroy sprites
    atk._end = true
end

function atk.Update(dt)
    if (not attacked) then
        if (Controller.GetState("confirm") == 1) then
            attacked = true
            -- Compute damage, play sound, notify animation
        end
    else
        -- Play the closing performance, then call atk.Destroy() when done
    end
end

return atk

_end MUST be set to true

The engine polls _end to determine "is this swing finished". Forget to set it, and the battle will permanently freeze on this swing, with no error message.

docs.title: Coordinating with Enemy Animations
docs.text:
The attack pattern should not directly manipulate a particular monster's sprite — it only handles settlement; the visuals go to the animation.

These two notification functions exist for this purpose:

  • Attack(data) Called the instant confirm is pressed; the enemy can dodge, block, or telegraph in OnAttack.
  • Hurt() Called when the damage actually takes effect; the enemy can do the hit-shake in Hurt.

This way the same attack pattern can be applied to any monster without changing the attack pattern to swap enemies.

How the Notification Actually Reaches the Animation

Both functions do only one thing: get the target animation instance from enemy.animation, then call its same-named method.

local anim = enemy.animation
if (type(anim) == "table" and anim._bound and anim.Hurt) then
    anim.Hurt()
end

That is, the monster animation must implement Hurt() / OnAttack(data) itself to react, and at the end of New(pos) it must have called Battle.BindAnimation(self, this module) to get _bound, otherwise this notification is silently skipped (no error). See Battle Initialization → Enemy Animation for how to write the animation side.

docs.title: Turn Script
docs.text:
Everything that happens during the enemy's turn is written in the Turn Script (Wave): how bullets come out, when they come out, and when they finish after coming out.

Path: Game/Waves/ (Game area, priority), Scripts/Waves/ (engine default, fallback). The name resolution rules are in Battle Initialization → Turn Script.

docs.title: What Happens in a Turn
docs.text:
Player's turn ends (press for enemy turn)
  ↓
Battle.Defending()
  ├─ Soul returns to (320, 320)
  ├─ Main battle box activates and shrinks to 155x130
  └─ Battle.LoadWave(...) loads and executes your wave file (top-level code runs only this once)
  ↓
wave.Update(dt) called every frame
  ↓
You call EndWave() inside it
  ↓
Engine destroys wave.objects, clears the imported library cache
  ↓
State returns to ACTIONSELECT, battle box smoothly restores to 565x130

Top-Level Code Runs Only Once

The wave file is required in — top-level code executes only once when loaded. "Things to do every frame" must be written into wave.Update; "initialize once when entering the turn" goes in the top level.

docs.title: File Skeleton
docs.text:
local wave = ImportFile("Battle.Waves")
local EndWave = wave.EndWave
local Arena = Battle.mainarena

-- Let the player move
Player.canMove = true
-- Switch to blue Soul
Player.SetSoul(6)

-- Bullet mask: follows the battle box
local mask = Masks.New("rectangle", 320, 320, 155, 130, 0, 0)

local time = 0
function wave.Update(dt)
    mask:Follow(Arena.black)

    -- TODO: spawn bullets, advance logic

    time = time + 1
    if (time == 300) then
        EndWave()
    end
end

return wave

The first line is fixed: ImportFile("Battle.Waves") gets the table shared by all waves, which the engine uses to wrap up.

docs.title: Wave Available Methods
docs.text:
Wave Methods

  • EndWave() End this turn. Destroys all objects in wave.objects, clears the library cache imported via wave.Import, and sets ENDED to true.
  • Import(path) Import an engine library; on error it only prints, doesn't crash.
    • path The library path, e.g. "Attacks.Bones".
  • objects A table you stuff things into yourself. EndWave auto-destroys everything inside, saving you from writing cleanup by hand.
  • Update(dt) Defined by you, called by the engine every frame.
  • ENDED Whether this turn has ended (the engine reads it).

Global Values Commonly Used in Waves

  • Battle.mainarena The main battle box; change its shape here (see Battle Box).
  • Battle.TIME_F How many frames have passed since the battle started.
  • Battle.TIME_R How many seconds have passed since the battle started.
  • Player.canMove Whether the player can control the Soul; remember to set it back to true at the start.
  • Player.SetSoul(id) Switch Soul.
  • Arenas The battle box library. This is a global (mounted when the battle library loaded).
  • Player / UI Are also globals, directly usable.

The Bullet Library Is NOT a Global

Bones, Blasters are not mounted on the global; using them directly gets nil. Bones is obtained via the wave's own wave.Import("Attacks.Bones"); Blasters needs the battle scene itself to ImportFile("Attacks.Blasters") and mount it as a global (the engine's own scene_battle_init.lua, scene_battle_template.lua do exactly this), so it becomes visible in waves.

Remember to Restore What You Changed

Player.canMove, Player.SetSoul, battle box size, etc. are not automatically restored at the end of the turn. If a wave switches the Soul to blue and the next wave doesn't switch it back, the player stays blue. Get into the habit of explicitly setting them once at the start of every wave.

docs.title: Spawning Bullets
docs.text:
The bullet library must be Imported first, then you manually call its Update — if the wave doesn't write bones.Update(dt), the bones simply won't move.

local wave = ImportFile("Battle.Waves")
local EndWave = wave.EndWave
local Arena = Battle.mainarena

local bones = wave.Import("Attacks.Bones")
local mask  = Masks.New("rectangle", 320, 320, 155, 130, 0, 0)

-- A bone falling from the top edge
local bone = bones.New2D("sans", 40, {320, 180}, 0, {0, 2})
bone:SetStencils({mask})
table.insert(wave.objects, bone)

function wave.Update(dt)
    mask:Follow(Arena.black)
    bones.Update(dt)

    if (Battle.TIME_R > 5) then
        EndWave()
    end
end

return wave

For the complete method list of bones and blasters, see Bullet Library.

docs.title: Making Your Own Bullets
docs.text:
You don't have to use the bullet library. Any sprite with isBullet = true gets included in the player's collision check:

local bullet = Sprites.CreateSprite("bullet.png", "Bullets")
bullet:Scale(2, 2)
bullet:MoveTo(320, 240)
bullet:SetStencils({mask})
bullet.isBullet = true
table.insert(wave.objects, bullet)

Don't Forget to Stuff It Into wave.objects

If you don't, EndWave won't destroy it, and it will stay on screen and still be visible in the next turn.

docs.title: Multi-Phase Waves
docs.text:
To split a turn into several phases of performance, using time as a state machine is the most direct approach:

Three-Phase Wave 
local wave = ImportFile("Battle.Waves")
local EndWave = wave.EndWave
local Arena = Battle.mainarena
local bones = wave.Import("Attacks.Bones")

local time = 0

-- Phase 1: bone rain
local function phase1()
    local b = bones.New2D("sans", 40, {math.random(220, 420), 200}, 0, {0, 3})
    b:SetStencils({Arena.mask and {Arena.mask} or {}})
    table.insert(wave.objects, b)
end

function wave.Update(dt)
    bones.Update(dt)

    if (time < 120 and time % 20 == 0) then
        phase1()
    elseif (time == 180) then
        Arena:Resize(200, 130)       -- Phase 2: box widens
    elseif (time == 300) then
        Arena:RotateTo(15)           -- Phase 3: box rotates
    elseif (time == 480) then
        EndWave()
    end

    time = time + 1
end

return wave

docs.title: Cache and Hot Reload
docs.text:
The wave module may have cache in both locations; Battle.ClearWaveModule clears both at once:

Cache Methods

  • Battle.ClearWaveModule(wave_name) Clear a wave's module cache; leaves the current Battle.wave empty.
  • Battle.waveModule The full module name that actually loaded successfully last time, e.g. Game.Waves.bones.wave1, usable to confirm whether the Game-area override took effect.

The engine auto-clears once at the end of the turn, so during normal play you don't need to worry about it. Only when you changed the wave file while debugging but it didn't take effect do you need to handle it manually.

docs.title: Bullet Library
docs.text:
The bullet library is ready-made parts that encapsulate the original game's bones, walls, and blasters.

Path: Scripts/Libraries/Attacks/. Import in the wave via wave.Import("Attacks.Bones") and the like (see Turn Script for details).

After importing, you must manually call its Update every frame, otherwise the bullets won't move or collide.

docs.title: Bones Bones
docs.text:
local bones = wave.Import("Attacks.Bones")
bones.Update(dt)

docs.title: Regular Bone
docs.text:
Creation Method

  • bones.New2D(whose, length, position, angle, velocity) Create a bone, returns the bone object.
    • whose Whose bone, "sans" or "papyrus", decides the sprite and thickness. A wrong value prints a warning and falls back to "sans".
    • length The bone-body length (pixels).
    • position Center coordinates {x, y}, default {320, 240}.
    • angle Angle (degrees), default 0.
    • velocity Per-frame displacement {x, y}, default {0, 0}.

Bone Properties

  • x / y / rotation / length Position, angle, length; directly modifiable.
  • velocity Per-frame displacement.
  • isBullet Whether it participates in player collision, default true.
  • layer The layer it sits on, default "Bullets".
  • width Bone thickness; sans is 10, papyrus is 13.

Bones and Pixel Snapping

A bone is a composite of three sprites — head / body / tail. If you snap each to whole pixels individually, the seams would jitter. The engine's approach: all three parts are set with pixel_snap = false (see New2D in Bones.lua), then inside bones.Update the shared anchor for all three is rounded only once (Sprites.SnapEdge(ax + dx, half_x), where half_x is the rotation-aware AABB half-width), and from this integer anchor the three coordinates are computed. So you don't need and shouldn't manually change the bone's pixel_snap; to disable snapping globally set Sprites.pixel_snap = false; details in Basic Development → Sprites → Pixel Snapping.

Bone Methods

  • SetLayer(layer) Change layer (a bone is composed of head, body, tail sprites; changing layer must be done wholesale).
  • SetPivot(xp, yp) Set the pivot, values 0 ~ 1.
    • xp Horizontal, 0 and 1 are the two sides of the width, 0.5 is centered.
    • yp Vertical, 0 is the head end, 1 is the tail end, 0.5 is the center of the whole bone.
  • SetStencils(stencils) Apply mask, usually bone:SetStencils({mask}).
  • ToDown(arena) / ToUp(arena) / ToLeft(arena) / ToRight(arena) Stick the bone to one edge of the battle box (handy for "grows out from the edge").
  • SetMode(mode, color) Set the damage mode and color.
    • mode Written into the sprite's HurtMode; values see Player and Soul → Bullet Color.
    • color The bone color; omitted means unchanged.
  • SetColor(color) Only change color; reverts to MainColor when omitted.
  • Destroy() Destroy. This method is idempotent; repeated calls won't error.

docs.title: 3D Bone
docs.text:
Give a set of 3D vertices; the engine projects them to 2D and connects them into bones, suitable for rotating 3D frames.

Creation Method

  • bones.New3D(points, percent, mode) Create a 3D skeleton, returns the skeleton object.
    • points The 3D point list, each point is {x, y, z}. Points with fewer than three components are auto-filled with 0.
    • percent The length ratio of the connecting line to the whole edge, default 0.5.
    • mode Projection method, "orthographic" (orthographic, default) or "perspective" (perspective).

Skeleton Properties

  • x / y / z Center coordinates. Directly assigning moves all vertices together (implemented via metatable internally).
  • points The original 3D point list.
  • bulge The "bulge" coefficient in orthographic mode; 0 is pure orthographic; greater than 0 means closer to the viewer is larger.
  • xscale / yscale The 2D scale after projection, purely visual, doesn't affect 3D data.

Skeleton Methods

  • MoveTo(x, y, z) Move the center to the specified position.
  • Move(x, y, z) Translate by an increment.
  • Rotate(axis, angle) Rotate around the center.
    • axis "x" / "y" / "z".
    • angle Angle (degrees).
  • Link(whose, point_1, point_2, percent_) Connect a 2D bone between two vertices.
    • point_1 / point_2 The vertices' 1-based indices in points.
    • percent_ This bone's length ratio; omitted uses the percent from creation.
  • Scale(sx, sy) Set the 2D scale.
  • SetLayer(layer) Change layer (applies to all linked bones).
A Rotating Cuboid Skeleton 
local bones = wave.Import("Attacks.Bones")

local cube = bones.New3D({
    {-50, -50, -50}, { 50, -50, -50},
    { 50,  50, -50}, {-50,  50, -50},
    {-50, -50,  50}, { 50, -50,  50},
    { 50,  50,  50}, {-50,  50,  50},
}, 0.9, "perspective")

cube:MoveTo(320, 320, 0)

-- 8 vertices, connect 12 edges
cube:Link("sans", 1, 2)
cube:Link("sans", 2, 3)
cube:Link("sans", 3, 4)
cube:Link("sans", 4, 1)
cube:Link("sans", 5, 6)
cube:Link("sans", 6, 7)
cube:Link("sans", 7, 8)
cube:Link("sans", 8, 5)
cube:Link("sans", 1, 5)
cube:Link("sans", 2, 6)
cube:Link("sans", 3, 7)
cube:Link("sans", 4, 8)

function wave.Update(dt)
    cube:Rotate("y", 1)
    cube:Rotate("x", 0.5)
    bones.Update(dt)
end

docs.title: Bone Wall
docs.text:
A whole wall pushed in from an edge, with a warning bar flashing.

Wall Methods

  • bones.Wall(arena, whose, warntime, staytime, length, direction, rotation, interval, animation)
  • bones.WallComplex(arena, whose, warntime, staytime, length, direction, rotation, interval, animation)
    • arena The reference battle box (usually pass Battle.mainarena).
    • whose "Sans" or "Papyrus".
    • warntime How many frames the warning bar flashes.
    • staytime How many frames to stay fully extended.
    • length The wall's length.
    • direction Which side it comes from: "up" / "down" / "left" / "right".
    • rotation Angle (degrees).
    • interval Bone spacing (WallComplex only).
    • animation The easing table, see below.

Wall Object Methods

  • SetStencils(masks) Apply mask to the warning bar and all bones.
  • Destroy() Tear down this wall early.

Wall is a single long-sprite strip sliding in; WallComplex has 20 bones per side extending individually. Both have exactly the same parameters.

The animation table is written like this:

{
    In  = "SineOut",   -- ease-in name
    Out = "BackIn",    -- ease-out name
    It  = 15,          -- frames used for ease-in
    Ot  = 60           -- frames used for ease-out
}

The Easing Name Gets Lowercased

Internally Tween resolves via ("" .. In):lower(), so "SineOut" actually looks up sineout. Just write it as "Sine" + "Out" in two concatenated segments; don't write it like "sineOut".

docs.title: Blasters Blasters
docs.text:
Blasters = ImportFile("Attacks.Blasters")

Blasters Are Driven by the Scene

Blasters is not mounted on the wave; Blasters.Update(dt) must be written in the battle scene's scene.update:

function scene.update(dt)
    Battle.Update(dt)
    Blasters.Update(dt)
end

If written only in the wave's Update, the blasters stop once you leave that turn.

Creation Method

  • Blasters.New(start_pos, final_pos, angles, wait_time, fire_time, gb_sprites, gb_sounds) Create a blaster.
    • start_pos Spawn position {x, y}, default {320, -100}.
    • final_pos Where to move to (the firing position), default {320, 240}.
    • angles {initial angle, final angle}, default {180, 0}.
    • wait_time Frames to move into position, default 40.
    • fire_time Frames the firing lasts, default 20.
    • gb_sprites Sprite folder name (optional).
    • gb_sounds Sound folder name (optional).
  • Blasters.NewTween(pos_tween, angles_tween, move_time, fire_time, gb_sprites, gb_sounds) The tween version, where you can specify easing curves.
    • pos_tween {start coords, end coords, easing name}, default {{320, -100}, {320, 240}, "QuartOut"}.
    • angles_tween {start angle, end angle, easing name}, default {180, 0, "QuartOut"}.
    • move_time Move frames, default 30.

Blaster Methods

  • Beam(angle) Manually fire a beam (relative to the blaster body angle). By default it auto-fires one when wait_time is reached.
  • Destroy() Destroy this blaster and all its beams early.

The engine auto-plays snd_intro.wav (entrance) and snd_fire.wav (firing).

docs.title: Blaster Resource Locations
docs.text:
Sprites and sounds are kept separate; both are Game area priority:

Content Game area Engine directory Sprites Game/Resources/Sprites/Blaster/<folder>/ Resources/Sprites/Blaster/<folder>/ Sounds Game/Resources/Sounds/Blaster/<folder>/ Resources/Sounds/Blaster/<folder>/

The file names inside the folder are fixed and cannot be changed:

  • spr_gasterblaster_0.png ~ spr_gasterblaster_5.png — the 6 frames from entrance to firing
  • beam.png — the beam
  • snd_intro.wav — entrance sound
  • snd_fire.wav — firing sound

Silently Falls Back to Default When Not Found

When the specified folder lacks spr_gasterblaster_0.png, the engine prints a warning and falls back to the Default folder. The sound side has one more layer of compatibility: when not found in the subfolder, it first tries the old flat layout (Blaster/snd_intro.wav), then falls back to Default.

[Attacks - Blasters] WARNING: blaster sprites 'MyBlaster' not found at Blaster/MyBlaster/spr_gasterblaster_0.png, using 'Default' instead.

docs.title: Wrap-Up
docs.text:
Global Cleanup

  • bones.Clear() Destroy all walls and 2D bones.
  • bones.Update(dt) Advance all bones, skeletons, and walls.

bones.Clear() Won't Run Itself

Across the whole library, bones.Clear() only has a definition, no caller — the engine won't call it for you at the end of the turn. Normally it's invisible, because you stuffed the bones into wave.objects, and EndWave() destroys everything in that table one by one (each bone object's own Destroy() also tears down its parts). But if you didn't stuff the bones into wave.objects, or there are long-lived walls, you need to call bones.Clear() at the right time yourself. It only clears this library's own internal list, and won't touch other libraries.

docs.title: Battle Scene and Callbacks
docs.text:
The battle's flow is handled by the engine, the battle's content is handled by the encounter file, and the layer in between — "what exactly happens in this battle" (e.g. how much healing an item gives, what to play on flee) — is written in the battle scene.
