docs.title: JSON Library
docs.text:
The engine ships with two JSON libraries: the low-level dkjson and SafeJson, which wraps around it.

Library Path Purpose dkjson Scripts/Libraries/Utils/dkjson.lua Pure encode/decode, fast, no restrictions, use it for data you wrote yourself and trust SafeJson Scripts/Libraries/Utils/SafeJson.lua Adds three safety checks on top of dkjson, for externally supplied, untrusted JSON

The engine itself uses them:

Location Which What for Scripts/Libraries/Global.lua dkjson Reading/writing the global save global_save.json Scripts/Libraries/Localize.lua dkjson Reading the Localization/*.json translation tables Scripts/Libraries/GamejoltAPI.lua dkjson Parsing network API return values Scripts/Libraries/Controller/VirtualKeyboard.lua SafeJson Player-customized virtual keyboard layout files

Import method

Both libraries live under the Utils subdirectory, so you must include the prefix, writing ImportFile("Utils.dkjson"). ImportFile("dkjson") will fail to find the file.

docs.title: dkjson
docs.text: local json = ImportFile("Utils.dkjson")

docs.title: Decode
docs.text:
local data, pos, err = json.decode(str, startPos, nullValue)
  • str JSON string.
  • startPos which character to start parsing from, defaults to 1. Almost never needs to be passed.
  • nullValue what a JSON null should decode to, defaults to nil.
  • The return value is three values: data, pos, err.
Case Return value Success data = table/number/string/boolean, pos = end position of parse, err = nil Failure data = nil, pos = error position, err = error description (includes line number)

Always check the third return value

local data = json.decode(str) gives data = nil when the JSON is malformed but does not raise an error. It only blows up later when you do data.xxx, and the error site is far from the real cause. Just write it properly:

local data, pos, err = json.decode(text)
if (err) then
    print("JSON parse failed (around character " .. pos .. "): " .. err)
    return
end

docs.title: Encode
docs.text:
local text = json.encode(value, options)
  • value any Lua value, usually a table.
  • options optional table; the two commonly used fields:
Key Effect indent When true, outputs a readable format with indentation and line breaks; if omitted, a single-line compact format keyorder Array of strings, specifies the output order of keys in the object

encode throws on error instead of returning nil

dkjson internally writes error(msg, 2). When it hits values that cannot be encoded — circular references, functions, userdata — json.encode will abort the entire call stack directly. Wrap saves in pcall:

local ok, text = pcall(json.encode, myTable)
if (not ok) then
    print("Encode failed: " .. tostring(text))
    return
end

docs.title: How a table becomes an array or object
docs.text:
JSON cannot tell Lua "arrays" and "dictionaries" apart. dkjson's rule is:

Your table Encoded result Note {1, 2, 3} [1,2,3] Integer keys 1..n contiguous → array {a = 1} {"a":1} Has non-integer keys → object {[1] = "a", [3] = "c"} ["a",null,"c"] A gap still counts as an array, the missing slot is filled with null (not demoted to object) {} {} Empty table is an object {1, 2, x = 3} {"1":1,"2":2,"x":3} Mixed with non-integer keys → object

The rule itself is isarray(tbl) (dkjson.lua line 81): as long as every key is an integer >= 1, it is treated as an array, then it loops from 1 to the maximum key value max, filling nil positions with null.

The only exception: too many holes demotes it to an object

At the end of isarray there is a line:

if max > 10 and max > arraylen and max > n * 2 then
    return false -- don't create an array with too many holes
end

In plain terms: only when the maximum key exceeds 10 AND the actual element count is less than half the max key is it encoded as an object (keys become strings). For example {[1]="a", [50]="b"}: max = 50, n = 2, 50 > 2 * 2, so it demotes to {"1":"a","50":"b"}. But {[1]="a",[3]="c"} stays an array because max = 3 does not exceed 10.

A round trip will deform it

Stored as [1,2,3], read back as {1,2,3}; but a gapped array stored as ["a",null,"c"] reads back as {1 = "a", 3 = "c"} — the middle slot simply does not exist in Lua (nil), so t[2] returns nil; only when it falls into the "too many holes" branch above and becomes an object do the read-back keys become the string "1", which t[1] cannot retrieve — you need tonumber(k) as a fallback.

Either keep lists in save files contiguous, or run every key through tonumber on read.

docs.title: Special values
Real examples in the engine
docs.text:
Global.lua save read/write (simplified) 
local json = ImportFile("Utils.dkjson")
local file_name = "global_save.json"

-- read
local contents = SE.filesystem.read(file_name)
local decoded, _, err = json.decode(contents)
if (not decoded) then
    print("Save corrupted: " .. tostring(err))
end

-- write
local encoded = json.encode(global._saveData or {})
SE.filesystem.write(file_name, encoded)

Path is relative to the save directory

SE.filesystem.read / write go through LÖVE's save directory (on mobile, the app's private directory). Just pass a relative path; do not pass an absolute path like C:\....

docs.title: SafeJson
docs.text:
local safejson = ImportFile("Utils.SafeJson")

It adds three layers of checks on the parse direction, to handle "JSON someone else gives you" (network responses, player-hand-edited saves, exported share codes).

docs.title: Parse
docs.text:
local data, err, errType = safejson.parse(jsonString, options)
  • Success: data is the parsed value, err and errType are both nil.
    • Most of the time it is a table, but when the JSON top level is directly a number / string / boolean / null, data is that scalar (null decodes to nil). So do not unconditionally #data.
  • Failure: data is nil, err is an English description, errType is the error type number.
errType Constant name Meaning 1 MALFORMED JSON syntax error (including BOM header) 2 UNSAFE_KEY A key or value hit the blacklist; debug hook detection also counts as this type 3 CIRCULAR Circular reference (currently unreachable, see below) 4 OVER_LIMIT Exceeds count/depth/length limit

errType == 3 is an unreachable branch

In SafeJson.lua, error_types.CIRCULAR = 3 is defined but never returned anywhere. The reason is parse goes through dkjson's decode (text → table), and the decode stage cannot possibly produce circular references between tables; the encode side (encode) has no safety check at all. So when writing errType checks, covering 1 / 2 / 4 is enough; 3 can never be hit.

docs.title: What the three checks are
docs.text:
Order Check Note ① check_bom Rejects files with a UTF-8 BOM header outright ② precheck_json + blacklist scan Before parsing, lowercases the entire text and searches the blacklist substrings one by one ③ check_object_safety After parsing, recursively checks every key and value

Default limits for ③:

Limit Default max_depth 100 levels max_items 12000 max_string_length 1e6 characters

To change them, override in the second parameter (internally setmetatable(options, {__index = default config}), so unspecified fields fall back automatically):

local data, err, t = safejson.parse(text, {max_items = 100, max_depth = 10})

Setting enable_precheck to false skips only step ②'s whole-string scan (step ③ still checks key names).

docs.title: What is in the blacklist
docs.text:
safejson.config.badwords is a {["word"] = true} table covering two categories:

  • Lua side: __index, getmetatable, require, os.execute, io.popen, function, coroutine …
  • Web side: __proto__, constructor, prototype, eval, fetch, XMLHttpRequest, localStorage, javascript:, onload, iframe …

These checks are designed for the case where "JSON will be fed into another parser or written into a web page".

docs.title: Encode
docs.text:
local text = safejson.encode(value)

The encode direction has no safety check

It is just a forward to safejson.json.encode(value), equivalent to dkjson's encode, and will also error. SafeJson's "safe" only applies to parse.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
The blacklist is substring matching and will falsely reject normal content

check_object_safety uses lower_v:find(word, 1, true) — plain substring search, no word boundaries. That means:

  • Key global_volume contains global → rejected
  • Key functions contains function → rejected
  • Value "The process of..." contains process → rejected
  • Value "Import complete" contains import → rejected

It does not affect your own Chinese content much, but English text easily trips it. Conclusion: always use dkjson for JSON you generate and trust yourself; only use safejson.parse when the source is untrusted.

parse lowercases \uXXXX escapes

normalize_unicode first replaces every \uXXXX in the text with the corresponding character and calls :lower(), then hands it to dkjson. So "\u0041BC" becomes "abc" — the case information is lost. Chinese generally does not use \u escapes and is unaffected; but be careful with ASCII strings containing uppercase letters.

parse fails while a debugger is attached

anti_tamper_check checks debug.gethook(). As long as a debug hook is currently set (breakpoint debugging, some profiling tools), it returns "Debug hook detected". If parse mysteriously fails during debugging, detach the debugger first and try again.

Rejects parsing when global memory exceeds 100MB

check_resource_limits uses collectgarbage("count"). If it exceeds 100MB it returns an error directly. In large projects this function may "work sometimes, fail sometimes", depending on whether GC just ran at the moment of the call.

precheck only scans the first max_string_length characters

Default 1e6, basically the whole text, but if you shrink it for performance, the part beyond it will not be scanned.

docs.title: Complete examples
docs.text:
Write a readable config file yourself

local json = ImportFile("Utils.dkjson")

local config = {
    version = 3,
    player = {name = "Frisk", lv = 1, hp = 20},
    flags = {met_sans = true, spare = false}
}

local text = json.encode(config, {
    indent = true,
    keyorder = {"version", "player", "flags"}
})

SE.filesystem.write("my_config.json", text)

Read an external JSON that may have been edited by someone

local safejson = ImportFile("Utils.SafeJson")

local text = SE.filesystem.read("download/layout.json")
if (not text) then return end

local data, err, errType = safejson.parse(text)
if (not data) then
    -- errType: 1=syntax error 2=dangerous content/debug hook 4=over limit (3 currently unreachable)
    print("Rejected load (type " .. tostring(errType) .. "): " .. tostring(err))
    return
end

print("Load succeeded, control count: " .. #(data.controls or {}))

docs.title: ShaderToy Conversion Library
docs.text:
ShaderToy has a large number of ready-made GLSL fragment shaders. This library automatically rewrites their mainImage style into a Shader that LÖVE can compile, saving you the manual porting work.

Path: Scripts/Libraries/ShaderToy/

File Responsibility init.lua Entry point: create Shader, multi-pass project, update uniforms each frame convert.lua Text rewriting (detect uniforms, wrap mainImage, replace function names) rules.lua Rewrite rule table; edit here to extend support 
local shadertoy = ImportFile("ShaderToy")

It is not a render pipeline

This library only handles "translating code into a LÖVE Shader" and "feeding uniforms each frame". Where to draw and how big is still decided by the sprite's SetShaders or your own setCanvas. For the engine's regular Shader usage, see Shaders.

docs.title: Quickest start
docs.text:
The engine has a directly runnable test scene Scripts/Scenes/TEST/scene_shader.lua. Just paste the ShaderToy code as-is into convert():

local shadertoy = ImportFile("ShaderToy")
local s = shadertoy.convert([[
void mainImage( out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord )
{
    vec2 uv = fragCoord/iResolution.xy;
    vec3 col = 0.5 + 0.5*cos(iTime+uv.xyx+vec3(0,2,4));
    fragColor = vec4(col,1.0);
}
]])

local bg = Sprites.CreateSprite("px.png", 0)
bg:Scale(640, 480)
bg:SetShaders({s.shader})

function scene.update(dt)
    s:update(dt)      -- must be called every frame, otherwise iTime does not advance
end

s.shader is the real Shader

convert() returns a wrapper object. When passing it to SetShaders / love.graphics.setShader, use its .shader field.

docs.title: What it changes for you
docs.text:
convert.lua does the following to the original code (the rules are all in rules.lua):

Original Changed to Reason texture(tex, uv) Texel(tex, uv) LÖVE's sampling function has a different name gl_FragCoord screen_coords LÖVE has no gl_FragCoord iChannelResolution[0] iChannelResolution0 GLSL ES 1.0 does not support indexing array uniforms like this precision ... float; deleted LÖVE does not need it, and keeping it actually causes an error void mainImage(...) {...} vec4 effect(...) {...} Replace with LÖVE's entry function

At the same time, it automatically inserts the uniform declarations it detects at the very top of the code, so you do not write extern yourself:

Appears in code Auto-inserted Auto-assigned each frame iTime extern number iTime; Seconds accumulated from dt iResolution extern vec3 iResolution; {CANVAS_WIDTH, CANVAS_HEIGHT, 1} iMouse extern vec4 iMouse; x, y from Keyboard.GetMousePosition() iFrame extern int iFrame; Frame count, +1 each update iChannel0 ~ iChannel3 extern Image iChannelN; See next section iChannelResolution extern vec3 iChannelResolutionN; Width/height of each channel's texture

Declarations not appearing in the code are not inserted and not assigned — so deleting unused variables saves a bit of overhead.

docs.title: How fragCoord is computed
docs.text:
The converted effect function begins like this:

vec2 fragCoord = vec2(texture_coords.x * iResolution.x,
                      iResolution.y - texture_coords.y * iResolution.y);

fragCoord comes from the drawn shape's UV, not screen coordinates

It is computed as texture_coords (sprite UV) × iResolution. Only a shape that fills the whole screen equals the screen coordinates on ShaderToy. Attach it to a 32×32 small sprite and you will see "the entire shader compressed into that 32×32 area".

There is also a line at the end, fragColor *= vec4(1.0,1.0,1.0, Texel(texture, texture_coords).a);: the result is multiplied by the sprite's alpha. px.png (1×1 white) is the easiest; if the sprite has transparent areas, the colors there get multiplied to 0.

docs.title: Channel textures
docs.text:
ShaderToy's iChannel0~3 default to noise images. This library's approach:

  • At conversion time, whenever it detects iChannelN used in the code, it generates a 256×256 random noise texture to stand in for it (rules.DEFAULT_NOISE_SIZE), so it will not fail to compile even if you do nothing.
  • To swap in your own image, use setChannel.
s:setChannel(0, myImage)      -- channel 0 uses myImage

docs.title: Audio channel
docs.text:
setAudioChannel(id, filepath) turns audio into a 512×2 texture and feeds it into the shader:

Row Content Value Row 0 (y=0) FFT spectrum RGB all written the same value v Row 1 (y=1) Waveform R channel written wave * 0.5 + 0.5 
s:setAudioChannel(0, "Resources/Music/mus_battle.ogg")

FFT is a naive O(N²) implementation

simpleFFT does a double loop over 512 samples, about 260,000 trig operations per frame, and it is recomputed every frame. On mobile this is real overhead; do not leave it on constantly on mobile.

docs.title: Methods of a single Shader
docs.text:
The object returned by convert(code) (called s below):

Method Effect s:update(dt) Call every frame. Advance iTime / iFrame / iMouse / iResolution and re-send channel textures s:apply() setShader(s.shader) s:use() Alias of apply() s:clear() setShader() to cancel s:setChannel(id, texture) Assign a texture to channel id (0-3) s:setAudioChannel(id, filepath) Connect audio to channel id and loop it s:unload() release() to free GPU resources s:printCode(mode, savePath) Print/save the converted code, a debugging godsend s:generateNoiseTexture(size) Manually generate a noise texture

Fields: s.shader (the real Shader), s.original (original text), s.code (after conversion), s.externs (inserted declarations), s.runtimeFlags (which uniforms were detected), s.time / s.frame.

When it won't convert, look at the conversion result first

s:printCode()                       -- print final GLSL
s:printCode("original")             -- print original text
s:printCode("extern")               -- print only inserted declarations
s:printCode("final", "out.glsl")    -- save to file to study slowly
The vast majority of "compile failures" can be spotted at a glance this way: whether some uniform was not detected, or whether parentheses broke the mainImage match.

docs.title: Multi-pass project
docs.text:
ShaderToy's "Buffer A / Buffer B / Image" is called a pass here. The output of the previous pass is automatically fed to the iChannel of the next pass (pass j → iChannel(j-1)).

local proj = shadertoy.newProject()

proj:addPass("bufferA", codeA)
proj:addPass("image",   codeB)

-- every frame
proj:update(dt)

-- draw (pick your own timing)
proj:draw()
Method Effect newProject() Create a new project proj:addPass(name, code) Add a pass; internally creates two canvases each for ping-pong proj:update(dt) Accumulate project time/frame count, and call update(dt) on each pass proj:draw() Render all passes in order, and draw the last result to screen proj:unload() Free all canvases and shaders

Multiple passes eat video memory

Each pass creates two full-screen canvases (CANVAS_WIDTH × CANVAS_HEIGHT). 3 passes means 6 full-screen canvases; weigh that on mobile. Remember to unload() when switching scenes.

docs.title: Pitfalls and limits
docs.text:
Only GLSL ES 1.0 is accepted

LÖVE's Shader is GLSL ES 1.0. Shaders on ShaderToy that use textureLod, textureSize, integer arithmetic, switch, in / out variables, #version 300 es will definitely fail to compile. When searching, pick older shaders tagged "Sound"/"Buffer" that are simple and have no cubemap — they have the highest success rate.

Unsupported uniforms are not auto-added

iDate, iChannelTime, iSampleRate, iKeyboard etc. are not in rules.UNIFORM_RULES. If the code references them, conversion will not insert a declaration → compile error "undefined variable". To support them, add the rule to rules.lua yourself (add the extern text + flag, then add a send block in init.lua's update).

Functions other than mainImage are kept verbatim

The conversion only does a regex replacement on the mainImage block; all other functions are copied as-is. This is usually good (helper functions work normally), but if the original has another function matching the void mainImage(...) shape (e.g. a commented-out version), it will be rewritten too, causing a duplicate definition.

Compile failure is an error, not a returned nil

convert() internally calls SE.graphics.newShader directly, so a syntax error throws. When loading someone else's shader, always wrap it in pcall, otherwise the whole scene fails to start:

local ok, s = pcall(shadertoy.convert, code)
if (not ok) then
    print("Shader compile failed: " .. tostring(s))
    return
end

iTime accumulates dt and is not affected by battle pause

Inside update(dt), self._time = self._time + dt keeps going up. If the pause menu does not call update, it stops; if it does, it keeps going. To make the animation follow the game's rhythm, pass in a processed dt yourself.

The Y axis is flipped

Screen coordinate y is positive downward; the conversion already applies a flip (see the fragCoord formula above). But if the math copied from ShaderToy itself relies on "y up", it will visually be upside down — just flip the sign in the formula.

docs.title: Shaders
docs.text:
Shaders are small GLSL programs that run on the GPU. You hand the frame to it, and per the rules you wrote, it decides pixel by pixel what color each point ends up being.

In LÖVE, most of the time you only need to write a fragment shader (the effect function) — it is like a "filter that every pixel goes through".

This page covers the engine's regular Shader usage. If you want to directly port ready-made effects from the web, see ShaderToy Conversion Library; if you want to understand the "ping-pong" drawing flow of screen shaders, see Canvas and Screen; the underlying LÖVE drawing API list is in With LÖVE → Graphics Drawing.

docs.title: The smallest possible Shader
docs.text:
The smallest runnable Shader is just this function:

vec4 effect(vec4 color, Image tex, vec2 tex_coords, vec2 screen_coords) {
    vec4 pixel = Texel(tex, tex_coords);
    return pixel * color;
}

The effect of this code is doing nothing — it takes the texture out as-is, multiplies by the draw color, and returns. Understand this one line and you understand the entire skeleton of a Shader.

docs.title: The four parameters of effect
docs.text:
Parameter Type Meaning color vec4 The current draw color, from setColor or the sprite's color / alpha tex Image The texture being drawn — usually the image itself tex_coords vec2 Texture UV, range 0~1, computed per drawn shape screen_coords vec2 Screen coordinates, unit is pixels

Its return value is the final color of this pixel (including alpha), directly deciding what you see on screen.

Sampling a texture must use Texel

In LÖVE the function to get a texture's color is Texel(tex, uv), not the standard GLSL texture(). A wrong write will fail to compile directly.

tex_coords is the shape's own UV, not screen coordinates

For an image that fills the whole screen, tex_coords happens to equal "the normalized screen coordinates". Attach it to a 32×32 small image, and tex_coords still only runs between 0~1 — the effect gets "compressed into that 32×32 area" instead of filling the screen. This is fundamentally different from ShaderToy's fragCoord (see the ShaderToy page for details).

docs.title: Want to change shape, not color?
docs.text:
Then use the vertex shader entry position, which decides where each vertex is drawn:

vec4 position(mat4 transform_projection, vec4 vertex_position) {
    return transform_projection * vertex_position;
}

The vertex entry is used far less. For everyday effects, just focus on effect.

docs.title: uniform: let Lua feed parameters in
docs.text:
The shader itself is "dead". To make it move, you rely on uniform — parameters sent in from outside each frame.

GLSL side declares with extern:

extern number time;        // in LÖVE, number is equivalent to float
extern vec2 amplitude;
extern Image mask;

Lua side assigns with send:

shader:send("time", 1.5)
shader:send("amplitude", {0.02, 0.05})
shader:send("mask", someImage)

docs.title: Type correspondence
docs.text:
GLSL declaration Value passed to send in Lua extern number x; A number extern vec2 / vec3 / vec4 v; {1, 2} / {1, 2, 3} / {1, 2, 3, 4} extern Image img; An Image / Canvas extern mat4 m; Matrix (rare) extern bool b; true / false

number is float

In LÖVE, number is an alias for float, and the engine's own shaders use both writings. Writing float is also completely fine.

Check before sending, to avoid silent failures

shader:hasUniform("time") tells you whether a uniform exists. When the name is misspelled, LÖVE may not error, yet the effect "doesn't move at all" — self-check with it first to save trouble:

if shader:hasUniform("time") then
    shader:send("time", t)
end

docs.title: Three usages, from small to large
docs.text:
Usage How to write Good for Sprite-level spr:SetShaders({shader}) Add an effect to a specific image / sprite Global screen Global.SetVariable("ScreenShaders", {shader}) Full-screen filter (to set the screen mood) Fully custom SE.graphics.setShader(shader) + your own setCanvas When you want full control of draw timing and target
  • The list of sprite-level methods (SetShaders / AddShader / InsertShader / RemoveShader / ClearShaders) is in Sprites → Common Methods. When multiple shaders are attached, the engine ping-pongs between two temporary canvases the same size as the sprite, stacking them one by one, so effects apply in list order.
  • The global-screen ScreenShaders goes through the main canvas ↔ intermediate canvas ping-pong flow, explained in Canvas and Screen.
  • The lowest-level newShader / setShader / validateShader are all wrapped under SE.graphics; the list is in Graphics Drawing.

docs.title: Write your first example quickest
docs.text: Three steps: write a .glsl file → write a test scene → set it as the startup scene.

docs.title: Step 1: create Scripts/Shaders/MyWave.glsl
docs.text:
extern number time;
extern number amplitude;

vec4 effect(vec4 color, Image tex, vec2 tex_coords, vec2 screen_coords) {
    // horizontal sine offset along the y axis: the lower you go, the more it twists
    vec2 uv = tex_coords;
    uv.x += sin(uv.y * 12.0 + time * 3.0) * amplitude;

    vec4 pixel = Texel(tex, uv);
    return pixel * color;
}

docs.title: Step 2: create test scene Scripts/Scenes/TEST/scene_my_shader.lua
docs.text:
local scene = {}

-- compile once, cache it. Never newShader every frame (that recompiles every frame)
local shader = SE.graphics.newShader("Scripts/Shaders/MyWave.glsl")

-- a white image that fills the screen, to "carry" the full-screen effect
local bg = Sprites.CreateSprite("px.png", 0)
bg:Scale(CANVAS_WIDTH, CANVAS_HEIGHT)
bg:SetShaders({shader})

local t = 0

function scene.update(dt)
    t = t + dt
    shader:send("time", t)          -- feed time every frame so the animation moves
    shader:send("amplitude", 0.02)
end

function scene.draw() end

function scene.clear()
    Layers.clear()
end

return scene

docs.title: Step 3: make it run on startup
docs.text:
In conf_pure.lua, point FirstRoom to it:

Global.SetVariable("FirstRoom", "TEST.scene_my_shader")

In the game you should see the whole screen gently swaying left and right. Change amplitude from 0.02 to 0.2, and the effect immediately grows tenfold — this is the best part of tweaking shaders: change one number and see the result instantly.

Two loading methods

  • SE.graphics.newShader("Scripts/Shaders/MyWave.glsl") — directly give the file path.
  • ImportFile("MyWave", "shader") — only give the name; the engine looks for .glsl under Scripts/Shaders/ itself, and throws a clear error with the path on compile failure, which makes debugging easier.

You can also pass the GLSL code directly as a string, skipping a file (ShaderToy Conversion Library does exactly this).

Compile failure throws, not returns nil

A Shader syntax error makes newShader throw directly. When loading a shader from an uncertain source, wrap it in pcall, otherwise the whole scene fails to start. To check syntax ahead of time separately, use SE.graphics.validateShader(code).

docs.title: The 7 shaders that ship with the engine
docs.text:
There are already 7 ready-to-use shaders in Scripts/Shaders/. The laziest starting point for practice is to take them apart and modify them.

File What it does Key uniforms ColorFilter.glsl Grayscale + tint (mix controls grayscale amount) grayscale tint_color Gradiant.glsl Four-corner color gradient, rotatable angle topLeftColor etc. four corners + angle WaveDistort.glsl Sine wave distortion, horizontal and vertical directions time amplitude frequency speed tex_size Glow.glsl Samples neighboring pixels for brightness difference, glows at edges glow_color glow_intensity threshold tex_size Dust.glsl Scanline dissolve fade-out (uses if branches and noise) dt scan_y etc. FourPoint.glsl Four-point deformation, solves UV with inverse bilinear interpolation, discard when out of bounds p1 ~ p4 PixelSmooth.glsl Uses dFdx/dFdy for pixel smoothing, fixes rotation aliasing texture_pixel_size

Suggested reading order: ColorFilter → WaveDistort → Glow → FourPoint. The first three are "change color / change UV / sample neighbors", covering 90% of daily needs; FourPoint is geometric-level, treat it as a math problem.

docs.title: How to practice further
docs.text: The Shader learning curve is "steep at the start, flat afterward": copy first, then modify, then write your own formula in the end.

docs.title: Stage 1: change constants (almost no math needed)
docs.text:
Push the existing shader's uniform to extremes and watch thephenomenon:

  • Move ColorFilter's grayscale from 0 up to 1 gradually, watch the screen turn gray.
  • Raise/lower Glow's threshold, watch the glowing area grow or shrink.
  • Pull WaveDistort's amplitude from 0 to 0.5, watch how the image gets twisted.

docs.title: Stage 2: change the formula (start touching math)
docs.text:
• Replace sin(...) with cos(...), abs(sin(...)), sqrt(...), watch how the waveform changes.
  • Change the two axes' sin frequencies in WaveDistort to different numbers, to make the difference between "water ripple" and "jitter".
  • Change uv.x += to uv.y +=, understand the symmetry of "horizontal distortion" and "vertical distortion".

docs.title: Stage 3: write small effects from scratch
docs.text:
Each does only one thing, run it on a full-screen white image:

Goal Hint Tint pixel.rgb * vec3(1.0, 0.5, 0.5) Grayscale dot(pixel.rgb, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) Invert 1.0 - pixel.rgb Brightness / contrast (pixel.rgb - 0.5) * contrast + 0.5 + brightness Scanline Use tex_coords.y with sin or step for stripes Radial vignette Use distance(tex_coords, vec2(0.5)) for bright center, dark edges Ripple Use sin(distance(uv, center) * k - time) for concentric circles

docs.title: Stage 4: combine and advance
docs.text:
• Use SetShaders to attach multiple shaders at once, and feel their sequential stacking effect.
  • Start touching neighbor sampling (like Glow sampling up/down/left/right pixels) and multi-sampling (blur, outline).
  • For big scenes, see ShaderToy Conversion Library, borrow community-ready code, then take it apart afterward.

docs.title: Recommended resources
docs.text:
• The Book of Shaders (thebookofshaders.com) — the best free tutorial for concepts, focus on the "color / shape / random / noise" chapters. Note its examples are WebGL style; when porting to LÖVE, switch to effect + Texel.
  • ShaderToy — a huge number of ready-made effects, usable directly with the engine's conversion library.
  • The 7 shaders that ship with the engine — the best "local examples", because their style is exactly the one this project maintains long-term.

docs.title: Performance and pitfalls
docs.text:
Never create a shader every frame

newShader triggers GPU compilation, which is very expensive. The correct approach is to compile once when the scene loads, cache it at the module top level, and only send uniforms each frame. send is cheap, call it freely.

Reset after drawing

SE.graphics.setShader(shader) stays in effect until the next setShader() call. Restore it immediately when done, otherwise it pollutes all subsequent drawing:

SE.graphics.setShader(shader)
-- ... your drawing ...
SE.graphics.setShader()      -- restore

Full-screen + neighbor sampling = expensive

effect runs once per pixel. A shader like Glow that samples 5 points at once is 5× the sampling on the whole screen; stack a few more passes and it grows multiplicatively. On mobile especially be restrained — this is also why the engine added caching optimization to PixelSmooth instead of setFilter every frame.

Only GLSL ES 1.0 is accepted

No switch, no #version 300 es, no dynamic array uniform indexing. When copying code from the web, confirm the version first; the concrete limits and "which writings definitely fail to compile" are listed in the pitfalls section of ShaderToy Conversion Library.

About the Y axis

Screen coordinate y is positive downward. When writing "bottom to top" math, it is normal that your first instinct is off — flip the sign in the formula, or draw a reference line first to confirm direction.

Use validateShader to catch errors early

After editing GLSL you do not have to enter the game every time to find errors: SE.graphics.validateShader(code) only does a compile check, does not actually replace the current shader, good for running once in a tool or at startup.

docs.title: Collision Library
docs.text:
The collision library handles the detection of "do two shapes overlap", without any movement or pushing.

Path: Scripts/Libraries/Collisions.lua

It is imported as the global Collisions in main.lua, so you can use it directly without your own ImportFile:

-- top of main.lua
Collisions = ImportFile("Collisions")

There is also a lowercase alias

The compat layer Scripts/Libraries/Engine/2_0.lua additionally mounts collisions (all lowercase). The two are the same table, but it is better to consistently write the uppercase Collisions — easier to find and won't collide with local variable names.

docs.title: Shape table
docs.text:
Every function in the library describes a rectangle/ellipse with the same "shape table":

{
    x = 320,    -- center x (world coordinates)
    y = 240,    -- center y (world coordinates)
    w = 32,     -- width
    h = 32,     -- height
    angle = 0   -- rotation angle, **unit is degrees**
}
  • x / y are the center, not the top-left corner.
  • angle is in degrees; the function internally calls math.rad itself. Do not pass radians.
  • w / h are edge lengths in a rectangle; in an ellipse they are the diameters of the two axes (see warning below).

docs.title: Method overview
docs.text:
All methods

Function Detection Note Collisions.FollowShape(sprite) —— Convert a sprite into a shape table Collisions.RectangleWithPoint(rect, point) rectangle × point point is {x = , y = } Collisions.CircleWithPoint(circle, point) ellipse × point see warning below, w/h used as radius Collisions.RectangleWithRectangle(rect1, rect2) rectangle × rectangle uses SAT, supports any rotation Collisions.RectangleWithCircle(rect, circle) rectangle × ellipse ellipse handled with w/2 semi-axis Collisions.CircleWithCircle(c1, c2) ellipse × ellipse two perfect circles use fast distance check

All return true / false, without any displacement.

CircleWithPoint's w/h unit is inconsistent with other functions

CircleWithPoint internally does local a, b = circ.w, circ.h then checks X²/a² + Y²/b² ≤ 1, which means it treats w/h as radius (semi-axis). Whereas CircleWithCircle and RectangleWithCircle both use w/2, treating it as diameter.

For the same {w = 16, h = 16} shape:

Function Actual coverage CircleWithPoint 32 × 32 CircleWithCircle / RectangleWithCircle 16 × 16

To work around it, pass values that are already divided by 2 to CircleWithPoint:

local c = {x = px, y = py, w = 8, h = 8, angle = 0}   -- want radius 8
Collisions.CircleWithPoint(c, {x = mx, y = my})

docs.title: Combining with sprites: FollowShape
docs.text:
Writing a shape table by hand is tedious. The real usage in the engine is to just throw a sprite in:

local shape = Collisions.FollowShape(mySprite)
-- -> {x, y, w, h, angle}

It reads these fields of the sprite:

Sprite field How it participates x / y World coordinates (no camera transform applied, consistent with the translation at draw time) width / height Original image size xscale / yscale Scale factor, w = width * xscale rotation Angle (degrees) xpivot_px / ypivot_px Pixel anchor, priority when non-zero xpivot / ypivot Ratio anchor, defaults to 0.5 (center)

Internal logic (simplified):

-- 1. offset from anchor to image center, in world units after scaling
local dx = (width * 0.5 - ox) * xscale
local dy = (height * 0.5 - oy) * yscale

-- 2. rotate this offset by the sprite's rotation angle into world direction (local -> world)
data_tab = {
    x = x + dx * cosA - dy * sinA,
    y = y + dx * sinA + dy * cosA,
    w = math.abs(w),
    h = math.abs(h),
    angle = angle
}

Scale() is a factor, not pixels

spr:Scale(2, 2) enlarges the image to 2×, w becomes width * 2. Only for a 1×1 pure-white image like px.png does Scale(155, 130) equal exactly 155×130 pixels (the battle box is drawn this way). For normal sprites don't treat Scale's arguments as pixels.

Negative scale is taken as absolute value

Both w / h go through math.abs. A sprite flipped horizontally (xscale = -1) keeps the same collision box size — which is correct, but if you use negative scale to mean "smaller", the collision box won't shrink with it.

docs.title: Real example in the engine: bullet hits Soul
docs.text:
Scripts/Libraries/Battle/Player/init.lua's Player.Update checks every bullet each frame:

for _, b in ipairs(Sprites.images) do
    if (b.isBullet) then
        local coll_b = Collisions.FollowShape(b)
        -- the Soul's own box: the sprite's geometric rectangle; if `_hitbox` is set, shrink to that size
        local coll_p = Sprites.GetHitbox(Player.sprite)

        if (Collisions.RectangleWithRectangle(coll_b, coll_p)) then
            -- rough hit. When either side enabled perfect pixel (SetPPCollision(true)),
            -- the real answer comes from the rectangulated shape; nil means neither side enabled, so use the rectangle result.
            local pp = Sprites.PPCollide(b, Player.sprite)
            if (pp == nil or pp == true) then
                Battle.OnHit(b)
                break
            end
        end
    end
end

Four things worth learning in this code:

  1. Iterate Sprites.images filtered by isBullet — this is the engine's convention field marking "I am a bullet", set on bones, cannons, homing shots when created.
  2. Sprites.GetHitbox(sprite) instead of hand-editing w/h — it shrinks the sprite's geometric rectangle to _hitbox (defaults to {4, 4}). The sprite may have a 32×32 glowing edge, but the check only uses the center 4×4, which is the key to the UNDERTALE feel (Soul hitbox far smaller than the image).
  3. FollowShape only computes x/y/angle — anchor and rotation are handled inside; size is left to GetHitbox.
  4. PPCollide is the "second gate" — only after the rectangle check hits do you do the pixel-level recheck; the order must not be reversed (reversed would send a huge number of impossible-to-hit bullets into the pixel algorithm).

docs.title: Change the Soul hitbox
docs.text:
Player.SetHitBox(width, height)           -- change main Soul
Player.SetHitBox(width, height, soulObj)  -- change a specific Soul object

Defaults to {4, 4}.

SetHitBox silently changes 0 and negative numbers to 1

The source is local w = (width > 0 and width or 1). To "disable the hitbox" passing 0 becomes 1, the hitbox still takes effect. To really disable it, you must skip the check loop yourself (e.g. temporarily set isBullet to false).

docs.title: Perfect pixel collision
docs.text:
The above is all rectangles and ellipses. If the art is a weirdly shaped figure (irregular rock, jagged edge, thin arrow), the rectangle check will visibly "slip".

The engine has built-in perfect pixel collision (Pixel-Perfect, underlying library in Scripts/Libraries/PerfectPixel/). The idea: read the sprite's real pixels, rectangulate the opaque parts into a bunch of small boxes, then compare those boxes against each other.

Toggle and query

  • sprite:SetPPCollision(enabled) toggles pixel-level collision for this sprite, returns (ok, rect_count).
    • ok whether a usable rectangulation result was formed (fails when the sprite is fully transparent).
    • enabled = false turns it off.
  • sprite:IsPPCollision() whether it is currently on.
  • Sprites.PPCollide(a, b) checks two sprites. Returns three states:
Return Meaning nil Neither side enabled — caller should keep the rectangle check's conclusion true At least one side enabled, and real pixels hit false At least one side enabled, but real pixels did not hit (false positive from rough check)
  • Sprites.GetPPRects(sprite) gets the rectangulation result in image space — a list {{x, y, w, h}, ...} (origin at sprite top-left, y down, no scaling/rotation applied), mainly for debugging.
  • Sprites.GetPPShapes(sprite) gets the result in world space — {{x, y, w, h, angle}, ...} isomorphic to Collisions.FollowShape, can be thrown directly into Collisions.RectangleWithRectangle.
  • Sprites.ClearPPCache() clears the pixel-cached sprites.

Rectangles overlap, they are not a jigsaw

The rectangulation algorithm aims for "maximum coverage area", not slicing the figure into disjoint small blocks, so adjacent rectangles overlap each other. This does not affect the check (every rectangle is inside the figure, the union is those opaque pixels), but do not use the rectangle count as an area estimate.

Why return nil instead of false

So the caller can write it as one line:

local pp = Sprites.PPCollide(bullet, player.sprite)
if (pp == nil or pp == true) then
    Battle.OnHit(bullet)
end

When pixel collision is off, pp is nil, the condition holds → keep the rectangle result; once on, pp is the real true / false → pixels decide. No need to check the toggle state outside.

Toggle the entire Soul at once

Player.SetPerfectPixel(true)    -- main Soul + all extra Souls on together
Player.SetPerfectPixel(false)   -- off together

The check loop in Battle is already wired to this chain (see the previous example), so you just flip the switch.

Enabling it makes the hitbox bigger, not smaller

The default _hitbox is 4×4 — far smaller than a 16×16 red heart. After enabling perfect pixel, the hitbox becomes the heart's real opaque pixels (area roughly 4× that of 4×4). The feel becomes noticeably "tighter". The original graze feel comes from the small hitbox, not from pixel-level checking — don't mix the two.

Debug with F7

Press F7 in battle (or call Battle.ToggleHitboxes(true)) to draw the hitbox overlay; where perfect pixel is on, it draws the real pixel outline instead of a rectangle, so you can see at a glance which side computed wrong.

Performance: pixel recheck is far more expensive than rectangle

Sprites.PPCollide is only worth calling after the rectangle rough check already hit (that's how the engine writes it). Don't use it as the first filter to iterate hundreds of bullets. Also there are two backends:

Backend Location Note C Scripts/Libraries/PerfectPixel/cpp.dll Fast, roughly 10× faster than pure Lua Pure Lua Scripts/Libraries/PerfectPixel/pure.lua Auto-falls back when the C library is unavailable, same result just slower

Source is in Scripts/Libraries/PerfectPixel/rectangulation.cpp, with init.lua uniformly picking the backend.

Both compute the "union of overlap regions", so you can only assert "what should not leak didn't leak, what should leak did leak", don't compare rectangle counts.

docs.title: Write your own collision
docs.text:
Click a sprite (mouse × rectangle)

Keyboard.GetMousePosition() returns world coordinates (already adjusted for scale and camera), in the same coordinate system as FollowShape's output, so you can compare directly:

local btn = Sprites.CreateSprite("button.png", 0)
btn:MoveTo(320, 400)

function scene.update(dt)
    local mx, my = Keyboard.GetMousePosition()
    local shape = Collisions.FollowShape(btn)
    if (Collisions.RectangleWithPoint(shape, {x = mx, y = my})) then
        btn.color = {1, 1, 0}       -- hover highlight
    else
        btn.color = {1, 1, 1}
    end
end

Custom bullet check (ellipse × rectangle)

-- a spherical bullet, compared against the Soul (rectangle hitbox)
local bullet = Sprites.CreateSprite("bullet.png", 0)
bullet.isBullet = true
bullet:MoveTo(320, 200)

local shape_b = Collisions.FollowShape(bullet)
local shape_p = Sprites.GetHitbox(Player.sprite)   -- auto-shrink to _hitbox (default 4x4)

if (Collisions.RectangleWithCircle(shape_p, shape_b)) then
    -- if you want this bullet checked by real pixels, add a recheck after the rough hit
    local pp = Sprites.PPCollide(bullet, Player.sprite)
    if (pp == nil or pp == true) then
        Battle.OnHit(bullet)
    end
end

Note Sprites.GetHitbox returns a brand-new shape table; editing it won't affect the sprite itself; but if you want to manually override the size, just edit the returned w / h (the old code's shape_p.w, shape_p.h = Player.sprite._hitbox[1], ... is now equivalent to this line).

Pure hand-written shape (no sprite needed)

Trigger zones, invisible walls, damage ranges can all skip creating a sprite:

local zone = {x = 500, y = 300, w = 120, h = 80, angle = 0}
if (Collisions.RectangleWithPoint(zone, {x = Player.sprite.x, y = Player.sprite.y})) then
    -- entered the zone
end

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Only checks, does not push

This library has no collision response. To push the player out of a box, or to slide along a wall, you must write it yourself. The battle box's push logic is in Scripts/Libraries/Battle/Arenas.lua, and it is implemented inline without calling Collisions.

Rotated rectangles must use RectangleWithRectangle

Don't use AABB-style writing like abs(dx) < w/2 and abs(dy) < h/2 to check a rotated box — after turning 45°, the result is completely wrong. RectangleWithRectangle uses SAT (Separating Axis Theorem), supporting any angle.

Overworld contact detection does not go through here

In Overworld, "walk next to an NPC and press Z to talk" / "step on a teleport point" is handled by Overworld's own FindObject / getTouchResult / getInteractResult (based on the Tiled object layer), unrelated to this library. See Overworld → Interaction and Dialogue.

Performance: with many bullets this is O(n), pixel recheck is even more expensive

Player.Update runs one FollowShape + one SAT per isBullet every frame. With bullets in the hundreds this is hundreds of trig operations per frame. On mobile keep the count down, or do your own rough filter first (compute the center distance, skip directly if beyond threshold).

Sprites.PPCollide internally does a cheap AABB rejection first (shapeHalfExtents); the expensive rectangulation comparison only runs when bounding boxes intersect. But again: rough check first, then pixels, don't use it as the first filter.

Coordinates are world coordinates, no camera

FollowShape explicitly does not go through love.graphics.transformPoint. The benefit is it is directly comparable to sprite.x/y; the cost is: if the sprite is under a scene with a Camera offset, the draw position and collision position are consistent (because the camera is applied at draw time), so don't worry about that — but if you manually applied a camera offset yourself, the two sides must be synchronized.

docs.title: Math Tutorial
docs.text:
This page doesn't cover math derivations; it only covers how to write it in SoulEngine and what it does.

Three parts: absolute value → trigonometric function A·sin(ωx + φ) → matrix transform (the rotating box's Soul).

Unit convention: angles in the engine are always in 'degrees'

The sprite rotation, Arena's angle, the shape table's angle — all are degrees. But Lua's math.sin / math.cos only take radians.

So the correct writing is always:

math.sin(math.rad(30))   -- correct
math.sin(30)             -- wrong! 30 radians ≈ 1718 degrees

Use math.deg for the reverse direction. math.atan2(dy, dx) returns radians; convert back to degrees before writing into rotation.

docs.title: Absolute value
docs.text: math.abs(x) flips negatives to positive. What it really expresses is three things.

docs.title: Distance
docs.text:
The difference dx between two coordinates may be positive or negative; "how far apart" only looks at the magnitude:

local dx = a.x - b.x
if (math.abs(dx) < 4) then
    -- already very close horizontally
end

Combined with dy it is the most common rough distance check. Note this is not a circular check (a real circle needs dx*dx + dy*dy < r*r), but as a "rough filter first" writing it is the cheapest.

docs.title: Symmetry
docs.text:
Make some effect symmetric left/right or up/down, or "the same no matter which way you move":

-- the further the Soul is from the box center, the redder (same on both sides)
local offset = math.abs(Player.sprite.x - arena.x)
Player.sprite.color = {1, 1 - offset / 200, 1 - offset / 200}

docs.title: Convergence
docs.text:
The "move a fixed step toward the target every frame" writing used everywhere in the engine (the local function smooth_value at the top of Arenas.lua, not mounted on the Arenas table):

local function smooth_value(value, target, speed)
    if (value > target) then return math.max(value - speed, target) end
    if (value < target) then return math.min(value + speed, target) end
    return value
end

There is no abs written here, but the distance itself is abs(target - value), and to know "how many frames until it arrives" you must compute it. Arenas.lua's ResizeWithTime reverses the speed this way:

local dw = math.abs(arena.target.width - arena.width)
arena.speeds.width = math.floor(dw / timew)   -- want to finish in timew frames

Common combinations

What to do Writing Clamp in a range math.max(min, math.min(v, max)) Check if close math.abs(a - b) < eps Amount of change math.abs(target - current) No error even with negative scale w = math.abs(width * xscale)

docs.title: Memorize these values first
docs.text:
Angle sin cos 0° 0 1 90° 1 0 180° 0 -1 270° -1 0 360° 0 1

sin's output always swings within [-1, 1], one full circle of 360°. cos is sin shifted forward 90° (cos(x) == sin(x + 90°)).

The screen's y axis points down

In math class y points up; on screen y points down. So +sin moves things down; to make something float up, write -A * sin(...) or use the -y direction.

docs.title: What each of the three parameters controls
docs.text:
y = A * sin(ω * x + φ)
    │      │       └─ φ (phase): where on the waveform to start
    │      └─ ω (angular speed): how fast one round trip is
    └─ A (amplitude): how big the swing is
Parameter Intuition Unit A Half-width of the swing. A = 20 means 20 pixels each side of center, 40 pixels total width pixels (or whatever unit you use) ω One circle is 360°, so period T = 360 / ω degrees / unit x φ Shifts the whole wave left/right. Two objects differing by φ differ in when they start degrees

What x is is up to you; the engine has two ready-made time sources:

Variable Meaning Note Battle.TIME_F Frame count since battle start, +1 per frame Simple, but speed follows frame rate Battle.TIME_R Seconds since battle start, +dt per frame Frame-rate independent, recommended

How long one swing, what ω to fill

Desired effect With frames TIME_F With seconds TIME_R One round trip per second (60fps) ω = 6 ω = 360 One round trip per 2 seconds ω = 3 ω = 180 Half-second round trip (fast jitter) ω = 12 ω = 720 Engine wave1 effect ω = 1 (6 seconds per trip) ——

docs.title: Scenario 1: back-and-forth patrol
docs.text:
The engine's built-in Scripts/Waves/bones/wave1.lua is written exactly like this:

p.image.x = 320 + 20 * math.sin(math.rad(Battle.TIME_F))

Broken down: center 320, A = 20, ω = 1°/frame → period 360 frames ≈ 6 seconds, φ = 0. The bone slowly sways between x = 300 and 340.

To make it sway twice as fast and a bit bigger:

p.image.x = 320 + 60 * math.sin(math.rad(Battle.TIME_F * 3))

docs.title: Scenario 2: float up and down
docs.text:
Item pickups, hint arrows, "interactable here" light points all use this:

-- float ±6 pixels in place, one trip per 2 seconds
local t = Battle.TIME_R
arrow.y = arrow_y0 - 6 * math.sin(math.rad(t * 180))

Why the minus sign

On screen larger y is lower, so -sin is "float up".

docs.title: Scenario 3: breathing scale
docs.text:
-- size breathes between 0.95× ~ 1.05×
local s = 1 + 0.05 * math.sin(math.rad(Battle.TIME_R * 180))
heart:Scale(s, s)

docs.title: Scenario 4: blink / invincibility frames
docs.text:
sin's range is [-1, 1]; to turn it into [0, 1] opacity, write 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(...):

-- alpha pulses between 0.2 ~ 1.0
Player.sprite.alpha = 0.6 + 0.4 * math.sin(math.rad(Battle.TIME_F * 12))

To do a hard "blink on and off" (not a gradient), binarize the result:

local v = math.sin(math.rad(Battle.TIME_F * 8))
Player.sprite.alpha = (v > 0) and 1 or 0.3

docs.title: Scenario 5: a row of bones in a wave (phase φ)
docs.text:
A row of 10 bones, each starting a bit later than the previous, forms a wave. The difference is all in φ:

for i = 1, 10 do
    local phi = i * 30                      -- each differs by 30°
    bone[i].y = 300 + 25 * math.sin(math.rad(Battle.TIME_F * 4 + phi))
end

φ differs by 30°, ω is 4°/frame, equivalent to "each bone moves 30/4 = 7.5 frames later than the previous".

docs.title: Scenario 6: circle / circular arrangement
docs.text:
cos controls x, sin controls y, together they are circular motion:

-- a bullet circles center (320, 320), radius 90, one lap per 3 seconds
local a = math.rad(Battle.TIME_R * 120)
bullet.x = 320 + 90 * math.cos(a)
bullet.y = 320 + 90 * math.sin(a)

To arrange N bullets in a ring (bullet ring), change φ to "each differs by 360/N degrees":

for i = 1, 12 do
    local a = math.rad(Battle.TIME_R * 120 + (i - 1) * 30)   -- 360 / 12
    local b = Attacks.New(...)
    b.x = 320 + 90 * math.cos(a)
    b.y = 320 + 90 * math.sin(a)
end

docs.title: Scenario 7: half period as easing
docs.text:
sin going from 0° to 180° is one full round trip of 0 → 1 → 0. Used as "progress", it is a natural ease-in-ease-out: slow at both ends, fast in the middle, no Tween needed.

-- t goes 0 to 1, value rises to 1 then falls back to 0
local t = progress            -- 0..1
local v = math.sin(math.rad(t * 180))

For a one-way 0 → 1 that is slow at start and slow at end, use the cos variant:

-- (1 - cos) / 2 : t=0 -> 0, t=1 -> 1, flat at both ends
local v = (1 - math.cos(math.rad(t * 180))) / 2

How to choose against Tween

Tween is good for "go from A to B, end when you arrive"; sin is good for "loop forever, need the current value anytime". Continuous motion in Waves basically all uses sin; one-time performances use Tween.

docs.title: Scenario 8: decaying shake
docs.text:
A shake should "get smaller as it goes", done by shrinking A itself:

shake_time = 30                                  -- shake for 30 frames
-- each frame:
if (shake_time > 0) then
    local amp = shake_time / 30 * 8              -- amplitude 8 -> 0
    sprite.x = base_x + amp * math.sin(math.rad(shake_time * 30))
    shake_time = shake_time - 1
else
    sprite.x = base_x
end

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Driving with frame count, speed follows frame rate

math.sin(math.rad(Battle.TIME_F * 6)) is one trip per second at 60fps, but 0.5 seconds per trip on a 120fps high-refresh screen. For frame-rate independence, uniformly use Battle.TIME_R * 360 / seconds.

Don't forget to multiply by A

math.sin(...) returns a value between ±1; writing it directly into x moves only 1 pixel. If "the animation is barely visible", check this item first.

sin's phase is added inside ω·x

To "start 0.5 seconds late", it is not sin(ω*x) + 0.5, but sin(ω*x + ω*0.5).

docs.title: Matrix transform: rotating box
docs.text: This is the hardest part of the page, but also the Soul of the battle box. Understand it and the big block of coordinate math in Arenas.lua is all the same pattern.

docs.title: What problem to solve
docs.text:
The battle box rotates: arena.rotation = 30. After rotating, "is the Player inside the box" can no longer be judged with x > left and x < right — the box edges are no longer horizontal and vertical.

The idea is not to compute the slanted edges, but to rotate the point "back" into the box's local coordinate system. In the box's own coordinate system, it is a proper, un-rotated rectangle:

      World coordinates (box rotated 30°)     Local coordinates (box not rotated)
        ／￣￣￣￣＼                    ┌────────┐
       ／    ·P    ＼        ==>        │   ·P    │
       ＼          ／                   │         │
        ＼＿＿＿＿／                    └────────┘
     All four edges are slanted        Four edges horizontal/vertical, compare directly

docs.title: Two formulas (just memorize them)
docs.text:
Let the box center be (cx, cy), rotation angle θ, cos = cos(θ), sin = sin(θ).

World → Local (use this to judge "is the point in this slanted box"):

local dx, dy = px - cx, py - cy
local lx = dx * cos + dy * sin      -- local x
local ly = dy * cos - dx * sin      -- local y
-- then treat the box as un-rotated:
local inside = (lx >= -w/2 and lx <= w/2 and ly >= -h/2 and ly <= h/2)

Local → World (use this when you know some position on the box and want to compute where it is on screen):

local wx = cx + lx * cos - ly * sin
local wy = cy + lx * sin + ly * cos

Memory trick

Local → World is the standard rotation matrix:

[ wx ]   [ cos  -sin ] [ lx ]
[ wy ] = [ sin   cos ] [ ly ]

World → Local is its inverse matrix, and the inverse of a rotation matrix = its transpose (flip the sign of sin):

[ lx ]   [  cos  sin ] [ dx ]
[ ly ] = [ -sin  cos ] [ dy ]

So the two formulas look almost the same, only the sign of sin changed. That is the entire content of "matrix transform" in this codebase.

docs.title: A computable example
docs.text:
The box is at (320, 320), width 155, rotated 30°. Where is its right edge midpoint on screen?

  • Local coordinates: (77.5, 0) (half the width, horizontal)
  • cos30 ≈ 0.866, sin30 = 0.5
wx = 320 + 77.5 * 0.866 - 0 * 0.5 = 387.1
wy = 320 + 77.5 * 0.5   + 0 * 0.866 = 358.75

The right edge midpoint ends up at (387, 359) — to the right and down, which is exactly what a 30° clockwise rotation should look like.

docs.title: Five real code spots in the engine
docs.text:
The same matrix appears five times in the engine:

① Judge if a point can stand — Arenas.lua's is_point_valid 
local dx, dy = px - a.x, py - a.y
local cos, sin = math.cos(math.rad(a.rotation)), math.sin(math.rad(a.rotation))
local lx = dx * cos + dy * sin
local ly = dy * cos - dx * sin

-- after that it's a normal rectangle comparison (shrunk in by 8 pixels, because the Soul is 16×16)
if (lx >= -w / 2 + 8 and lx <= w / 2 - 8 and ly >= -h / 2 + 8 and ly <= h / 2 - 8) then
    in_plus = true
end

Note this is a file-level local function (local function is_point_valid), not mounted on the Arenas table, and not exported globally — so you can't get it from outside, only be indirectly affected by its behavior through Arenas's public behaviors.

② Push the Player out of the minus box — compute locally then rotate back to world

In Arenas.lua it is inlined, with no separate function name, but every line is those two formulas:

-- world -> local: lx = dx·cos + dy·sin , ly = dy·cos − dx·sin
while ((p.x - arena.x) * math.cos(math.rad(arena.rotation))
     + (p.y - arena.y) * math.sin(math.rad(arena.rotation)) < -w / 2 + 8) do
    ...
end

-- after the loop, rotate back to world
p.x = arena.x + lx * cos - ly * sin
p.y = arena.y + lx * sin + ly * cos

The cos / sin in this block are recomputed every loop iteration, because arena.rotation may be changed mid-way.

③ Get a point on the box — GetCornerPos / GetCenterPos

Both methods use "compute the local offset first, then rotate to world":

-- GetCornerPos: the corner's local coords are just a (±corner_x, ±corner_y), then rotate out
res[1] = arena.x + corner_x * cos - corner_y * sin
res[2] = arena.y + corner_x * sin + corner_y * cos

GetCenterPos(side) looks a bit different (written as arena.x + length * sin / arena.y - length * cos cross form), but it is the same matrix in another form — side == "up" takes "the top edge midpoint of the rotated box": Arena:GetCenterPos("up") correctly follows rotation, and that is why.

④ Sprite to shape — Collisions.FollowShape 
-- anchor offset relative to image center (dx, dy), rotated to world by the sprite's rotation angle
x = x + dx * cosA - dy * sinA
y = y + dx * sinA + dy * cosA

The collision library uses the same matrix too, see Collision Library. The imageRectsToWorld inside the perfect-pixel collision set (Sprites.GetPPShapes) is a verbatim copy of this formula, so both check paths must describe the same box.

⑤ 3D bones too — Attacks/Bones.lua's _rotateZ 
return {
    center[1] + x * cos_a - y * sin_a,
    center[2] + x * sin_a + y * cos_a,
    point[3]
}

_rotateX / _rotateY / _rotateZ are all essentially the same 2×2 matrix, just applied to the three different axis pairs (y,z), (x,z), (x,y).

docs.title: After the Soul rotates: the probe
docs.text:
The blue Soul "flips over" (gravity points up), implemented by setting Player.sprite.rotation to 180. Then "below the feet" is no longer at the bottom of the screen, but at the local bottom.

Arenas.PlayerOnGround is written like this:

local psin, pcos = math.sin(math.rad(player.rotation)), math.cos(math.rad(player.rotation))
return side_touching(player, -psin * 10, pcos * 10)

The probe offset (-sin θ, cos θ) * 10 is the "local down" direction in world space:

Soul rotation Probe direction On screen 0 (0, 10) below feet ↓ 90 (-10, 0) left ← 180 (0, -10) top of head ↑ 270 (10, 0) right →

One matrix transform handles all four gravity directions.

PlayerOnCeiling flips BOTH x and y components' signs

Not just x reversed:

-- PlayerOnGround
return side_touching(player, -psin * 10,  pcos * 10)
-- PlayerOnCeiling
return side_touching(player,  psin * 10, -pcos * 10)

Each component flips its sign once, because that is the 180° opposite direction, not a mirror. Changing only one component gives a "side", the probe points left/right, and the judgment is naturally all wrong.

docs.title: Order of transforms
docs.text:
The correct order is always scale → rotate → translate:

  1. First take the point by local size (w/2, h/2) — scale is already baked into w/h
  2. Then multiply by the rotation matrix
  3. Last add the center coordinates cx, cy

Translating before rotating flings the box away

Writing x = (px + dx) * cos - ... is wrong. Translation must be the final step.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Wrong angle unit

The box's rotation is degrees; the matrix wants radians. Forgetting math.rad usually results in "the box spinning wildly", because 30 radians ≈ 1718 degrees.

Positive angle is clockwise on screen

Because the y axis points down. rotation = 90 is not "rotate 90° counterclockwise", it is visually 90° clockwise. Consistent with LÖVE's love.graphics.rotate.

Rotated rectangle can no longer use AABB

abs(dx) < w/2 and abs(dy) < h/2 only holds for an un-rotated box. Either go through the local coordinates above, or use Collisions.RectangleWithRectangle (internally SAT).

Arenas' speeds do not multiply by dt

arena.rotation = smooth_value(arena.rotation, arena.target.rotation, arena.speeds.rotation)

Here speeds.rotation = 15 is 15 degrees per frame, not per second. On a 120Hz machine the rotation is twice as fast. For frame-rate-independent rotation, scale speeds by dt yourself outside.

Scale only reads xscale/yscale

FollowShape's w = width * xscale only looks at the sprite's own scale field, not parents, not layer scale. For a sprite under a parent node, multiply in the parent's factor yourself.

docs.title: Working with LÖVE
docs.text:
SoulEngine is built on love, which means it's impossible to detach from love's underlying layer.

And love2d has many excellent APIs, and in some cases you must use these APIs for development — they aren't directly included in any single file of SoulEngine.

This topic covers how love2d's native APIs work together with SoulEngine.

docs.title: What is SE
docs.text:
The first thing loaded when main.lua starts up is it:

SE = ImportFile("Engine.FuncProtector")

FuncProtector returns a table, categorized by LÖVE's module names, where every function is a direct forward to the corresponding love.xxx:

SE.graphics.newCanvas(640, 480)            -- equivalent to love.graphics.newCanvas(640, 480)
SE.audio.newSource("a.wav", "static")      -- equivalent to love.audio.newSource("a.wav", "static")
SE.filesystem.read("config.json")          -- equivalent to love.filesystem.read("config.json")

So you don't need to learn a new API: just replace love. with SE.. Parameters, return values, and error behavior are all identical — the explanations on the LOVE2D wiki can be copied as-is.

Rewrite Rule

love.graphics.rectangle("fill", 0, 0, 10, 10)
SE.graphics.rectangle("fill", 0, 0, 10, 10)

Only change the module name at the start; nothing after it needs to move.

docs.title: Why This Extra Layer
docs.text:
Open Scripts/Libraries/Engine/FuncProtector.lua, and every function body looks like this:

newCanvas = function(...)
    -- TODO: Implement adaptation logic
    return love.graphics.newCanvas(...)
end,

That TODO (implement adaptation logic) is for later: certain behaviors differ across LÖVE versions and platforms, and when they actually need handling, only this layer needs to change — neither the engine internals nor your game code need to move.

Currently all functions are pure pass-throughs with no extra behavior, so you can safely treat it as love.

docs.title: What It Wraps
docs.text:
20 categories in total, 316 functions:

Table under SE Corresponding LÖVE module Function count SE.graphics love.graphics 101 SE.window love.window 36 SE.filesystem love.filesystem 31 SE.audio love.audio 26 SE.physics love.physics 22 SE.mouse love.mouse 18 SE.math love.math 16 SE.data love.data 10 SE.keyboard love.keyboard 9 SE.system love.system 8 SE.event love.event 6 SE.timer love.timer 6 SE.joystick love.joystick 6 SE.font love.font 5 SE._top LÖVE's own top-level functions 4 SE.thread love.thread 3 SE.touch love.touch 3 SE.image love.image 3 SE.sound love.sound 2 SE.video love.video 1

SE._top is special — it holds the top-level functions of the love table itself (functions not inside any submodule):

SE._top.getVersion()                      -- equivalent to love.getVersion()
SE._top.isVersionCompatible("11.4")

What's Not Wrapped

Event callbacks (keypressed, update, draw, etc.) aren't here — the engine forwards events to the scene; see Scenes for how to write them. LÖVE's object methods (source:play(), canvas:renderTo()) aren't here either; they travel with the object.

docs.title: Functions the Engine Added Itself
docs.text:
At the end of FuncProtector.lua there are two blocks that aren't pass-throughs but utilities written by the engine, available right now:

Tool Functions SE.tools

  • SE.tools.hexColor(hexcode) → {r, g, b}
    • Converts a hex color string into the three 0 ~ 1 numbers that setColor accepts. Supports both #RGB and #RRGGBB forms; the # is optional.
    • Returns nil (without error) when the input isn't a string or the length is wrong, so it's safe to use for parsing colors given by players/config files.

Drawing Shortcuts SE.draw_

  • SE.draw_.colorText(r, g, b, a, ...) → nothing
    • First setColor, then calls print with the remaining arguments, finally automatically restoring the color to white. Parameters are exactly the same as love.graphics.print.
    • This saves the step of "must restore color after drawing" — forgetting to restore will bleed onto everything drawn afterward; see the pitfalls in Image Drawing.
SE.draw_.colorText(1, 0, 0, 1, "Hello", 100, 200)

local c = SE.tools.hexColor("#C14949")
SE.graphics.setColor(c[1], c[2], c[3], 1)

conf_pure.lua sets the main color with these two lines (commented out by default; uncomment to change the main color):

Global.SetVariable("MainColor", SE.tools.hexColor("#C14949"))

docs.title: When Not to Use SE
docs.text:
SE is the low-level fallback, not the first choice. Prefer the engine's own wrapped versions, because they additionally handle Game area override, caching, volume following, and the like:

What you want to do First choice Instead of Load a sprite Sprites.New SE.graphics.newImage Load a font Fonts.New SE.graphics.newFont Play audio Audio.PlaySound / Audio.PlayMusic SE.audio.newSource

Conversely, for things the engine doesn't wrap (building a Canvas, writing a Shader, drawing shapes directly, reading/writing files…) just use SE with confidence. The engine internals do the same: Sprites.lua loads sprites at its lowest level with SE.graphics.newImage, it just wraps caching, Game area priority, and pixel snapping on top.

docs.title: Contents of This Topic
docs.text:
• Image Drawing — the relationship between SE.graphics and love.graphics, a full rundown of all 101 functions
  • Audio System — the division of labor between SE.audio and the engine's Audio library

Tip

Everything in this topic can also be found on the LOVE2D wiki, but here we only cover a few of the most commonly used ones.

docs.title: Graphics Drawing
docs.text:
The engine did not build its own drawing API; the principle of this section is just one sentence:

Start with SE.graphics, and the rest is exactly the same as love.graphics.

SE.graphics.setColor(1, 0, 0, 1)
SE.graphics.rectangle("fill", 100, 100, 40, 40)

The only reason to write SE.graphics instead of love.graphics is cross-platform adaptation (see this topic's home page); functionally there is no difference — the love.graphics.* docs on the wiki can be used directly.

Before drawing to the screen, first think about whether it should use MAIN_CANVAS

The engine's entire game picture is drawn on a canvas called MAIN_CANVAS (size = CANVAS_WIDTH x CANVAS_HEIGHT), then uniformly scaled and centered onto the window by the engine. So don't draw directly to the window yourself inside love.draw — window coordinates and in-game coordinates are different coordinate systems, and the window size also changes with the player's screen. Drawing inside a scene works normally with regular calls; the engine has already set up the canvas, scale, and offset before you enter the scene. Details in Screen and Canvas.

docs.title: Function overview
docs.text: Grouped by purpose below, listing all 101 SE.graphics functions in FuncProtector. The behavior, parameters, and return values of all functions are exactly the same as the same-named love.graphics functions; only a one-line description is given here, go to the wiki for details.

docs.title: Creation and loading
docs.text: Function Effect newImage Build a texture from a file or ImageData (in the engine, Sprites.New is preferred) newFont Build a font (in the engine, Fonts.New is preferred) newImageFont Build a font from a character-sheet image newText Build a text object whose content can be changed anytime later (underlying call is love.graphics.newTextBatch) newCanvas Build an off-screen canvas, i.e. a render target newQuad Crop a rectangular region from a texture newShader Compile a shader (can take GLSL source directly, or a file path) newMesh Build a vertex mesh newSpriteBatch Build a sprite batch, used when the same texture is drawn many times newParticleSystem Build a particle system newVideo Build a video object newArrayImage Build an array texture (multiple layers, use drawLayer to specify a layer) newVolumeImage Build a 3D texture newCubeImage Build a cube texture getDefaultFilter Read the default sampling filter for newly created textures setDefaultFilter Set the default sampling filter for newly created textures ("nearest" nearest / "linear" linear)

docs.title: Canvas and presentation
docs.text: Function Effect setCanvas Send subsequent drawing output to the specified canvas; no argument = output to screen getCanvas Read the current canvas present Present this frame (the engine calls it automatically after love.draw, don't call it yourself) isActive Whether currently in a drawable state discard Discard canvas / depth / stencil contents, for performance optimization

docs.title: Color and clearing
docs.text: Function Effect setColor Set the current draw color; all subsequent drawing is multiplied by it getColor Read the current color setBackgroundColor Set the background color, used when the window is cleared getBackgroundColor Read the background color setColorMask Mask writing of certain color channels getColorMask Read the current channel mask state clear Clear the current canvas with the current color (or a specified color) reset Restore all draw states to default

docs.title: Font and text
docs.text:
Function Effect setFont Set the current font getFont Read the current font setNewFont Two-in-one newFont + setFont print Draw a line of text (left-aligned, can rotate and scale) printf Auto-wrap within a given width, alignable by "left" / "center" / "right" / "justify"

Don't use print for formal text

Dialogue, menus, shop text all go through the engine's Typewriter, which has built-in wrapping, per-character typing, bubble width, and hanging asterisk indentation. print / printf are generally only for debug info and text with minimal alignment requirements.

docs.title: Blend, line style, points and shaders
docs.text: Function Effect setBlendMode Set blend mode ("alpha" default, "add" additive, "multiply" multiply …) getBlendMode Read the blend mode setLineWidth Line width getLineWidth Read the line width setLineStyle Line style ("smooth" default / "rough" hard edge, use the latter for pixel art) getLineStyle Read the line style setLineJoin Style at polyline joints getLineJoin Read the polyline joint style setPointSize Diameter of points drawn by points getPointSize Read the point diameter setWireframe Wireframe mode, for debug meshes isWireframe Whether in wireframe mode setShader Set the current shader; setShader() with no argument = release getShader Read the current shader validateShader Only compile-checks syntax, does not actually replace, used to catch shader errors early

docs.title: Shape drawing
docs.text: Function Effect draw Draw a texture / canvas / mesh / text object (in the engine, usually Sprites' spr:Draw()) drawLayer Draw only one layer of a sprite batch / mesh drawInstanced Instanced draw many times with the same vertex data flushBatch Immediately submit the current batch points Draw a set of points line Draw a polyline (vertex coordinates passed flat) rectangle Draw a rectangle ("fill" filled / "line" outlined, can take a corner radius) circle Draw a circle or arc sector ellipse Draw an ellipse arc Draw an arc polygon Draw a polygon

docs.title: Transform and stack
docs.text:
Function Effect push Save the current draw state ("transform" saves only transform / "all" saves everything) pop Restore the last saved state rotate Rotate the current coordinate system, argument is in radians translate Translate the current coordinate system scale Scale the current coordinate system shear Shear the current coordinate system origin Reset the transform back to origin applyTransform Stack a Transform object on top of the current transform replaceTransform Replace the current transform with a Transform object transformPoint World coordinates → local coordinates inverseTransformPoint Local coordinates → world coordinates getStackDepth How many layers currently pushed

Transforms are cumulative, and only affect subsequent drawing

A transform is not "setting a property on some object", it changes the current coordinate system. So the idiomatic writing is always push … draw … pop. Forgetting pop makes all subsequent drawing skew, and it is hard to debug.

docs.title: Clipping and stencil
docs.text: Function Effect setScissor Set a rectangular clip region; drawing outside the box is not shown intersectScissor Set a clip region, intersected with the current clip region getScissor Read the current clip region stencil Use a drawing result as a stencil; subsequent drawing only takes effect inside (or outside) the stencil range setStencilState Set the stencil comparison rule setStencilTest Toggle the stencil test getStencilTest Read the stencil test state

docs.title: 3D, depth and face culling
docs.text:
Function Effect setDepthMode Set depth test and writing getDepthMode Read the depth mode setMeshCullMode Set back-face culling getMeshCullMode Read the back-face culling setFrontFaceWinding Set which face counts as front getFrontFaceWinding Read the front-face determination

This group is only needed when doing 3D or custom meshes; 2D games basically don't touch it.

docs.title: Info and stats
docs.text: Function Effect getWidth / getHeight Width / height of the current render target (returns canvas size in canvas mode) getDimensions Get width and height at once getPixelWidth / getPixelHeight Actual pixel size (considering DPI) getPixelDimensions Get actual pixel width and height at once getDPIScale Current DPI scale getRendererInfo Renderer, GPU name, driver version getSupported Which features the current device supports (compression formats, stencil, GLSL version, etc.) getSystemLimits Hard upper limits (max texture size, texture unit count, etc.) getTextureTypes Supported texture types getStats Draw stats: drawcall count, texture switch count, VRAM usage … isGammaCorrect Whether sRGB correction is currently on captureScreenshot Save the current frame to a file getCanvasFormats Supported canvas pixel formats getImageFormats Supported texture pixel formats

docs.title: A complete drawing example
docs.text:
function MyScene:draw()
    SE.graphics.push()

    -- red filled circle
    SE.graphics.setColor(1, 0, 0, 1)
    SE.graphics.circle("fill", 320, 240, 40)

    -- white outline (change back to white before outlining)
    SE.graphics.setColor(1, 1, 1, 1)
    SE.graphics.setLineWidth(2)
    SE.graphics.circle("line", 320, 240, 40)

    -- centered text
    SE.graphics.printf("Hello LOVE", 0, 300, 640, "center")

    SE.graphics.pop()
end

push and pop are safer than manual restore

Color, font, line width, transform are all global state. push once, draw, pop once, and nothing changed in between leaks outside.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
Forgetting to restore color is the most common drawing bug

setColor is global state, retained until the next change. The classic crash is "drew a red text, forgot to change back to white", and after that all textures turn red. In the engine several draw functions end with a dedicated line setColor(1, 1, 1, 1) precisely to prevent this color bleed — do the same yourself: restore after drawing, or just use push / pop.

rotate takes radians, not degrees

SE.graphics.rotate(math.pi / 2) is 90°. But everywhere else in the engine (Soul facing, bone rotation, matrix math, etc.) uses degrees; don't mix the two units — remember math.rad(degrees) before passing in.

After setCanvas, the coordinate system and size both change

After setCanvas(c), getWidth() / getHeight() return the canvas size, and clear() also clears the canvas. Don't forget to switch back with setCanvas() (no argument).

captureScreenshot is asynchronous

It does not return an image immediately; it waits for LÖVE to finish a draw cycle and read the frame back, and gives you the result via a callback.
